metadata.caseLaw: In the matter of Joe G. Rivera, SC-31410218, at ┬╢12 (finding that as long as ΓÇ£direct contributions to and expenditures by the committee are properly disclosed by the committee, they need not be reported by the candidateΓÇ¥ because ΓÇ£such double-reporting for ΓÇÿalter-egoΓÇÖ committees would be redundant and burdensome on the candidate or office- holder and therefore unnecessary.ΓÇ¥). The CommissionΓÇÖs decision in Rivera demonstrates that the Commission will ignore the legal distinction between a political committee and a candidate when the committee is operated as the ΓÇ£alter egoΓÇ¥ of the candidate. The CommissionΓÇÖs use of the term ΓÇ£alter egoΓÇ¥ was a reference to the ΓÇ£alter-ego doctrine,ΓÇ¥ one of the common law stan- dards for piercing a corporate veil, which applies when ΓÇ£there is such unity between corporation and individual that the separateness of the corporation has ceased and holding only the corporation liable would result in injustice.ΓÇ¥ Castleberry v. Branscum, 721 S.W.2d 270, 272 (Tex. 1986) (superseded by statute on other grounds); see also SSP Partners v. Gladstrong Invs. Corp., 275 S.W.3d 444, 454 (Tex. 2008). The rationale is that if the shareholders of a corporation disregard the separation of the corporate enterprise, the law will also disregard it to avoid an unjust result or thwart an illegal purpose. Id. Miller v. Ziegler, 109 F.4 th 1045 (8 th Cir. 2024) This case is not controlling in Texas, but it worth noting that MissouriΓÇÖs two-year lobbying ban for prior legislators was held unconstitutional based on the state failing to show how less restrictive alternatives were insufficient on their own to rein in the specter of corruption.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: C/OH EXPENDITURES FOR OWN CAMPAIGN DO NOT TRIGGER 2 YEAR WAITING PERIOD. An officeholder who is not running for re-election may use campaign contributions for expenditure related to the maintenance of his campaign account (bank fees, storage of campaign assets, maintenance of campaign email accounts). These are not ΓÇ£direct campaign expen- dituresΓÇ¥ and do not trigger the 2 year waiting period under ┬º253.007. EAO 596. APPLICATION 	TO 	ALL 	(NON-FEDERAL) CANDIDATES AND OFFICES, NO ABILITY TO CURE, AND NO GIVING TO PACs. The prohibi- tions in 253.007 apply to all candidates and officeholders of non-federal Texas offices (including local C/OHΓÇÖs), not just legislative or state executive branch offices. Once the statute has been triggered, it cannot be cured by a refund or reimbursement, and the statute cannot be eschewed by giving to a PAC, no matter how the PAC ultimately disposes of the contribution. However, a person would not violate 253.007 simply by registering ΓÇ£ just to be safeΓÇ¥. The prohibition is on the acts that would require registration, not the act of registering itself. EAO 592. See also EAO 575 (2002), EAO 587 (2023). CANNOT CURE PAST VIOLATION OR LOBBY SOONER THAN 2 YEARS BY REIMBURSING CAMPAIGN WITH PERSONAL FUNDS. A for- mer legislator retires at the end of session and during the interim makes political contributions to legisla- tive candidates from their campaign account. Then they reimburse their campaign account with personal funds and want to begin lobbying. The plain language of Section 253.007 does not permit a person to cure a past violation or reduce the two-year waiting period by reimbursing the personΓÇÖs campaign with personal funds. Section 253.007 similarly prohibits a former member of the Legislature from crossing the lobby registration threshold if the former member has used political contri- butions he or she accepted as a C/OH to make political contributions to others within the past two years. EAO 587. But also see EAO 585 (2023) re: use of a GPAC to section off contributions, start lobbying, and wait two years for contributions. FORMER LEGISLATOR LOBBYIST MAY USE GPAC 	FOR 	POLITICAL 	CONTRIBUTIONS UNDER CERTAIN CIRCUMSTANCES. A former legislator who has registered to lobby contributed money from his political funds to a GPAC and wants to use those funds for political contributions. Although 253.007 imposes a two-year moratorium on registering to lobby from the date of the last political contribution they gave to a C/OH, the argument follows that under a plain and ordinary reading of HB 2677 (2019), a person can leave office and contribute money to a GPAC, do nothing with the GPAC for two years, make no political contributions or lobby expenditures during the same time period, and then register as a lobbyist. At which time, political expenditures from COH and SPAC accounts would still be prohibited, but the making of the same from GPAC accounts would be permissible under Section 253.006(3) of the Election Code and Section 305.029(b) of the Government Code, which effectively restates Section 253.006 in the Government Code. EAO 585. See also EAO 575 (2022) SPAC 	ACTIVITY 	MAY 	TRIGGER 	LOBBY REGISTRATION BAN. Contributions accepted by a political committee controlled by a candidate or office- holder are accepted ΓÇ£as a candidate or officeholder.ΓÇ¥ Tex. Elec. Code ┬º 253.007(b). Furthermore, expenditures made by a political committee controlled by a candidate or officeholder are knowingly made or authorized by the candidate or officeholder. If the candidate or officeholder has the authority to control the contributions accepted and expenditures made by a specific-purpose commit- tee, those transactions will trigger the prohibitions in 253.007. EAO 575 (2022). Subchapter B. Candidates, Officeholders, and Political Committees

sections.title: CONTRIBUTION AND EXPENDITURE WITHOUT CAMPAIGN
sections.content: TREASURER PROHIBITED (a) 	A candidate may not knowingly accept a campaign contribution or make or authorize a campaign expenditure at a time when a campaign treasurer appointment for the candidate is not in effect. (b) 	A political committee may not knowingly accept political contributions totaling more than $500 $1,110 or make or authorize political expenditures totaling more than $500 $1,110 at a time when a campaign treasurer appointment for the committee is not in effect (see TEC Rule ┬º18.31). (c) 	A political committee may not knowingly make or authorize a campaign contribution or campaign expenditure supporting or opposing a candidate for an office specified by Section 252.005(1) in a primary or general election unless the committeeΓÇÖs campaign treasurer appointment has been filed not later than the 30 th day before the appropriate election day. (d) 	This section does not apply to a political partyΓÇÖs county executive committee that accepts political contributions or makes political expenditures, except that: (1) 	a county executive committee that accepts political contributions or makes political expenditures shall maintain the records required by Section 254.001; and (2) 	a county executive committee that accepts political contributions or makes political expenditures that, in the aggregate, exceed $25,000 $41,460 in a calendar year shall file (see TEC Rule ┬º18.31): (A) a campaign treasurer appointment as required by Section 252.001 not later than the 15th day after the date that amount is exceeded; and (B) the reports required by Subchapter F, Chapter 254, including in the political committeeΓÇÖs first report all political contributions accepted and all political expenditures made before the effective date of the campaign treasurer appointment. (e) 	This section does not apply to an out-of-state political committee unless the committee is subject to Chapter 252 under Section 251.005. (f) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 1991, 72nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.04, eff. Jan. 1, 1992; Acts 1993, 73rd Leg., ch. 531, Sec. 2, eff. Sept. 1, 1993. Amended by Acts 2005, 79th Leg., Ch. 1079 (H.B. 1647), Sec. 1, eff. June 18, 2005. cross -refereNce Federal Candidates and Officeholders, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 22.11 Termination of Campaign Treasurer Appointment, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.207 Thresholds for Campaign Treasurer Appointment, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.301 Appointment of Campaign Treasurer, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.303 Thresholds for Appointment of Campaign Treasurer by a General-Purpose Committee, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.401 Record of Contributions and Expenditures and Contents of Report, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.525 Certain Campaign Treasurer Appointments Required before Political Activity Begins, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 22.1 P ractice Notes In Catholic Leadership Coalition of Texas v. Reisman, 764 F. 3d 409 (5th Cir. 2014), the Fifth Circuit struck down parts of the Election Code that have since been repealed from statute. In the same case, the Fifth Circuit declined to strike down provisions at issue in ┬º253.031, Election Code, which require a campaign treasurer appointment prior to mak- ing $500 in expenditures or accepting more than $500 in contributions. The court reasoned that the appointment requirement is nothing more than a registration requirement for political committees and that free speech rights are not abridged in requiring registration with the Commission.

metadata.ethicsOpinions: TREASURER APPOINTMENT MUST REMAIN ACTIVE WHILE MAKING EXPENDITURE. An expenditure made by a person to obtain a refund of money previously paid by the person to a service provider in connection with the personΓÇÖs campaign is a campaign expenditure. 	The person must therefore maintain an active campaign treasurer appointment when the expen- diture is made. 	A person is not required to maintain an active campaign treasurer appointment to receive a refund of personal funds used to make a campaign expenditure. EAO 493. DUES PAYMENTS TO CLUB TO SUPPORT A GPAC 	ARE 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	SUBJECT 	TO $500 	THRESHOLD 	UNLESS 	EARMARKED FOR PURPOSES NOT REGULATED BY TITLE 15. Membership dues paid to a club which qualifies as a political committee due to its involvement in political campaigns and advertising are ΓÇ£political contributionsΓÇ¥ that count toward the $500 contribution threshold for purposes of Election Code section 253.031(b), unless spe- cifically earmarked for purposes not governed by Title 15 of the Election Code. Contributions earmarked to cover the general administrative costs of a political committee are still political contributions. EAO 394. See also EAO 161, EAO 132, EAO 131, EAO 344. PRECINCT 	CHAIR 	OF 	A 	PARTY 	WISHING TO SOLICIT CONTRIBUTIONS MUST FILE TREASURER APPT FOR GPAC. A precinct chair of a political party wishing to solicit political contributions to be used on campaign activities for his partyΓÇÖs candi- dates must file an appointment of campaign treasurer of a general-purpose committee before exceeding $500 in political contributions or political expenditures, because the precinct chair would necessarily be working in con- cert with contributors to accept political contributions and make political expenditures. The treasurer of the committee would be required to follow the recordkeep- ing and reporting requirements of chapter 254 of the Election Code. EAO 320. JUDICIAL 	CANDIDATE 	FOR 	NEWLY CREATED 	DISTRICT 	COURT 	MAY ACCEPT 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	AND 	MAKE EXPENDITURES. Under the federal Voting Rights Act, any new judicial district must be pre-cleared by the United States Department of Justice. At this time, the matter of the new courtΓÇÖs pre-clearance is still pending with that office. A judicial candidate for a newly created district court may accept political contributions and make political expenditures despite the fact that the new district has yet to be approved, provided that the candi- date has filed a campaign treasurer appointment and a Judicial Declaration of Intent form with the proper filing authority for the newly created district court. EAO 288. FUNDS 	COLLECTED 	BY 	LEGISLATORSΓÇÖ SPECIFIC-PURPOSE 	COMMITTEE 	ARE OFFICEHOLDER CONTRIBUTIONS. Because the lawsuit is being pursued by legislators in their status as officeholders, funds collected to promote the lawsuit are to defray expenses incurred by officeholders engaging in an activity in connection with their office and are there- fore officeholder contributions. If the committee collects more than $500 in political contributions or spends more than $500 on political expenditures, it must file an appointment of campaign treasurer as well as periodic reports of political contributions and expenditures. EAO 270. PAC 	PROHIBITED 	FROM 	EXPENDITURES OVER $500 UNLESS CAMPAIGN TREASURER APPOINTMENT FILED 30 OR MORE DAYS PRIOR TO RELEVANT ELECTION. A political committee may not knowingly make or authorize a campaign contribution or campaign expenditure that in the aggregate exceeds $500 supporting or opposing a candidate for a statewide office, the state legislature, the State Board of Education, or a multi-county district office in a primary or general election unless the com- mitteeΓÇÖs campaign treasurer appointment has been filed not later than the 30 th day before the appropriate election day. A general-purpose committee may not knowingly make or authorize political expenditures totaling more than $500 unless the committee has (1) filed its campaign treasurer appointment not later than the 60 th day before the date the expenditure is made that causes the total expenditures to exceed $500, and (2) accepted political contributions from at least 10 persons. EAO 161.

sections.title: LIMITATION ON CONTRIBUTION BY OUT-OF-STATE COMMITTEE
sections.content: (a) 	In a reporting period, a candidate, officeholder, or political committee may not knowingly accept political contributions totaling more than $500 $1,140 from an out-of-state political committee unless, before accepting a contribution that would cause the total to exceed $500 $1,140, the candidate, officeholder, or political committee, as applicable, receives from the out-of-state committee (see TEC Rule ┬º18.31): (1) 	a written statement, certified by an officer of the out-of-state committee, listing the full name and address of each person who contributed more than $100 $230 to the out-of-state committee during the 12 months immediately preceding the date of the contribution (see TEC Rule ┬º18.31); or (2) 	a copy of the out-of-state committeeΓÇÖs statement of organization filed as required by law with the Federal Election Commission and certified by an officer of the out-of-state committee. (b) 	This section does not apply to a contribution from an out-of-state political committee if the committee appointed a campaign treasurer under Chapter 252 before the contribution was made and is subject to the reporting requirements of Chapter 254. (c) 	A person who violates Subsection (a) commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. (d) 	A candidate, officeholder, or political committee shall include the statement or copy required by Subsection (a) as a part of the report filed under Chapter 254 that covers the reporting period to which Subsection (a) applies. (e) 	A candidate, officeholder, or political committee that accepts political contributions totaling $500 $1,140 or less from an out-of-state political committee shall include as part of the report filed under Chapter 254 that covers the reporting period in which the contribution is accepted (see TEC Rule ┬º18.31): (1) 	the same information for the out-of-state political committee required for general-purpose com- mittees by Sections 252.002 and 252.003; or (2) 	a copy of the out-of-state committeeΓÇÖs statement of organization filed as required by law with the Federal Election Commission and certified by an officer of the out-of-state committee. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 1995, 74th Leg., ch. 996, Sec. 7, eff. Sept. 1, 1995. cross -refereNce Information about Out-of-State Committees, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.29 Contribution from Out-of-State Committee, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 22.7

metadata.ethicsOpinions: TX 	CANDIDATE 	MAY 	ACCEPT 	IN-KIND CONTRIBUTION FROM OUT-OF-STATE PAC IF CERTAIN REQUIREMENTS MET. Title 15 of the Election Code does not prohibit a candidate from accept- ing an in-kind political contribution from an out-of-state political committee if the contribution is made from a permissible source and the candidate properly complies with applicable disclosure requirements. Before accept- ing political contributions totaling more than $500 in a reporting period, including the value of any in-kind contributions, from an out-of-state political committee, a candidate must receive certain information from the out- of-state political committee, found at ┬º253.032, Election Code. EAO 519. RECIPIENTS OF OUT OF STATE POLITICAL COMMITTEE 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	IN 	EXCESS OF $500. A Texas candidate, officeholder, or political committee must obtain a new certified copy of the out- of-state political committeeΓÇÖs statement of organization filed with the Federal Election Commission for each reporting period in which the Texas candidate, office- holder, or political committee receives more than $500 in contributions from the out-of-state committee. EAO 166. Superseded by TEC rule ┬º22.7(d) USING 	CORPORATE 	FUNDS 	TO 	PAY 	FOR POSTCARDS 	ADVOCATING 	FOR 	SPECIFIC CANDIDATES IS IMPERMISSIBLE. Paying for postcards advocating the election of identified candi- dates is a political expenditure. Therefore, a corporation may not make such payments. Such postcards would be ΓÇ£political advertisingΓÇ¥ and the name of an individual or group that entered into an agreement to have the cards printed would have to appear on the postcards as part of the disclosure statement. EAO 77. See also EAO 37, EAO 74. Modified by Acts 1993, 73rd Leg., ch. 531, ┬º 2 (amending Elec. Code ┬º 253.032(b)) Modified by Acts 2005, 79th Leg., ch. 1081, ┬º 1 (adding Elec. Code ┬º 254.1541)

sections.title: CASH CONTRIBUTIONS EXCEEDING $100 PROHIBITED
sections.content: (a) 	A candidate, officeholder, or specific-purpose committee may not knowingly accept from a contribu- tor in a reporting period political contributions in cash that in the aggregate exceed $100. (b) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. cross -refereNce Cash Contributions Exceeding $100 Prohibited, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 22.9

sections.title: RESTRICTIONS ON CONTRIBUTIONS DURING AND FOLLOWING
sections.content: REGULAR LEGISLATIVE SESSION (a) 	During the period beginning on the 30 th day before the date a regular legislative session convenes and continuing through the 20 th day after the date of final adjournment, a person may not knowingly make a political contribution to: (1) 	a statewide officeholder; (2) 	a member of the legislature; or (3) 	a specific-purpose committee for supporting, opposing, or assisting a statewide officeholder or member of the legislature. (b) 	A statewide officeholder, a member of the legislature, or a specific-purpose committee for supporting, opposing, or assisting a statewide officeholder or member of the legislature may not knowingly accept a political contribution, and shall refuse a political contribution that is received, during the period prescribed by Subsection (a). A political contribution that is received and refused during that period shall be returned to the contributor not later than the 30 th day after the date of receipt. A contribution made by United States mail or by common or contract carrier is not considered received during that period if it was properly addressed and placed with postage or carrier charges prepaid or prearranged in the mail or delivered to the contract carrier before the beginning of the period. The date indicated by the post office cancellation mark or the common or contract carrier documents is considered to be the date the contribution was placed in the mail or delivered to the common or contract carrier unless proven otherwise. (c) 	This section does not apply to a political contribution that was made and accepted with the intent that it be used: (1) 	in an election held or ordered during the period prescribed by Subsection (a) in which the person accepting the contribution is a candidate if the contribution was made after the person appointed a campaign treasurer with the appropriate authority and before the person was sworn in for that office; (2) 	to defray expenses incurred in connection with an election contest; or (3) 	by a person who holds a state office or a member of the legislature if the person or member was defeated at the general election held immediately before the session is convened or by a specif- ic-purpose political committee that supports or assists only that person or member. (d) 	This section does not apply to a political contribution made to or accepted by a holder of an office to which Subchapter F applies. (e) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 1991, 72nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.05, eff. Jan. 1, 1992; Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 1134, Sec. 4, eff. Sept. 1, 1997; Acts 2003, 78th Leg., ch. 249, Sec. 2.05, 2.06, eff. Sept. 1, 2003. Amended by Acts 2009, 81st Leg., R.S., Ch. 426 (H.B. 2065), Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2009. cross -refereNce Prohibition on Contributions during Regular Session, 1 Tex. Admin. metadata.ethicsOpinions: USE OF LLC OFFICE SPACE BY HOUSE MEMBER THROUGH SESSION . A member of the legislature may accept the use of office space contributed by an LLC, provided the contributing LLC is not engaged in a business specified by 253.093 and the contributing LLC is not owned in whole or in part by a corporation. As long as a person subject to Section 253.034 of the Election Code accepts and receives a political contribution in the form of office space before the beginning of the legis- lative moratorium, the person may continue to use the office space during the period covered by the morato- rium. EAO 618 (2025). See also, EAO 495 (2010), EAO 383 (1997), EAO 239 (1994). OFFICEHOLDER ACCEPTANCE OF TRANSPO- RTATION 	& 	LODGING 	AT 	CONFERENCE DURING MORATORIUM. A legislator who accepts transportation, lodging and meals at a conference which they actively participate in are not accepting an honorarium and do not violate the moratorium since 36.07(b-1), Penal Code states that the acceptance of these are not political contributions. EAO 553. See also EAO 401, EAO 273, EAO 54, EAO 17. TEXAS 	SECRETARY 	OF 	STATE 	NOT 	A ΓÇ£STATEWIDE OFFICEHOLDERΓÇ¥ UNDER TITLE 15. Title 15 contains certain restrictions and reporting requirements that apply to a ΓÇ£statewide officeholderΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£holder of a statewide office in the executive branch.ΓÇ¥ The secretary of state is an office with statewide juris- diction to exercise certain constitutional and statutory powers.4 However, the Election Code defines the term ΓÇ£statewide office,ΓÇ¥ as it appears in the Election Code, as ΓÇ£an office of the federal or state government that is voted on statewide.ΓÇ¥ The Texas Constitution provides that the secretary of state shall be appointed by the Governor and is not elected by the qualified voters of the state. Tex. Const. art. IV, ┬º┬º 2, 21. We therefore conclude that the secretary of state is not a statewide officeholder or a holder of a statewide office in the executive branch for purposes of Title 15. EAO 549. See also EAO 234. REPLACEMENT 	CHECK 	DURING MORATORIUM. Although delivery of the invalid checks may have constituted pledges to the legislators, receipt of the pledged contributions did not take place because there were no funds in the account on which the checks were drawn. Under Election Code section 253.034, therefore, a member of the legislature may not take possession of a replacement check during the mor- atorium because that would amount to the receipt of a contribution at a time when such receipt is prohibited. EAO 411. MORATORIUM 	EXCEPTION 	FOR 	SPECIAL ELECTION. A member of the House of Representatives who intends to run for the Senate in a special election that has not yet been ordered but which will almost certainly be ordered and held during the 1997 Legislative Session may rely on the exception set out in section 253.034(c) (1) of the Election Code. EAO 354. See generally ┬º201.025, Election Code, ┬º203.013, Election Code. INCUMBENT JUSTICES OF HIGH COURTS. Justices and justices-elect of the Supreme Court and the Court of Criminal Appeals who had an opponent in the Nov. 1996 general election may accept political contribu- tions in accordance with the Judicial Campaign Fairness Act until March 5, 1997. EAO 351. Affirmed by Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 1134, ┬º4 (amending Elec. Code ┬º253.034(d)) ATTENDING FUNDRAISER OF NONPROFIT AS A ΓÇ£DRAWΓÇ¥ FOR ATTENDANCE. An officeholder contribution is a contribution given with the intent that it defray expenses incurred in connection with duties or activities of the office. If the legislatorΓÇÖs presence at the fundraiser is a ΓÇ£drawΓÇ¥ for others to attend rather than to defray expenses or with intent to make a contribution, the organization would not be making a political con- tribution by providing the officeholder an opportunity to appear at the organizationΓÇÖs fundraiser. EAO 346. See also EAO 71. MORATORIUM DOES NOT APPLY TO STATE DISTRICT JUDGES. The moratorium on political contributions during the legislative session does not apply to state district judges. EAO 253. See also EAO 234. Affirmed by Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 1134, ┬º 4 (amending Elec. Code ┬º 253.034(d)). OFFICE 	SPACE 	IN-KIND 	CONTRIBUTION BEFORE MORATORIUM. As long as a person sub- ject to section 253.034 accepts and receives a political contribution in the form of office space before the begin- ning of the moratorium on political contributions set out in section 253.034, the person may continue to use the office space during the period covered by the morato- rium. EAO 239. MEMBER 	OF 	SBOE 	NOT 	SUBJECT 	TO MORATORIUM 	ON 	CONTRIBUTIONS. The Education Code states that the State Board of Education members are elected from multi-county dis- tricts throughout the state, not statewide. Educ. Code ┬º 11.2101. Therefore, a member of the State Board of Education is not a statewide officeholder for purposes of section 253.034 and is not subject to the moratorium on contributions before and during the regular legislative session. EAO 234.

sections.title: RESTRICTIONS ON CONTRIBUTIONS TO LEGISLATIVE
sections.content: CAUCUSES DURING AND FOLLOWING REGULAR LEGISLATIVE SESSION (a) 	During the period beginning on the 30 th day before the date a regular legislative session convenes and continuing through the 20 th day after the date of final adjournment, a person not a member of the caucus may not knowingly make a contribution to a legislative caucus. (b) 	A legislative caucus may not knowingly accept from a nonmember a contribution, and shall refuse a contribution from a nonmember that is received, during the period prescribed by Subsection (a). A contribution that is received and refused during that period shall be returned to the contributor not later than the 30 th day after the date of receipt. A contribution made by United States mail or by common or contract carrier is not considered received during that period if it was properly addressed and placed with postage or carrier charges prepaid or prearranged in the mail or delivered to the contract carrier before the beginning of the period. The date indicated by the post office cancellation mark or the common or contract carrier documents is considered to be the date the contribution was placed in the mail or delivered to the common or contract carrier unless proven otherwise. (c) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. (d) 	A person who knowingly makes or accepts a contribution in violation of this section is liable for dam- ages to the state in the amount of triple the value of the unlawful contribution. (e) 	In this section, ΓÇ£legislative caucusΓÇ¥ means an organization that is composed exclusively of members of the legislature, that elects or appoints officers and recognizes identified legislators as members of the organization, and that exists for research and other support of policy development and interests that the membership hold in common. The term includes an entity established by or for a legislative caucus to conduct research, education, or any other caucus activity. An organization whose only nonlegislator members are the lieutenant governor or the governor remains a ΓÇ£legislative caucusΓÇ¥ for purposes of this section.

metadata.ethicsOpinions: CAUCUS 	ACCEPTING 	RETURN 	OF MISAPPROPRIATED 	FUNDS 	DOES 	NOT VIOLATE MORATORIUM. A legislative caucus would not be required to disclose the misappropriation of its funds by a former employee as an expenditure or disclose the return of those funds by the former employee as a contribution. The legislative moratorium on contri- butions to the caucus from nonmembers would not pro- hibit the caucus from accepting the return of those mis- appropriated funds by the former employee. EAO 542. ENTITY 	ESTABLISHED 	BY 	OR 	FOR 	A LEGISLATIVE CAUCUS. An entity established by or for a legislative caucus to conduct research or education is itself a legislative caucus if the research or education is a ΓÇ£caucus activity.ΓÇ¥ A ΓÇ£caucus activityΓÇ¥ is an activity that supports the policy development and interests that the members of the establishing caucus hold in common. EAO 384. LEGISLATIVE CAUCUS CONTRIBUTIONS OF PERSONAL SERVICES. A legislative caucus must refuse contributions of personal services from nonmem- bers during the moratorium period imposed by Election Code section 253.0341 even if the agreement to provide the services was entered into before the start of the mor- atorium period. EAO 357. See also EAO 239.

sections.title: RESTRICTIONS ON PERSONAL USE OF CONTRIBUTIONS
sections.content: (a) 	A person who accepts a political contribution as a candidate or officeholder may not convert the contribution to personal use. (b) 	A specific-purpose committee that accepts a political contribution may not convert the contribution to the personal use of a candidate, officeholder, or former candidate or officeholder. (c) 	The prohibitions prescribed by Subsections (a) and (b) include the personal use of an asset purchased with the contribution and the personal use of any interest and other income earned on the contribution. (d) 	In this section, ΓÇ£personal useΓÇ¥ means a use that primarily furthers individual or family purposes not connected with the performance of duties or activities as a candidate for or holder of a public office. The term does not include: (1) 	payments made to defray ordinary and necessary expenses incurred in connection with activities as a candidate or in connection with the performance of duties or activities as a public officeholder, including payment of rent, utility, and other reasonable housing or household expenses incurred in maintaining a residence in Travis County by members of the legislature who do not ordinarily reside in Travis County, but excluding payments prohibited under Section 253.038; or (2) 	payments of federal income taxes due on interest and other income earned on political contributions. (e) 	Subsection (a) applies only to political contributions accepted on or after September 1, 1983. Subsection (b) applies only to political contributions accepted on or after September 1, 1987. (f) 	A person who converts a political contribution to the personΓÇÖs personal use in violation of this section is civilly liable to the state for an amount equal to the amount of the converted contribution plus reasonable court costs. (g) 	A specific-purpose committee that converts a political contribution to the personal use of a candidate, officeholder, or former candidate or officeholder in violation of this section is civilly liable to the state for an amount equal to the amount of the converted contribution plus reasonable court costs. (h) 	Except as provided by Section 253.0351 or 253.042, a candidate or officeholder who makes politi- cal expenditures from the candidateΓÇÖs or officeholderΓÇÖs personal funds may reimburse those personal funds from political contributions in the amount of those expenditures only if: (1) 	the expenditures from personal funds were fully reported as political expenditures, including the payees, dates, purposes, and amounts of the expenditures, in the report required to be filed under this title that covers the period in which the expenditures from personal funds were made; and (2) 	the report on which the expenditures from personal funds are disclosed clearly designates those expenditures as having been made from the personΓÇÖs personal funds and that the expenditures are subject to reimbursement. (i) 	ΓÇ£Personal useΓÇ¥ does not include the use of contributions for: (1) 	defending a criminal action or prosecuting or defending a civil action brought by or against the person in the personΓÇÖs status as a candidate or officeholder; or (2) 	participating in an election contest or participating in a civil action to determine a personΓÇÖs eligi- bility to be a candidate for, or elected or appointed to, a public office in this state. (j), (k) Repealed by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.20, eff. Jan. 1, 1992. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 1991, 72nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.06, eff. Jan. 1, 1992; Acts 1995, 74th Leg., ch. 996, Sec. 9, eff. Sept. 1, 1995; Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 864, Sec. 240, eff. Sept. 1, 1997. cross -refereNce Total Politics Contributions Maintained, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.50 Final Disposition of Unexpended Contributions, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.237(c) Disposition of Unexpended Contributions, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.289 Prohibition on Personal Use of Political Contributions, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 22.17 General Restrictions on Reimbursement of Personal Funds, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 22.19 Expenditures to Vendors, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º20.56 Use of Funds for Informal Settlements Prohibited, Texas House Housekeeping Resolution, ┬º5.10 Constitutional Prohibition on Use of Public Resources for Nonpublic Purposes, Tex. Constituent. Art. III, ┬º51 Reporting the Use and Reimbursement of Personal Funds, 1 Tex. Admin. Code ┬º20.63 P ractice Notes The Ethics Commission approved EAO 547 (below) in June of 2018 and created a new ΓÇ£but forΓÇ¥ test for campaign expenditures. The test states that if an expenditure would not have had to be made but for the candidate running for office, then it can be made out of campaign funds. The case at issue related to childcare expenses for a stay-at-home mom who would not have had the expenses except that she was required to be out of the house for the campaign. And it was mostly based on a Federal Election Commission ruling that laid out the same conclusion. That scenario was simple enough, but the commission acknowledged that there would likely be challenges to the breadth of the testΓÇÖs application. One such hypothetical was a farmer who worked his land for a living and who needed to hire someone to take it over while he campaigned. Commissioners indicated that they may be apt to allow that expenditure from campaign funds, although it would need to come before the commission to make a binding determination. The case also did not address elected officials who had already been elected using political contributions for the same purpose. Practitioners should expect additional challenges to the personal use statute through opinion requests to further define this test.

metadata.ethicsOpinions: GENERAL CANDIDATE/OH MAY NOT CONTROL GPAC AND DRAW SALARY. While the personal use statute does not apply to GPACs, candidates and officeholders who set up GPACs and control them may run afoul of the statute anyway. The Ethics Commission states that all contributions accepted by a C/OH-controlled GPAC are deemed ΓÇ£accepted by candidate or officeholderΓÇ¥ and thus may not be converted to personal use by that C/ OH, including by paying himself a salary, even if the C/ OH is employed by the GPAC to provide professional services. The reasoning comes down to 1. controlling the GPAC, and 2. being paid by the GPAC (subject to Penal Code restrictions). The Commission states that a C/OH may do one or the other, but not both. Depending on the circumstances, the payment may be subject to standards of conduct limitations in Ch. 572, or Penal Code bribery provisions in Ch. 39. EAO 569. See also EAO 508 (2013), EAO 371 (1997), EAO 358 (1997), EAO 192 (1994), EAO 156 (1993), EAO 148 (1993), EAO 47 (1992), EAO 41 (1992). CHILDCARE 	EXPENSES 	OKAY 	WITH CAMPAIGN FUNDS UNDER NEW ΓÇ£BUT FORΓÇ¥ TEST. A candidate may use political contributions to pay childcare expenses to facilitate the candidateΓÇÖs participation in campaign activities. The commission created a new ΓÇ£but forΓÇ¥ test regarding otherwise per- sonal expenditures to state: if an expenditure would not be necessary but for the person running for office, then it may be paid for out of political contributions without being considered ΓÇ£personal useΓÇ¥. EAO 547 (2018). See also, EAO 546 (2018), EAO 423 (1999), EAO 267 (1995), EAO 247 (1995), EAO 157 (1993), EAO 149 (1993). CONTRIBUTIONS 	FOR 	DONOR 	BUILDING; SPOUSE/CHILDREN. 	An 	SPAC 	supporting 	a candidate may use political contributions to purchase tickets to entertainment events for a candidate when the purpose of attendance is building relationships with donors (or for a campaign event), and may also use polit- ical contributions for an officeholder when the purpose of attendance is due to official capacity. The SPAC may not pay for attendance of spouse/children if attending for ΓÇ£donor relationship buildingΓÇ¥, but the SPAC may pay for their attendance as campaign assistants. EAO 521. See also EAO 483, EAO 407, EAO 405, EAO 378, EAO 356, EAO 111. REIMBURSING 	INDIVIDUAL 	PERSONAL EXPENSES WITH CONTRIBUTIONS. The use of political funds to make a reimbursement of expenses to a staff member that occurred due to clerical error is not a use that primarily furthers individual or family purposes not connected with the performance of duties or activ- ities as an officeholder. Therefore, the use of political contributions to make the reimbursement is permissible. EAO 502. CONTRIBUTIONS TO TRUST FUND FOR NON- FAMILY MEMBER FOR MEDICAL BILLS. The exemptions under 254.204 for personal use of campaign contributions are narrowly tailored. Contributing to a trust fund for a non-family-member campaign manager who had a stroke and has excessive medical bills is a pro- hibited personal use for the benefit of a single person. EAO 483. See also EAO 47. See generally ┬º254.203-204, Election Code. USING 	PERSONAL 	FUNDS 	TO 	PURCHASE TICKETS 	WHICH 	COULD 	HAVE 	BEEN PURCHASED WITH PUBLIC FUNDS. A school board member who chooses not to accept the school dis- trictΓÇÖs offer of a free pass to all district events and instead uses personal funds to purchase tickets for events that he attends is not entitled to reimbursement from public funds. He could have avoided the expenditures in the first place by accepting the districtΓÇÖs offer of free passes, but after he made the expenditures, he had no right to repayment from government funds. EAO 460. UNEXPENDED 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	TO 	POLI- TICAL PARTY. Personal use does not include a remit- tance to the political party with which the person was affiliated when the personΓÇÖs name last appeared on a ballot. Therefore, a contribution to any generally recog- nized affiliate of the party would be a permissible use of unexpended political contributions. EAO 437. See also EAO 47. CANDIDATE 	MAY 	PAY 	RELATIVE 	FOR CAMPAIGN WORK AT FAIR MARKET VALUE. A candidate may use political contributions to pay a niece or nephew for campaign work in a situation in which the amount of compensation is based on the fair market value of the work performed. EAO 434. SURPLUS CONTRIBUTIONS TO REIMBURSE EXPENSES CONNECTED WITH POSITION AS BOARD MEMBER OF POLITICAL SUBDIVISION. As a general rule, the provisions of title 15 of the Election Code apply to ΓÇ£officeholders,ΓÇ¥ which is defined in title 15 to include only persons who hold an elective public office (and the secretary of state). Consequently, an appointed member of the board of an appraisal district may use surplus political contributions to pay travel expenses incurred in connection with his activities as a member of the board of a political subdivision. EAO 417. See also EAO 279. CAMPAIGN 	LOAN 	PAID 	WITH 	PERSONAL FUNDS. A candidate who uses personal funds to make payments on a campaign loan is making a political expenditure from personal funds. This means that a candidate who properly reports such payments may use political contributions to reimburse himself for the pay- ments, subject to any applicable limit on reimbursement. EAO 400. See also EAO 389. JUDICIAL CANDIDATE CONTRIBUTIONS TO HOLD VICTORY PARTY IN CONJUNCTION WITH 	CHARITY 	GOLF 	TOURNAMENT. 	A judicial candidate may spend political contributions to purchase amenities at a charity golf tournament to hold a victory party in the skybox. EAO 314. See generally ┬º253.168, Election Code. CAMPAIGN 	FINANCE 	LAW 	PROHIBITS CONVERSION OF ASSETS PURCHASED WITH CONTRIBUTIONS TO PERSONAL USE. The Aircraft Pooling Board no longer permits use of state air- planes with reimbursement by candidates/officeholders because providing flights not paid for wholly with state funds would subject flights operated by the board to addi- tional and costly federal regulations. Letter from Bob Dulaney, Executive Director, Aircraft Pooling Board (March 27, 1995). The campaign finance law prohibits the conversion of an asset purchased with political con- tributions to personal use. An officeholder may not use a state plane for purposes other than those authorized by section 2205.036 even if the officeholder pays for such use. The basis for reimbursement for personal use of an airplane paid for with campaign funds is the reasonable value of the personal use. EAO 269. See also EAO 116. CONTRIBUTIONS TO STATE TREASURY NOT CONVERSION TO PERSONAL USE. An unre- stricted donation of political contributions to the state to offset the cost of staff salaries is not a conversion of those political contributions to ΓÇ£personal use.ΓÇ¥ EAO 244. SEPARATE ACCOUNTS FOR POLITICAL AND PERSONAL FUNDS IS NOT NECESSARY. Title 15 of the Election Code does not require that political contributions be kept in an account separate from other funds, or even that political contributions be kept in an account at all. If a candidate or officeholder maintains more than one account, a transfer of political contri- butions from one of those accounts to another is not an expenditure; nor does the transfer trigger any reporting requirements. Similarly, the withdrawal of cash from one of those accounts is not, by itself, an expenditure; nor does the withdrawal itself trigger any reporting require- ments. EAO 230. Modified by Acts 2003, 78th Leg., ch. 249, ┬º2.09 (adding Elec. Code ┬º253.04) USE OF CONTRIBUTIONS FOR INVESTMENT PURPOSES. Using political contributions to pur- chase stock for personal gain would be impermissible. Additionally, an investment could constitute a conversion to personal use if the investment instrument itself could be converted to personal use. Nothing in title 15 makes degree of risk a basis for concluding that a particular investment is or is not permissible. The only limit title 15 places on a candidateΓÇÖs or officeholderΓÇÖs investment of political contributions is that an investment may not constitute a conversion of a political contribution to the personal use of the candidate or officeholder. Agency policies should also ensure that state resources are not used for private commercial purposes and that only incidental amounts of employee timeΓÇötime peri- ods comparable to reasonable coffee breaks during the dayΓÇöare used to attend to personal matters. EAO 372. See also EAO 134. See generally ┬º39.02, Penal Code. Modified by Acts 1999, 76th Leg., ch. 1499, ┬º1.33 (adding GovΓÇÖt Code ┬º2203.004, to codify General Appropriations Act, 74 th Leg., ch. 1063, art. IX, ┬º135) Modified by Acts 1999, 76th Leg., ch. 1499, ┬º1.44 (repealing GovΓÇÖt Code ┬º403.273(d)) PURCHASING 	DECORATIVE 	ITEMS 	FOR CAPITOL OFFICE. Use of political contributions to purchase items to decorate an officeholderΓÇÖs Capitol office is a use connected with officeholder activities and is therefore not a violation of the personal use prohibition. Items purchased with political contributions may not be converted to personal use at the end of an officeholderΓÇÖs tenure in office. EAO 296. See also EAO 241, 237. PAYING FOR REQUIRED CONTINUING LEGAL EDUCATION COURSES. Like senior judges, for- mer judges sitting by assignment have all the powers of active judges when sitting by assignment, are required to take continuing legal education courses to be eligible for assignment by the presiding judge of an adminis- trative region, and file personal financial statements as state officers. Aa former judge sitting by assignment may use unexpended political contributions to pay for required continuing legal education courses. EAO 291. See also EAO 279; ┬º74.059, Government Code; ┬º74.055, Government Code. PAYING 	FOR 	EVENTS 	IN 	CONNECTION WITH 	ACTIVITIES 	AS 	CANDIDATE 	OR OFFICEHOLDER. As long as the payments for social events are in connection with a judgeΓÇÖs activities as a candidate or officeholder, the judge may use political contributions to make those payments. EAO 284. PAYING FOR CONTINUING LEGAL EDUCA- TION COURSES. A senior judge is a retired judge who elects to be a judicial officer subject to assignment. Therefore, payment for continuing legal education courses is connected with a senior judgeΓÇÖs duties as a holder of public office, and may be made from the judgeΓÇÖs surplus political contributions. EAO 279. See also EAO 196, 245; ┬º75.001, Government Code; Attorney General Opinion H-526 (1975). EXPENSES INCURRED CONCERNING DUTIES OR ACTIVITIES OF OFFICE. A judge may use polit- ical contributions remaining from his previous re-elec- tion campaign to pay expenses incurred in connection with a course of study related to the judgeΓÇÖs duties or activities of office. EAO 267. See also EAO 247. USING COMPUTERS OWNED BY THE STATE FOR PERSONAL PURPOSES. It is up to the legis- lature to determine whether there are circumstances in which a member of the legislature may use for personal purposes computers owned by the state and reimburse the state for any costs to the state. EAO 260. See also EAO 172, 164; See generally, ┬º39.02, Penal Code. SUPPLEMENTING THE SALARIES OF STATE EMPLOYEES. A salary supplement paid by a legisla- tor to state employees who work for the officeholder is permissible under section 36.10(a)(2) of the Penal Code. EAO 254. See also EAO 139, 130, 118, ┬º┬º 36.08 & 36.10, Penal Code. EXPENSES 	INCURRED 	IN 	CONNECTION WITH A COURSE RELATED TO THE JUDGEΓÇÖS DUTIES. A judge may use political contributions to pay expenses incurred in connection with a course of study related to the judgeΓÇÖs duties or activities of office (in this case in the preparation of a thesis required for a Masters of Law in the Judicial Process). EAO 247. PAYING STATE BAR DUES. For judges required to be licensed to practice law in Texas, the payment of state bar dues is a purpose connected with the duties or activi- ties of a judicial candidate or officeholder. Consequently, such judicial candidates and officeholders may use polit- ical contributions to pay state bar dues without violating Election Code section 253.035, the ΓÇ£personal useΓÇ¥ pro- hibition. EAO 245. SENDING CONGRATULATORY LETTERS TO CONSTITUENTS. It is permissible for an officeholder to use political contributions to purchase, prepare, and mail congratulatory letters to parents upon the birth of a child and certificates to students upon graduation from high school or college. The attorney general is the appropriate source for determining whether the constitu- tion permits the use of state resources for such purposes. EAO 209. See also EAO 190, Attorney General Opinion MW-36 (1979). USE OF POLITICAL CONTRIBUTIONS FOR SELF PORTRAIT. An expenditure to purchase a por- trait of a retiring judge for the county courthouse where the judge presided is connected to the duties and activi- ties associated with the office and is therefore a permissi- ble use of political contributions. EAO 199. SPANISH LESSONS TO IMPROVE COMMU- NICATION WITH CONSTITUENCY. A state repre- sentative whose district has a large Hispanic population may use political contributions to pay for Spanish lessons in order to communicate with his or her constituency. Such expenditures would not constitute a prohibited per- sonal use of political contributions under section 253.035 of the Election Code. EAO 157. DRYCLEANING 	BILLS 	IN 	AUSTIN. 	Laundry expenses are neither connected with maintaining a res- idence, such as rent and utility payments, nor are they considered in connection with the performance of duties or activities as an officeholder. Even if there are rules of the House or Senate establishing a dress code for legisla- tors, the clothes worn by members of the legislature are ordinary clothing that can be worn in places other than the Capitol. Thus a legislator may not use political con- tributions to pay for laundry and dry cleaning expenses incurred in Austin. EAO 104. Modified by EAO 407 (1998) PERSONAL 	AND 	BUSINESS 	CALLS 	NOT INVOLVING STATE BUSINESS. A member of the legislature may not place business and personal phone calls not involving state business from his Austin office to his hometown. Because the calls in question are business and personal calls ΓÇ£not involving state business,ΓÇ¥ paying for the calls out of political contributions would be an illegal personal use of political contributions. EAO 78. Overruled by EAO 241 (1995) ELECTRONIC EQUIPMENT FOR OFFICIAL USE IN COURTROOM. A judge may use political contri- butions to purchase electronic equipment for official use in the judgeΓÇÖs courtroom or chambers but may not con- vert the asset to personal use. The asset would be subject to the various provisions of title 15 of the Election Code applicable to an asset purchased with political contribu- tions. EAO 25.

sections.title: LOANS FROM PERSONAL FUNDS
sections.content: (a) 	A candidate or officeholder who makes political expenditures from the candidateΓÇÖs or officeholderΓÇÖs personal funds may report the amount expended as a loan and may reimburse those personal funds from political contributions in the amount of the reported loan. (b) 	Section 253.035(h) applies if the person does not report an amount as a loan as authorized by Subsection (a). (c) 	A candidate or officeholder who deposits personal funds in an account in which political contribu- tions are held shall report the amount of personal funds deposited as a loan and may reimburse the amount deposited as a loan from political contributions or unexpended personal funds deposited in the account. The reimbursement may not exceed the amount reported as a loan. Personal funds deposited in an account in which political contributions are held are subject to Section 253.035 and must be included in the reports of the total amount of political contributions maintained required by Sections 254.031(a)(8) and 254.0611(a).

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1995, 74 th Leg., ch. 996, Sec. 8, eff. Sept. 1, 1995. Amended by Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 864, Sec. 241, eff. Sept. 1, 1997. Amended by Acts 2011, 82nd
metadata.ethicsOpinions: PERSONAL 	MONEY 	REIMBURSED 	WITH COMMERCIALLY REASONABLE INTEREST. A candidate or officeholder may use political contributions to reimburse himself or herself with interest at a com- mercially reasonable rate for political expenditures made from the candidateΓÇÖs or officeholderΓÇÖs personal funds. For judicial candidates, there is a cap on the total amount a judicial candidate may reimburse himself or herself from political contributions. The caps on reimbursement set out in Election Code section 253.162 are the total amounts judicial candidates and officeholders may pay themselves to compensate themselves for political expen- ditures made from personal funds. Any interest paid is included in determining whether a candidate or office- holder has reached the applicable cap. EAO 375. See also EAO 349, EAO 258. CANDIDATE MAY REIMBURSE HIMSELF FOR USE OF PERSONAL FUNDS AS LOANS TO HIS CAMPAIGN IF REPORTED AND DOES NOT EXCEED AMOUNT SPENT FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES. It is permissible for a candidate to reim- burse himself from political contributions for political expenditures made from personal funds and reported as loans from the candidate on Schedule E of the candidate report of contributions and expenditures (Form C/OH). Although the technically correct way to report the use of personal funds is to disclose expenditures made from these funds on Schedule G, we believe that a candidate who has reported his use of personal funds for political expenditures as loans to his campaign is not prohibited from reimbursing himself from political contributions in the amount of the personal funds spent for political purposes. EAO 258. See also EAO 195, 230, State Ethics Advisory Commission Opinion 84-27. Affirmed by Acts 1995, 74th Leg., ch. 996, ┬º8 (adding Elec. Code ┬º253.0351)

sections.title: OFFICEHOLDER CONTRIBUTIONS USED IN CONNECTION WITH
sections.content: CAMPAIGN An officeholder who lawfully accepts officeholder contributions may use those contributions in connection with the officeholderΓÇÖs campaign for elective office after appointing a campaign treasurer. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987.

sections.title: RESTRICTIONS ON CONTRIBUTION OR EXPENDITURE BY
sections.content: GENERAL-PURPOSE COMMITTEE (b) 	A general-purpose committee may not knowingly make a political contribution to another gener- al-purpose committee unless the other committee is listed in the campaign treasurer appointment of the contributor committee. (d) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 1993, 73rd Leg., ch. 531, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1993. Amended by Acts 2019, 86th Leg., R.S., Ch. 209 (H.B. 3580), Sec. 5(1), eff. metadata.ethicsOpinions: DUES PAYMENTS TO CLUB TO SUPPORT A GPAC. Membership dues paid to a club which qualifies as a political committee due to its involvement in polit- ical campaigns and advertising are ΓÇ£political contribu- tionsΓÇ¥ that count toward the $500 contribution threshold for purposes of Election Code section 253.031(b), unless specifically earmarked for purposes not governed by Title 15 of the Election Code. Contributions earmarked to cover the general administrative costs of a political committee are still political contributions. EAO 394. See also EAO 161, EAO 132, EAO 131, EAO 344. POLITICAL 	EXPENDITURES 	ONLY 	REPOR- TABLE 	FOR 	TEXAS 	CAMPAIGNS 	AND MEASURES. This opinion is solely concerned with reporting requirements in regard to expenditures and does not address contributions. General-purpose political com- mittees are not required to report political expenditures made in connection with out-of-state campaigns, office- holders, or measures on reports filed under chapter 254 of the Texas Election Code. EAO 208. See Letter from Jack M. Rains, Texas Secretary of State, to Aubrey B. Calvin, Office of Calvin, Dylewski, Gibbs, Maddox, Russell & Verner (Dec. 2, 1988). GPAC 	EXPENDITURES 	RELATED 	TO POLITICAL FUNDRAISING AND EDUCATIO- NAL 	PURPOSES. 	General-purpose 	committee expenditures related to political fundraising are subject to the 60-day waiting period of Election Code section 253.037(a). If a general-purpose committee receives as an in-kind contribution brochures (which discuss the political concerns of the PAC to be used for education and fundraising purposes) costing more than $500 to produce, its distribution of the brochures constitutes a political expenditure subject to the 60-day waiting period. EAO 177. See also EAO 161, EAO 77, EAO 74. Modified by Catholic Leadership Coalition of Tex. v. Reisman ex rel., No. 13-50582, 2014 U.S. App. LEXIS 15558 (5 th Cir. Aug. 12, 2014) EXPENDITURES 	OVER 	$500/CAMPAIGN TREASURER 	APPOINTMENT 	FILED 	30 	OR MORE DAYS PRIOR TO RELEVANT ELECTION. A political committee may not knowingly make or autho- rize a campaign contribution or campaign expenditure that in the aggregate exceeds $500 supporting or oppos- ing a candidate for a statewide office, the state legislature, the State Board of Education, or a multi-county district office in a primary or general election unless the com- mitteeΓÇÖs campaign treasurer appointment has been filed not later than the 30 th day before the appropriate election day. A general-purpose committee may not knowingly make or authorize political expenditures totaling more than $500 unless the committee has (1) filed its campaign treasurer appointment not later than the 60 th day before the date the expenditure is made that causes the total expenditures to exceed $500, and (2) accepted political contributions from at least 10 persons. EAO 161. Modified, in part, by Catholic Leadership Coalition of Tex. v. Reisman ex rel., No. 13-50582, 2014 U.S. App. LEXIS 15558 (5 th Cir. Aug. 12, 2014) RESTRICTED USE CONTRIBUTIONS. If funds are given to a political committee with the restriction that they be used to hire a lobbyist to work on legisla- tive matters, the political committee is not required to report the funds as a political contribution since it does not fit the definition of campaign contribution or office- holder contribution. If, on the other hand, funds are not restricted to uses not regulated by title 15, the funds must be reported as a political contribution. Incurring post- age, telephone and personal travel costs by the PAC or its directors do not by themselves require lobbyist registra- tion. EAO 131. See also EAO 3, EAO 89. CONTRIBUTIONS TO OUT OF STATE GROUP. If an out-of-state employee group is a ΓÇ£general-purpose committeeΓÇ¥ under the Texas Election Code, then a Texas general-purpose committee is required to include the name and address of the out-of-state employee group in its appointment of campaign treasurer as a ΓÇ£general-purpose committee to whom the committee intends to make polit- ical contributionsΓÇ¥ before the Texas committee may make a contribution to the out-of-state committee. EAO 65.

sections.title: PAYMENTS MADE TO PURCHASE REAL PROPERTY OR TO RENT
sections.content: CERTAIN REAL PROPERTY PROHIBITED (a) 	A candidate or officeholder or a specific-purpose committee for supporting, opposing, or assisting the candidate or officeholder may not knowingly make or authorize a payment from a political contribu- tion to purchase real property or to pay the interest on or principal of a note for the purchase of real property. (a-1) A candidate or officeholder or a specific-purpose committee for supporting, opposing, or assisting the candidate or officeholder may not knowingly make or authorize a payment from a political contribu- tion for the rental or purchase of real property from: (1) 	a person related within the second degree by consanguinity or affinity, as determined under Chapter 573, Government Code, to the candidate or officeholder; or (2) 	a business in which the candidate or officeholder or a person described by Subdivision (1) has a participating interest of more than 10 percent, holds a position on the governing body, or serves as an officer. (b) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this subsection is a Class A misdemeanor. (c) 	This section does not apply to a payment made in connection with real property that was purchased before January 1, 1992.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.07, eff. Jan. 1, 1992. Amended by Acts 2007, 80th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1087 (H.B. 3066), Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2007;
metadata.ethicsOpinions: RENT ON SPOUSEΓÇÖS SEPARATE PROPERTY NOT ILLEGAL PURCHASE OF REAL PROPERTY. A legislatorΓÇÖs use of political contributions to make a rental payment to his spouse for the use of her separate property does not constitute a payment to purchase real property and does not violate section 253.038 of the Election Code. Nor is such a payment a conversion to personal use as long as the payment does not exceed the fair market value of the use of the property. EAO 319. See also EAO 129, EAO 116. Limited by Acts 2007, 80 th Leg., H.B. 3066 (adding Elec. Code ┬º253.038(a-1)) IF AN ASSET IS PURCHASED IN PART WITH POLITICAL CONTRIBUTIONS, THE PERSONAL USE RESTRICTIONS APPLY. An item is not con- verted to personal use if the candidate or officeholder reimburses his political funds on the basis of the reason- able value of any personal use. If political contributions are used to pay part of the purchase price of an asset, a proportional amount of any income from the asset is sub- ject to the prohibition on personal use in section 253.035 of the Election Code. EAO 248. See also, EAO 13, 116.

sections.title: CONTRIBUTIONS IN CERTAIN PUBLIC BUILDINGS PROHIBITED
sections.content: (a) 	A person may not knowingly make or authorize a political contribution while in the Capitol or a courthouse to: (1) 	a candidate or officeholder; (2) 	a political committee; or (3) 	a person acting on behalf of a candidate, officeholder, or political committee. (b) 	A candidate, officeholder, or political committee or a person acting on behalf of a candidate, office- holder, or political committee may not knowingly accept a political contribution, and shall refuse a political contribution that is received, in the Capitol or a courthouse. (c) 	This section does not prohibit contributions made in the Capitol or a courthouse through the United States postal service or a common or contract carrier. (d) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. (h) 	In this section, ΓÇ£courthouseΓÇ¥ means any building owned by the state, a county, or a municipality, or an office or part of a building leased to the state, a county, or a municipality, in which a justice or judge sits to conduct court proceedings.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.07, eff. Jan. 1, 1992. Amended by Acts 2009, 81st Leg., R.S., Ch. 1219 (S.B. 1152), Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2009.

sections.title: SEPARATE ACCOUNTS
sections.content: (a) 	Except as provided by Section 253.0351(c), each candidate or officeholder shall keep the personΓÇÖs campaign and officeholder contributions in one or more accounts that are separate from any other account maintained by the person. (b) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class B misdemeanor.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 2003, 78 th Leg., ch. 249, Sec. 2.09, eff. Sept. 1, 2003. Amended by Acts 2011, 82nd Leg., 1st C.S., Ch. 4 (S.B. 1), Sec. 76.02, eff. September 28, 2011.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: POLITICAL FUNDS FROM PRIOR JUDICIAL CAMPAIGN. Even if a candidate chooses to keep con- tributions from different campaigns in separate accounts, a transfer from one of those accounts to the other is not a contribution or expenditure for purposes of the cam- paign finance law and is not reportable on a campaign finance report. Transfers between a specific-purpose political committee and the candidate or officeholder supported by that committee are not subject to the con- tribution limits in the Judicial Campaign Fairness Act. EAO 418. See also EAO 230, EAO 271, EAO 281. Modified by ┬º253.040, Election Code, in 2003. SEPARATE ACCOUNTS FOR POLITICAL AND PERSONAL FUNDS IS NOT NECESSARY. Title 15 of the Election Code does not require that political contributions be kept in an account separate from other funds, or even that political contributions be kept in an account at all. If a candidate or officeholder maintains more than one account, a transfer of political contri- butions from one of those accounts to another is not an expenditure; nor does the transfer trigger any reporting requirements. Similarly, the withdrawal of cash from one of those accounts is not, by itself, an expenditure; nor does the withdrawal itself trigger any reporting require- ments. EAO 230. Modified by Acts 2003, 78th Leg., ch. 249, ┬º2.09 (adding Elec. Code ┬º253.040)

sections.title: RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN PAYMENTS
sections.content: (a) 	A candidate or officeholder or a specific-purpose committee for supporting, opposing, or assisting the candidate or officeholder may not knowingly make or authorize a payment from a political contribu- tion if the payment is made for personal services rendered by the candidate or officeholder or by the spouse or dependent child of the candidate or officeholder to: (1) 	a business in which the candidate or officeholder has a participating interest of more than 10 per- cent, holds a position on the governing body of the business, or serves as an officer of the business; or (2) 	the candidate or officeholder or the spouse or dependent child of the candidate or officeholder. (b) 	A payment that is made from a political contribution to a business described by Subsection (a) and that is not prohibited by that subsection may not exceed the amount necessary to reimburse the business for actual expenditures made by the business. (c) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this subsection is a Class A misdemeanor.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.07, eff. Jan. 1, 1992.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: CORPORATION STOCK OWNED BY SPOUSE. The stock of the corporation granting the option is owned by the spouse of a legislator as community prop- erty. This provision would therefore not prevent the corporation owned by the legislatorΓÇÖs spouse from selling the property to the prospective buyer. We note that arti- cle III, section 18, of the Texas Constitution also restricts a legislator from entering into a contract with the state. The Texas Ethics Commission has no authority to inter- pret constitutional provisions. EAO 263. USE OF CORPORATE OWNED AIRPLANE FOR TRAVEL. A member of the legislature may use politi- cal contributions to pay for transportation to and from Austin for legislative purposes. A payment from political contributions to a business in one of the categories listed in section 253.041(a) must not exceed the amount neces- sary to reimburse the business for actual expenditures made by the business. Use of a corporate plane for a charge less than necessary to reimburse the corporation for the use of the plane may be a political contribution in the form of an officeholder contribution. A candidate may use political contributions to pay for transportation for campaign purposes. Because both section 253.041 and section 253.094 would apply to a payment from political contributions for campaign use of the plane in question, the payment to the corporation for use of the plane would have to be in the amount reasonably neces- sary to reimburse the corporation for its expenses. EAO 249. See also, EAO 35, 139. ITEM PURCHASED WITH POLITICAL FUNDS REIMBURSED WITH PERSONAL FUNDS. An item is not converted to personal use if the candidate reim- burses his political funds on the basis of the reasonable value of the use. A candidate or officeholder may use a personal asset for political purposes and it is not required to be reported. Similarly, a candidate or officeholder may reimburse his personal funds from political contributions for the use of a personal asset for political purposes. EAO 116. See also EAO 13, EAO 50. CANDIDATE INTEREST IN CORPORATION. A candidate who owns 50 percent of the stock in a cor- poration engaged in the advertising business may make a payment from a political contribution to the corporation to purchase advertising services and supplies if the pay- ment is in the amount necessary to reimburse the corpo- ration for actual expenditures. A payment greater than that amount would be in violation of section 253.041. A payment less than that amount would be an impermissi- ble corporate contribution. EAO 35.

sections.title: RESTRICTIONS ON REIMBURSEMENT OF PERSONAL FUNDS
sections.content: AND PAYMENTS ON CERTAIN LOANS (a) 	A candidate or officeholder who makes political expenditures from the candidateΓÇÖs or officeholderΓÇÖs personal funds may not reimburse those personal funds from political contributions in amounts that in the aggregate exceed the following amounts for each election in which the personΓÇÖs name appears on the ballot: (1) 	for a statewide office other than governor, $250,000; and (2) 	for governor, $500,000. (b) 	A candidate or officeholder who accepts one or more political contributions in the form of loans, including an extension of credit or a guarantee of a loan or extension of credit, from one or more persons related to the candidate or officeholder within the second degree by affinity or consanguinity may not use political contributions to repay the loans in amounts that in the aggregate exceed the amount prescribed by Subsection (a). (c) 	The total amount of both reimbursements and repayments made by a candidate or officeholder under this section may not exceed the amount prescribed by Subsection (a). (d) 	A person who is both a candidate and an officeholder covered by Subsection (a) may reimburse the personΓÇÖs personal funds or repay loans from political contributions only in one capacity. (e) 	This section does not prohibit the payment of interest on loans covered by this section at a commer- cially reasonable rate, except that interest on loans from a candidateΓÇÖs or officeholderΓÇÖs personal funds or on loans from the personal funds of any person related to the candidate or officeholder within the second degree by affinity or consanguinity is included in the amount prescribed by Subsection (a), (b), or (c). (f) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. (g) 	The commission shall study possible restrictions on amounts of reimbursements under Subsection (a) in connection with the offices of state senator and state representative and shall make appropriate recommendations to the legislature on those matters.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.07, eff. Jan. 1, 1992. Amended by Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 864, Sec. 242, eff. Sept. 1, 1997.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: CAMPAIGN 	LOAN 	PAID 	WITH 	PERSONAL FUNDS. A candidate who uses personal funds to make payments on a campaign loan is making a political expenditure from personal funds. This means that a candidate who properly reports such payments may use political contributions to reimburse himself for the pay- ments, subject to any applicable limit on reimbursement. EAO 400. See also EAO 389. CANDIDATEΓÇÖS USE OF CONTRIBUTIONS TO REPAY A BANK LOAN. The result of a candidateΓÇÖs use of political contributions to reimburse personal funds is that the political contributions become available for the candidateΓÇÖs unrestricted personal use. A loan repay- ment, in contrast, makes funds available to a third party. Therefore, a candidateΓÇÖs use of political contributions to repay a bank loan does not count toward the limit on reimbursement set out in section 253.162. EAO 389. See also EAO 258, EAO 230.

sections.title: POLITICAL CONTRIBUTIONS USED IN CONNECTION WITH
sections.content: APPOINTIVE OFFICE A former candidate or former officeholder who lawfully accepts political contributions may use those con- tributions to make an expenditure to defray expenses incurred by the person in performing a duty or engaging in an activity in connection with an appointive office of a state board or commission.

sections.title: CORPORATIONS COVERED
sections.content: This subchapter applies only to corporations that are organized under the Texas Business Corporation Act, the Texas For-Profit Corporation Law, the Texas Non-Profit Corporation Act, the Texas Nonprofit Corporation Law, federal law, or law of another state or nation. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. Amended by Acts 2007, 80th Leg., R.S., Ch. 481 (H.B. 2492), Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2007. cross -refereNce Corporations and Certain Associations Covered, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 24.1 P ractice Notes Practitioners should keep in mind the federal one-third rule as a guidepost when fundraising for corporately affiliated PACΓÇÖs. The federal rule states that in order to avoid an appearance of impropriety, a fundraiser which accepts auction prizes and entertainment from corporate entities must raise at least three times the cost (or fair market value) of the auction items donated and entertainment provided. This rule is designed to keep corporations from donating costly items to a PAC for auction, but only valuing them or charging the PAC a minimal amount of money to obtain it. Then once the PAC auctions off the item for a large amount, the corporation has essentially just worked around making a prohibited corporate contribution of a large sum of money to that PAC. As an example, if the fair market value of auction items and entertainment (if entertainment is the draw for the event, e.g. if Willie Nelson were playing or if the event centered around casino games as an entertainment draw) is $3,000, then the event must raise at least $9,000. If the event does not raise that amount, then a complicated formula is required to refund portions of that money until it reaches the required benchmark. Note that this formula does not apply to the cost of venue, food, drinks or anything else. While this is a federal rule, the TEC has applied the rule and mentioned it in two ethics opinions: EAO 280, and EAO 163. The TEC did not require adherence to this rule, but merely offered it as a guidepost for safe harbor purposes in Texas. attorNey G eNeral oPiNioNs APPLICATION OF ACT TO CERTAIN ACTIVITIES. A contribution by a business corporation to a non-profit organization conducting non-partisan research for a legislative caucus is not necessarily prohibited by or subject to the Texas Business Corporation Act, article 1349 of the Revised Statutes, the Political Funds Reporting and Disclosure Act, the Lobby Act, or chapter 36 of the Texas Penal Code. AttΓÇÖy Gen. Op. JM-50. See also AttΓÇÖy Gen. Ops MW-48 (1979); H-743 (1975); H-486, H-252 (1974); H-189 (1973); H-1175(1978); H-191 (1973); H-265 (1974). JM-50 case law cited: State v. Duke, 137 S.W. 654, 65 (Tex. 1911). Texas State Board of Medical Examiners v. McClellan, 307 S.W.2d 317 (Tex. Civ. App.ΓÇö Houston 1957, writ refΓÇÖd n.r.e.). First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti, 435 U.S. 765 (1978).

metadata.caseLaw: King Street Patriots et. al. v. Texas Democratic Party et. al., No. 15-0320 (Tex. June 30, 2017) ΓÇ£Adhering to the United States Supreme CourtΓÇÖs decision in Federal Election Commission v. Beaumont, as we are obliged to do, we conclude that legislatively enacted bans on corporate political contributions are constitutional under the First Amendment.ΓÇ¥ (p.4) ΓÇ£Section 253.094ΓÇÖs current incarnation reflects a 2011 amendment that removed a limitation on political expenditures in response to the United States Supreme CourtΓÇÖs decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission. Restrictions on corporate political contributions remained intact, however, presumably because the Supreme CourtΓÇÖs Citizens United decision did not overturn its earlier holding in Federal Election Commission v. Beaumont that laws barring corporate political contributions are ΓÇ£consistent with the First AmendmentΓÇ¥ and are not subject to strict scrutinyΓÇ¥ (p.21) Only the Supreme Court has the ΓÇ£prerogative . . . to overrule one of its precedents.ΓÇ¥ Thus even if BeaumontΓÇÖs rationale is in doubt, we are bound to follow it unless and until the Supreme Court overrules it. Our unanimous acknowledgment that Beaumont is binding Supreme Court precedent terminates our inquiryΓÇªOur role is simply to ΓÇ£say what the law is,ΓÇ¥ not prognosticate how the law could change. Applying Beaumont, we conclude sections 253.091 and 253.094 of the Texas Election Code are not unconstitutional.ΓÇ¥ (p.22)

sections.title: TREATMENT OF INCORPORATED POLITICAL COMMITTEE
sections.content: If a political committee the only principal purpose of which is accepting political contributions and making political expenditures incorporates for liability purposes only, the committee is not considered to be a corporation for purposes of this subchapter. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987.

metadata.ethicsOpinions: POLITICAL 	COMMITTEE 	INCORPORATED FOR LIABILITY PURPOSES ONLY. A political committee 	that 	incorporates 	under 	the 	Nonprofit Corporation Act for liability purposes only and states that its only purpose for incorporating is to accept contri- butions and make expenditures as a political committee is formed for liability purposes only within the meaning of section 253.092 of the Election Code. Such an incor- porated political committee is not subject to the prohibi- tions generally applicable to corporations under title 15. EAO 165.

sections.title: CERTAIN ASSOCIATIONS COVERED
sections.content: (a) 	For purposes of this subchapter, the following associations, whether incorporated or not, are con- sidered to be corporations covered by this subchapter: banks, trust companies, savings and loan associations or companies, insurance companies, reciprocal or interinsurance exchanges, railroad companies, cemetery companies, government-regulated cooperatives, stock companies, and abstract and title insurance companies. (b) 	For purposes of this subchapter, the members of the associations specified by Subsection (a) are con- sidered to be stockholders. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. P ractice Notes EAOΓÇÖs 614 and 601 below are interesting regarding the differences in how a corporation is treated by the Commission vs. how trusts are treated. The opinions reach different conclusions about trusts (which are not treated as a separate entity) and corporations (which are, except when theyΓÇÖre not) in the question of how and why the entity could be required to form as a PAC. In both opinions, they cite Lake Travis Citizens Council and restate an argument the Commission used in that case, that ΓÇ£a nonprofit corporation is not at risk of regulation as a political committee because it is a nonprofit corporation and therefore treated as a single person, not a group of persons, under the Texas Election Code.ΓÇ¥ See above for a summary of the case. However, in EAO 614, the Commission specifically flips its position on this issue and says that ΓÇ£the same logic would also exempt a political committee, because a political committee also meets the Code Construction ActΓÇÖs definition of a ΓÇÿperson.ΓÇÖ (since the committee is also a legal entity and can sue and be sued). This is, of course, absurd.ΓÇ¥ So IΓÇÖm still not sure how we got here, but the new official position of the TEC is that a corporation CAN be consid- ered a political committee and is not necessarily a single person regardless of what EAO 601 says.
