Similarly, a trust is disregarded as a standalone entity, and thus the new principal purpose safe harbor of 49% (EAO 614 abolished the 25% safe harbor and later added the new safe harbor to TEC rule 20.1(17) in the definition of ΓÇ£principal purposeΓÇ¥) applies to the trust such that it could be considered a PAC if it goes over the 49% mark. The same now applies to a corporation.

metadata.caseLaw: Tex. Home Sch. Coal. AssΓÇÖn v. Tex. Ethics CommΓÇÖn, No. 03-17-00167-CV, (Tex. App. Nov. 7, 2018) The Coalition sued for declaratory and injunctive relief, seeking to challenge the validity of a Commission rule referred to as ΓÇ£the Principal Purpose Rule.ΓÇ¥ Despite its efforts to show that it intends to engage in conduct arguably affected by the rule, the CoalitionΓÇÖs arguments as to standing essentially come down to these questions: What if the CoalitionΓÇÖs circumstances change in the future so as to trigger the ruleΓÇÖs limits on spending or contributions? And what if the Commission changes its mind and attempts to enforce the rule against the Coalition as a distinct legal entity and not part of a group? We accept that the Coalition has sincere concerns about these future hypotheticals. However, on this record, those concerns do not suffice to establish a justiciable controversy under Texas law. Lake Travis Citizens Council v. Ashley, No. 1:14-CV-994-LY, (W.D. Tex. Mar. 14, 2016) Citizens Council alleges that it curtailed its spending before the March 2016 election out of fear that engaging in its desired advocacy would subject Citizens Council to classification as a political committee under Texas Election Code, Section 251.001(12). Ashley argues that Citizens Council is not at risk of regulation as a political committee because it is a nonprofit corporation and therefore treated as a singular person, not a group of persons, under the Texas Election Code. See Tex. GovΓÇÖt Code ┬º 311.005(2). The court agrees.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: NO MORE 25% SAFE HARBOR FOR PRINCIPAL PURPOSE. NEW MULTIFACTOR TEST FOR PAC FORMATION. By definition, two or more persons must act in concert with a principal purpose of making polit- ical expenditures or accepting political contributions to form a political committee. If a group of persons form a nonprofit corporation that has as a principal purpose accepting political contributions or making political expenditures, the corporation is a political committee. To determine whether a group has a principal purpose of making political expenditures, the TEC will presume that a corporation who spends 50% or more of its time/ resources on political activity should be organized as a political committee. The previous 25% safe harbor for political activity is repealed. An organization that spends less than 50% of its time/resources on political activity may still qualify as a political committee based on the facts and circumstances concerning the groupΓÇÖs actual and planned activities related to making political expen- ditures, including: 1. The proportion of the groupΓÇÖs total expenditures that constitute political expenditures; 2. The amount of the groupΓÇÖs staff or volunteer time, equipment, or other resources allocated to making political expenditures; 3. The content of the groupΓÇÖs public statements regard- ing its goals or support of or opposition to candidates, officeholders, or measures; 4. The groupΓÇÖs government filings and organizational documents, including mission statements; and 5. The groupΓÇÖs other activities that are unrelated to making political expenditures. EAO 614 (2024). See also, EAO 518 (2014), EAO 147 (1993). TRUST IS NOT SEPARATE ENTITY, SO ALL TITLE 15 RULES APPLY TO FUNDERS AND MANAGERS OF TRUST. Purpose trusts were created by the 2023 Legislature which can be created for a non- charitable purpose without a definite beneficiary. The Commission states that unlike a corporation, a trust is not a separate legal entity and as such the individuals contributing to or managing the trust may be treated as a PAC if the group meets the principal purpose defini- tions. EAO 601 LLC OWNED IN WHOLE OR IN PART BY CORPORATION. A limited liability company owned in whole or in part by a corporation is subject to the restrictions in Election Code chapter 253, subchapter D. The restrictions also apply to associations engaged in certain types of business, regardless of how the associa- tions are organized, including out of state LLCΓÇÖs. Thus, a limited liability company is subject to the restrictions in Election Code chapter 253, subchapter D, if it engages in a type of business listed in Election Code section 253.093. EAO 383. See also EAO 221, EAO 215. CORPORATE MEMBER OF GENERAL PURPOSE COMMITTEE. The use of the associationΓÇÖs resources to solicit and process contributions to the general-purpose committee from its members would be permissible as a method of financing the solicitation costs of the politi- cal committee. If a member of the association is either a corporation or an entity considered to be a corpora- tion under Election Code section 253.093, the member would be allowed to contribute to the general-purpose committee only to finance the administration of the committee and the solicitation of funds for the commit- tee. Furthermore, the fact that the contributions would flow through the incorporated associationΓÇÖs general account before being deposited in the general-purpose committeeΓÇÖs account would not violate the prohibition on corporate political activity. EAO 181. See also EAO 108, EAO 163, EAO 132.

sections.title: CONTRIBUTIONS PROHIBITED
sections.content: (a) 	A corporation or labor organization may not make a political contribution that is not authorized by this subchapter. (b) 	A corporation or labor organization may not make a political contribution in connection with a recall election, including the circulation and submission of a petition to call an election. (c) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a felony of the third degree. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. Amended by Acts 2011, 82nd Leg., R.S., Ch. 1009 (H.B. 2359), Sec. 1, eff. June 17, 2011; Acts 2011, 82 nd Leg., R.S., Ch. 1009 (H.B. 2359), Sec. 2, eff. June 17, 2011. cross -refereNce DefinitionsΓÇöΓÇ£Principal PurposeΓÇ¥, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.1(20) Final Disposition of Unexpended Contributions, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.237 Reporting Schedule for Political Party Accepting Corporate or Labor Organization Contributions, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 24.529 Contributions to Direct Campaign Expenditure Only Committees, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º22.5 Reporting Direct Campaign Expenditures, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 22.6 Corporate Expenditures for Get-Out-the-Vote Campaigns Permitted, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 24.17 Designation of Contribution for Administrative Purposes, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º24.18. P ractice Notes Note: After the Texasn for Free Enterprise case (see below), the TEC acknowledged that it will no longer enforce subsection (a) above. After the Citizens United decision in 2010, corporate involvement in campaigns increased dramatically at all levels. But that decision isnΓÇÖt necessarily what allowed corporations to do so. Direct campaign expenditures (usually called independent expenditures on the federal level) were legal in Texas for years prior to Citizens United. The case merely brought the practice to light and cemented its place as a legitimate tool for corporations and labor organizations to get around corporate contribution prohibitions. The natural progression from corporate independent expenditures was to pool corporate money from multiple sources and make expenditures from a single source. From this idea, Super PACs arose and regulation followed, and some national organizations made headlines by using 501(c)(4) non-profit organizations to engage in political activity. One upside to this practice is that 501(c)(4)ΓÇÖs are tax exempt as long as their political activity does not cross a majority (50% +) threshold. The biggest advantage is that 501(c)(4) organizations do not have to disclose their contributors to the Federal Election Commission or the Texas Ethics Commission (ΓÇ£TECΓÇ¥). In fact, the IRS removed the require- ment that 501(c)(4) nonprofits disclose ΓÇ£largeΓÇ¥ donors who contribute over $5,000. So now, 501(c)(4)ΓÇÖs donΓÇÖt have to disclose their donors to anyone. The downside is the possible public perception of non-profits cheating the system. From 2012 to 2014, the term ΓÇ£dark moneyΓÇ¥ emerged to describe this practice in a negative connotation, and elected officials took notice. A number of bills were filed to address the issue, and Governor Abbott issued emergency declarations to pass meaningful ethics reform in both the 2015 and 2017 legislative sessions. However, a full omnibus reform never materialized even when the TEC was up for sunset review in 2025. In the meantime, the TEC made attempts to address issues at the regulatory level. Many of these changes were the result of the Ethics CommissionΓÇÖs considerable time spent in the courtroom defending itself and the laws under its jurisdiction, some of which are detailed below.

metadata.caseLaw: Virden v. City of Austin, No. 21-50597 (5th Circuit decision Oct. 25, 2021) This case originated out of an Austin city council race in which the plaintiff challenged the constitutionality of a one year moratorium on collecting contributions as a city council candidate for election. While the ordinance is of no import for state law purposes, the 5th CircuitΓÇÖs reasoning is of interest: ΓÇ£Supreme Court precedent regarding First Amendment campaign finance distinguishes between the First Amendment rights of a contributor and those of a candidate. See, e.g., Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1, 24, 44ΓÇô45 (1976) (per curiam). A contributor has a constitutionally protected right of association, typically expressed by donating money to candidates or political action committees (ΓÇ£PACsΓÇ¥). See id. at 24ΓÇô25. A candidate, on the other hand, has a constitutionally protected right of political expression, typically exercised by spending money on political communications. See id. at 19ΓÇô20. In other words, VirdenΓÇÖs constitutionally protected interest is in spending moneyΓÇönot receiving it.ΓÇ¥ King Street Patriots et. al. v. Texas Democratic Party et. al., No. 15-0320 (Tex. June 30, 2017) ΓÇ£Adhering to the United States Supreme CourtΓÇÖs decision in Federal Election Commission v. Beaumont, as we are obliged to do, we conclude that legislatively enacted bans on corporate political contributions are constitutional under the First Amendment.ΓÇ¥ (p.4) ΓÇ£Section 253.094ΓÇÖs current incarnation reflects a 2011 amendment that removed a limita- tion on political expenditures in response to the United States Supreme CourtΓÇÖs decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission. Restrictions on corporate political contributions remained intact, however, presumably because the Supreme CourtΓÇÖs Citizens United decision did not overturn its earlier holding in Federal Election Commission v. Beaumont that laws barring corporate political contributions are ΓÇ£consistent with the First AmendmentΓÇ¥ and are not subject to strict scrutinyΓÇ¥ (p.21) Only the Supreme Court has the ΓÇ£prerogative . . . to overrule one of its precedents.ΓÇ¥ Thus even if BeaumontΓÇÖs rationale is in doubt, we are bound to follow it unless and until the Supreme Court overrules it. Our unanimous acknowledgment that Beaumont is binding Supreme Court precedent terminates our inquiryΓÇª Our role is simply to ΓÇ£say what the law is,ΓÇ¥ not prognosticate how the law could change. Applying Beaumont, we conclude sections 253.091 and 253.094 of the Texas Election Code are not unconstitutional.ΓÇ¥ (p.22) Catholic Leadership Coalition of Texas v. Reisman, 764 F. 3d 409 (5th Cir. 2014) This case invalidated the 60 day layout period and 10 contributor minimum required before making over $500 in expenditures by a PAC. See practice notes of 20.401(d) of these rules for a full explanation of this case Texans for Free Enterprise v. Texas Ethics Commission, 732 F. 3d 535 (5th Cir. 2013) Texans for Free Enterprise (TFE) was a political committee which, by its own admission, did not have any intention on making contributions to candidates but rather only made direct campaign expenditures. Based on the Citizens United decision, TFE sued the TEC and filed an injunction to keep the TEC from enforcing a long-standing pro- hibition on PACs accepting corporate contributions to use in political expenditures. TFE argued that this prohibi- tion under the circumstances violated the First Amendment as applied to TFE. Ultimately the 5th Circuit agreed, and as a result, the Ethics Commission announced that it would no longer enforce ┬º253.094(a), Election Code and ┬º253.003(b), Election Code in certain circumstances. This case led to the creation of Direct Campaign Expenditure- Only Committees in Texas, which operate like federal Super PACs in that they can accept and pool corporate money from multiple sources and then turn around and spend that money only on direct campaign expenditures supporting or opposing candidates/measures. These committees are still prohibited from using any of the corporate money to contribute to candidates. The issue of dark money contributions and expenditures is still a moving target in regards to regulation, but Ethics Commission rules ┬º22.5 and ┬º22.6 and some ethics opinions referenced below show the recent attempts by the Ethics Commission to reign in hidden political activity. Ex parte Ellis, 309 SW 3d 71 (Tex. Crim. App. 2010) Under this statute, a corporation can contribute money to support or oppose a measure, but only if it gives that money to an entity devoted exclusively to measures, i.e. an entity that does not contribute to candidates. A corporation vio- lates the law if it makes a contribution to a political committee for the purpose of supporting or opposing a measure if that political committee also contributes to candidates. The exclusivity aspect of the provision seems designed to prevent diversion of funds from an acceptable purpose (supporting or opposing a measure) to an unacceptable purpose (supporting or opposing a candidate). A corporation can be confident that it is following the law if the con- tribution is given to a political committee devoted exclusively to measures because that political committee cannot make a contribution to a candidate. And a corporation can be equally confident that a political contribution given to an entity that is not devoted exclusively to measures is a violation of the law unless authorized by another provision of the Election Code. That a particular candidate may be associated with the measure has no effect on this authorization. As we also explained above, it is true that a corporation may not make a political contribution with respect to a measure to a political committee that also contributes to candidates. That is so, regardless of whether or not a particular candidate is associated with the measure in question. We decide that the prohibition against making corporate political contributions on a measure to a mixed-purpose political committee is ΓÇ£closely drawn to match a sufficiently important interest.ΓÇ¥ This prohibition serves to prevent the diversion of corporate ΓÇ£measureΓÇ¥ money to candidates, and thus ensures that the prohibition against corporate contributions to candidates will not be circumvented. The law is narrowly drawn because it addresses a narrow aspect of political association while allowing corporations several alternate avenues for political expression with respect to measures. First and most obviously, a corporation may contribute to a political committee devoted exclu- sively to measures. Second, a corporation may create its own political committee, which can then solicit contributions from the corporationΓÇÖs shareholders, employees, and their families, and any contributions received may then be con- tributed without being subject to corporate limitations. Finally, a corporation may make independent expenditures (e.g., buy its own issue ads), make press releases, and otherwise have its agents directly engage in communication with respect to a measure (or a candidate, for that matter). Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, 558 U.S. 310 (2010) The Supreme Court struck down portions of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (commonly referred to as the ΓÇ£McCain Feingold ActΓÇ¥) and a decision by the U.S. District Court in D.C. from Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce to state that prohibitions on independent expenditures by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment. The ruling upheld restrictions on corporate contributions directly to candidates but freed contributions and unions to spend directly on electioneering communications that advocate for the election or defeat of candidates. This is the seminal case that defined a corporation as a ΓÇ£personΓÇ¥ for the sake of constitutional (namely, First Amendment) protection. Federal Election CommΓÇÖn v. Beaumont, 539 U.S. 146, 123 S.Ct. 2200, 156 L.Ed.2d 179 (2003) Contribution regulations are justified so long as they are ΓÇ£closely drawn to match a sufficiently important interest,ΓÇ¥ while expenditure regulations must be ΓÇ£narrowly tailored to serve a compelling government interest.ΓÇ¥ (p. 161) Osterberg v. Peca, 12 S.W.3d 31 at 43 (Tex., 2000) ΓÇ£Though complexly phrased and structured, the Election Code has an unambiguous intended effect: an individual must report direct expenditures that total over $100 or the unreported expenditures become illegal and the spender may face civil and criminal penalties; if the spender reports the expenditures, he or she faces no penalties. As Peca argues, these provisions operate to impose a reporting requirement on direct campaign expenditures, rather than a ban or ceiling on those expenditures. Because in a candidate election the ultimate burden of these requirements is substantially similar to that of the federal reporting requirements, they fall into the genus of requirements that Buckley upheld as ΓÇ£a reasonable and minimally restrictive method of furthering First Amendment values by opening the basic processes of [the] election system to public view.ΓÇ¥ Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1 at 82 (1976).ΓÇ¥ Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1 (1976) (Overruled by McCutcheon v. FEC) In Buckley, the Court upheld limitations on the amount of money a person may contribute to another personΓÇÖs campaign but struck down limitations on independent expenditures (ΓÇ£direct campaign expendituresΓÇ¥ in Texas). Although a limitation upon the amount of money a person or group may contribute to a candidate or political committee ΓÇ£entails only a marginal restriction upon the contributorΓÇÖs ability to engage in free communication,ΓÇ¥ a limitation upon independent expenditures ΓÇ£heavily burdens core First Amendment expression.ΓÇ¥ The Court found that contribution limitations were sufficiently justified by the danger of corruption or the appearance of corruption, while these dangers were not sufficient to justify limitations on independent expenditures.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: CORPORATE SHAREHOLDERS MAY CAUSE WHOLE LLC TO BE CONSIDERED CORPORATE. A Texas LLC that is owned by a partnership whose shares are publicly traded on an exchange is subject to the Chapter 253 corporate contribution prohibition if any share of the partnership is owned by a corporation. EAO 606. See also EAO 383 (1997), EAO 221 (1994), EAO 215 (1994). COMMON WEB PORTAL BT CORP & CORP- CONTROLLED 	PAC 	FOR 	CONTRIBUTIONS OKAY. Parent organizations that have related entities, including PACs, can use a common payment portal for all organizations. Flowing through corporate payment processing before reaching the PAC account does not violate the prohibition on corporate political activity as long as the corporate payment processing is operating solely as a conduit for contribution acceptance and deliv- ery to the PAC. EAO 581. See also, EAO 181 (1994), EAO 163 (1993), EAO 132 (1993). NONPROFIT 	PRO 	BONO 	LEGAL 	SERVICES TO 	CANDIDATES 	TO 	CHALLENGE 	LAWS UNDER TEC JURISDICTION ARE POLITICAL CONTRIBUTIONS. Legal services provided without charge to candidates or PACs are in-kind contributions. They are not considered permissible discounts under TEC rule 20.66 (which are allowable as long as they are provided across the spectrum in the usual and normal practice of the industry, with no favoritism for those in politics) because it must apply broadly to the industry as a whole. Here, the TEC defined the industry as ΓÇ£legal servicesΓÇ¥, and not ΓÇ£nonprofits that offer pro bono legal servicesΓÇ¥. EAO 580. See also, EAO 574 (2022), EAO 533 (2015), EAO 498 (2011), EAO 433 (2001), EAO 329 (1996), EAO 222 (1994), EAO 219 (1994), EAO 105 (1992). CORPORATE 	ADVERTISEMENTS 	COORDI- NATED WITH CANDIDATES & PARTY ARE PROHIBITED. Texas law prohibits corporations from making campaign contributions, which includes making an expenditure for advertisements coordinated with a candidate or political committee that criticize or praise a candidate or the candidateΓÇÖs opponent. Such advertise- ments are campaign contributions because they consti- tute things of value given with the intent that they be used in connection with a campaign for elected office and with the prior consent or approval of the candidate or committee on whose behalf the expenditure is made. EAO 574 (2022). GPAC MAY NOT USE CORP CONTRIBUTIONS IT RECEIVES TO THEN CONTRIBUTE TO POLITICAL PARTY. While a general purpose com- mittee may accept corporate contributions from corpo- rate sources for administrative & solicitation uses, and a political party may accept corporate contributions for administrative purposes as well, a general purpose committee may not use political contributions accepted from a corporation for its own administrative use to turn around and make a contribution of corporate money to a political party for the partyΓÇÖs administrative costs. EAO 527. See also EAO 489, EAO 383, EAO 221, EAO 176. ΓÇ£PRINCIPAL PURPOSEΓÇ¥ OF A PAC DEPENDS ON CIRCUMSTANCE, BUT 20% OR LESS SAFE HARBOR. A 501(c)(4) nonprofit that plans to make direct campaign expenditures from 20% of its total expenditures and staff time to expressly advocate for the election or defeat of clearly identified candidates for state and local offices in Texas and make no contributions does not have a principal purpose of accepting political contributions or making political expenditures and is not required to register as a political committee. This opin- ion provides a safe harbor at 20%. A political commit- tee is defined as a group with ΓÇ£a principal purpose,ΓÇ¥ as opposed to the principal purpose, of accepting political contributions or making political expenditures. There are a number of factors to rely on when determining a principal purpose: 1. The proportion of the groupΓÇÖs total expenditures that constitute political expenditures; 2. The amount of the groupΓÇÖs staff or volunteer time, equipment, or other resources allocated to making political expenditures; 3. The content of the groupΓÇÖs public statements regard- ing its goals or support of or opposition to candidates, officeholders, or measures; 4. The groupΓÇÖs government filings and organizational documents, including mission statements; and 5. The groupΓÇÖs other activities that are unrelated to making political expenditures. EAO 518. See also EAO 168, EAO 131, EAO 331, EAO 440, EAO 77, EAO 74, EAO 320, EAO 242, EAO 332, EAO 177. See TEC rule 20.1(5), 20.1(14) and 20.1(20). CORPORATION AND CANDIDATE SHARING A COMMON VENDOR. The single fact that a corpora- tion shares a common vendor with a candidate would not constitute a campaign contribution by the corporation to the candidate, but it depends on what the vendor is doing for each client and if they are sharing information. Specifically, if there is a firewall policy in place with the vendor that employees working on one client do not share information with other employees working with other clients, that would be evidence that the corporationΓÇÖs expenditure would not constitute a prohibited campaign contribution (assuming the corporation has not commu- nicated with the candidate regarding the vendor and the expenditures at issue). EAO 503. TEC 	CANNOT 	ENFORCE 	┬º253.094 	OR ┬º253.002 	ELECTION 	CODE 	TO 	PROHIBIT CORPORATIONS/LABOR 	ORGANIZATIONS FROM 	MAKING 	DIRECT 	CAMPAIGN EXPENDITURES. On January 21, 2010, the United States Supreme Court issued an opinion in the case of Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (hereaf- ter, Citizens United), in which it considered the consti- tutionality of certain federal statutes. The legislature intended title 15 to require a corporation, labor organi- zation, or other person that makes one or more direct campaign expenditures from its own property in con- nection with an election of a candidate to comply with section 253.062 as if it were an individual. Therefore, a corporation, labor organization, or other person that makes such expenditures must comply with the disclo- sure requirements that apply to an individual under sec- tion 253.062. EAO 489. See also EAO 331. Superseded by statute: H.B. 2359, 82 nd Leg. R.S. (2011) (amending Elec. Code ┬º┬º253.094, 253.036, 254.061; adding Elec. Code Subchapter J, 254.261, 254.262; repealing Elec. Code ┬º┬º253.002, 253.097, 254.036(f), and Subchapter C, ┬º┬º253.061, 253.062, 253.063) CAMPAIGN MATERIALS AVAILABLE TO COR- PORATIONΓÇÖS EMPLOYEES. A corporation that provides all candidates the same opportunity to make campaign materials available to corporate employees would not be making a campaign contribution. In this context ΓÇ£the same opportunityΓÇ¥ means not only that all candidates must be given the opportunity to provide information, but also that the corporate communications to each candidate regarding the opportunity to provide information must be essentially the same and that the corporation must handle each candidateΓÇÖs information in the same way. EAO 336. See also EAO 198, EAO 327, EAO 37. Superseded, in part, by statuteΓÇöH.B. 2359, 82 nd Leg., R.S. (2011) (amending Elec. Code ┬º┬º253.094, 253.036, 254.061; adding Elec. Code Subchapter J, 254.261, 254.262; repealing Elec. Code ┬º┬º253.002, 253.097, 254.036(f), and Subchapter C, ┬º┬º253.061, 253.062, 253.063) CORPORATE CONTRIBUTIONS TO CANDI- DATE FOR COUNTY CHAIR OF POLITICAL PARTY. Title 15 of the Election Code does not prohibit a corporation from making contributions to a candidate for county chair of a political party. EAO 301. See also EAO 198. Superseded, in part, by statute Acts 2003, 78 th Leg., ch. 249, ┬º2.24, 2.25 (amending Elec. Code ┬º257.005) USE OF COPORATE OWNED AIRPLANE FOR TRAVEL. A member of the legislature may use polit- ical contributions to pay for transportation to and from Austin for legislative purposes. A payment from political contributions to a business in one of the categories listed in section 253.041(a) must not exceed the amount neces- sary to reimburse the business for actual expenditures made by the business. Use of a corporate plane for a charge less than necessary to reimburse the corporation for the use of the plane may be a political contribution in the form of an officeholder contribution. A candidate may use political contributions to pay for transportation for campaign purposes. Because both section 253.041 and section 253.094 would apply to a payment from political contributions for campaign use of the plane in question, the payment to the corporation for use of the plane would have to be in the amount reasonably neces- sary to reimburse the corporation for its expenses. EAO 249. See also, EAO 35, 139. CONTRIBUTION MADE BY PARTNERSHIP & PROFITS 	ATTRIBUTABLE 	TO 	CORPORATE PARTNER. The Federal Election Commission has developed complex regulations governing the appor- tionment and attribution of partnership contributions and expenditures as to the individual partners in order to insure that corporate funds are not spent on political activity in violation of the law. The Ethics Commission believes that any similar treatment of contributions and expenditures under Texas law should result from the legislative process rather than from the Texas Ethics CommissionΓÇÖs rulemaking or advisory opinion func- tions. EAO 221. See also EAO 163, EAO 215, Fed. Elec. Commission AO 1980-132; 11 C.F.R. 110.1(e). ANONYMOUS 	CONTIRUBTION 	TRANSFER- RED 	TO 	A 	REOCOGNIZED 	TAX-EXEMPT CHARITABLE ORGANIZATION. Despite the need to know the source of a political contribution, filers do sometimes receive anonymous contributions. There is no violation of title 15 of the Election Code if a candidate, officeholder, or political committee transfers an anony- mous contribution to a recognized tax-exempt charitable organization. A candidate, officeholder, or political com- mittee is not required to report the anonymous contribu- tion under title 15 of the Election Code. EAO 207. CORPORATE 	EXPENDITURES 	CONSTITU- TING EXPRESS ADVOCACY. A corporation may not make expenditures to communicate concerning an election to its employees, retirees, and their family members if it contains express advocacy. Whether a communication was ΓÇ£express advocacyΓÇ¥ depends on its inclusion of words such as ΓÇ£vote for,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£elect,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£support,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£defeat,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£reject,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£Smith for Congress,ΓÇ¥ etc. Whether an actual communication constitutes express advocacy can be answered only on a case-by-case basis. EAO 198. See also EAO 37, EAO 77. Superseded, in part, by statuteΓÇöH.B. 2359, 82 nd Leg., R.S. (2011) (amending Elec. Code ┬º┬º 253.094, 253.036, 254.061; adding Elec. Code Subchapter J, 254.261, 254.262; repealing Elec. Code ┬º┬º 253.002, 253.097, 254.036(f), and Subchapter C, ┬º┬º 253.061, 253.062, 253.063) LEFTOVER 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	FROM CAMPAIGN DONATED TO TAX-EXEMPT NON- PROFIT. By specifying that the use of campaign con- tributions must not primarily serve individual or family purposes, the legislature has indicated that a use is not a prohibited personal use merely because it may have some incidental benefit to the individual candidate or officeholder. An officeholder may use political contribu- tions left over from a campaign to make a donation to a tax-exempt, nonprofit organization serving physically, mentally, and developmentally challenged citizens with- out violating the prohibition on conversion of political contributions to personal use. EAO 149. See also EAO 47. See generally ┬º253.035, Election Code, ┬º254.204, Election Code. CORPORATE 	ASSETS 	FOR 	CAMPAIGN/ OFFICEHOLDER PURPOSES. A candidate or office- holder may not use corporate assets for campaign or officeholder purposes since the corporationΓÇÖs permitting the candidate or officeholder to use these assets would be a corporate contribution. EAO 116. See also EAO 13, EAO 50. POSTCARDS 	ADVOCATING 	FOR 	SPECIFIC CANDIDATES. Paying for postcards advocating the election of identified candidates is a political expendi- ture. Therefore, a corporation may not make such pay- ments. Such postcards would be ΓÇ£political advertisingΓÇ¥ and the name of an individual or group that entered into an agreement to have the cards printed would have to appear on the postcards as part of the disclosure state- ment. EAO 77. See also EAO 37, EAO 74. Modified by Acts 1993, 73rd Leg., ch. 531, ┬º 2 (amending Elec. Code ┬º 253.032(b)) Modified by Acts 2005, 79th Leg., ch. 1081, ┬º 1 (adding Elec. Code ┬º 254.1541) EXPENDITURE 	OF 	SURPLUS 	CAMPAIGN FUNDS FOR ANY PURPOSES UNDER ┬º254.204 ELECTION CODE. We think the legislature meant to identify certain expenditures that it did not consider to be personal ones even if they are not necessarily political expenditures. Therefore, we conclude that an expendi- ture of political contributions for one of the purposes set out in section 254.204 is not a personal use of political contributions under title 15. EAO 47. See also State Ethics Advisory Commission Opinion No.2. NONPARTISAN NOTICE TO EMPLOYEES RE: UPCOMING ELECTION. An expenditure on a non- partisan notice that contains only nonpartisan material to inform employees about an election and encouraging people to register to vote is not a political expenditure because it is not made in connection with a campaign for an elective office or on a measure, nor is it an office- holder expenditure. Therefore a corporate expenditure to provide such a notice is not prohibited by the Election Code. EAO 37. Superseded, in part, by statuteΓÇöH.B. 2359, 82 nd Leg., R.S. (2011) (amending Elec. Code ┬º┬º 253.094, 253.036, 254.061; adding Elec. Code Subchapter J, 254.261, 254.262; repealing Elec. Code ┬º┬º 253.002, 253.097, 254.036(f), and Subchapter C, ┬º┬º 253.061, 253.062, 253.063)

sections.title: PUNISHMENT OF AGENT
sections.content: An officer, director, or other agent of a corporation or labor organization who commits an offense under this subchapter is punishable for the grade of offense applicable to the corporation or labor organization. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987.

sections.title: CONTRIBUTION ON MEASURE
sections.content: A corporation or labor organization may make campaign contributions from its own property in con- nection with an election on a measure only to a political committee for supporting or opposing measures exclusively. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. cross -refereNce Contributions to Direct Campaign Expenditure Only Committees, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º22.5 P ractice Note Generally, for tax purposes, when a specific purpose PAC is created to be involved in an upcoming ballot measure election, that type of committee would be considered a type of Section 501c4 organization (i.e., to promote social welfare purposes) by the IRS because the SPAC would only be supporting or opposing a ballot measure and none of its activity would be related to supporting or opposing candidates/officeholders (which is what Section 527 PACs do). So when the ballot measure committee is created, then after it gets itsΓÇÖ EIN, it should also file Form 8976 with the IRS. A 501c3 organization should be able to contribute to the 501c4 (the ballot measure committee) as long as the 501c3 can justify that the making of the contribution to the ballot measure committee falls within their c3ΓÇÖs program exempt purposes for which they were organized.

metadata.caseLaw: Cook v. Ministries, 385 S.W.3d 592 (Tex. App. 2012) ΓÇ£Appellees argued that ΓÇ£the circulation and submission of recall petitions by [corporations] represents core First Amendment activityΓÇ¥ and falls within the protection of the Supreme CourtΓÇÖs ruling in Citizens United. In Ex parte Ellis, a post-Citizens United case, the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals determined that Citizens United had no effect upon the jurisprudence relating to corporate contributions. Let us be clear. The Election Code has not and does not prohibit any and all corporate contributions in connection with recall elections. It merely prescribes the parameters under which contributions may be made. Appellees were not barred from pursuing the November 2010 ballot initiative through the special purpose committee known as EPTFV, nor were they banned from speaking. They spoke and spoke loudly. They are not banned from speaking now. They must simply follow the protocol established in the Election Code with which they are already familiar. All they needed to do was ΓÇ£re-purposeΓÇ¥ EPTFV or create a new special purpose committee. ΓÇ£Why?ΓÇ¥, one might ask. Why are these procedures necessary? Citizens United tells us precisely why: The First Amendment protects political speech; and disclosure permits citizens and shareholders to react to the speech of corporate entities in a proper way. This transparency enables the electorate to make informed decisions and give proper weight to different speakers and messages.ΓÇ¥ Ex parte Ellis, 309 SW 3d 71 (Tex. Crim. App. 2010) Under this statute, a corporation can contribute money to support or oppose a measure, but only if it gives that money to an entity devoted exclusively to measures, i.e. an entity that does not contribute to candidates. A corporation vio- lates the law if it makes a contribution to a political committee for the purpose of supporting or opposing a measure if that political committee also contributes to candidates. The exclusivity aspect of the provision seems designed to prevent diversion of funds from an acceptable purpose (supporting or opposing a measure) to an unacceptable purpose (supporting or opposing a candidate). A corporation can be confident that it is following the law if the con- tribution is given to a political committee devoted exclusively to measures because that political committee cannot make a contribution to a candidate. And a corporation can be equally confident that a political contribution given to an entity that is not devoted exclusively to measures is a violation of the law unless authorized by another provision of the Election Code. That a particular candidate may be associated with the measure has no effect on this authorization. As we also explained above, it is true that a corporation may not make a political contribution with respect to a measure to a political committee that also contributes to candidates. That is so, regardless of whether or not a particular candidate is associated with the measure in question. We decide that the prohibition against making corporate political contributions on a measure to a mixed-purpose political committee is ΓÇ£closely drawn to match a sufficiently important interest.ΓÇ¥ This prohibition serves to prevent the diversion of corporate ΓÇ£measureΓÇ¥ money to candidates, and thus ensures that the prohibition against corporate contributions to candidates will not be circumvented. The law is narrowly drawn because it addresses a narrow aspect of political association while allowing corporations several alternate avenues for political expression with respect to measures. First and most obviously, a corporation may contribute to a political committee devoted exclusively to measures. Second, a corporation may create its own political committee, which can then solicit contributions from the corporationΓÇÖs shareholders, employees, and their families, and any contributions received may then be contrib- uted without being subject to corporate limitations. Finally, a corporation may make independent expenditures (e.g., buy its own issue ads), make press releases, and otherwise have its agents directly engage in communication with respect to a measure (or a candidate, for that matter).

sections.title: CONTRIBUTION FROM CORPORATION OR LABOR ORGANIZATION
sections.content: A corporation or labor organization may make campaign contributions from its own property to a political committee that has filed an affidavit with the committeeΓÇÖs campaign treasurer appointment in accordance with Section 252.003(a)(4) or 252.0031(a)(2).

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 2019, 86 th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1127 (H.B. 2586), Sec. 5, eff. September 1, 2019.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: OUT-OF-STATE PAC RUN BY C/OH CANNOT ACCEPT CORPORATE MONEY AND CONTRI- BUTE TO CANDIDATES. The requestor is a politi- cally-active organization that the requestor states meets the definition of a political committee (the Committee). The Committee incorporated for liability purposes only. The Committee is currently controlled by a non-fed- eral Texas candidate and officeholder. The Committee accepts corporate political contributions but maintains those contributions in a separate account from its non-corporate contributions. The Committee uses its corporate contributions to make direct campaign expen- ditures in states where corporate political contributions are prohibited and political contributions in states where corporate contributions are permitted. The committee is not registered with the Federal Election Commission or any other state campaign finance regulator and files its regular contribution and expenditure reports with the Internal Revenue Service. They wish to collect corpo- rate contributions into a separate account and make con- tributions to candidates with its noncorporate account. But because the committee is controlled by a candidate/ officeholder, it cannot complete the required affidavit under ┬º253.097 stating that it is not established or con- trolled by a candidate or officeholder, so it is not legally allowed to make contributions in Texas. It may continue to make direct campaign expenditures, however. EAO 628 (2025).

sections.title: COMMUNICATION WITH STOCKHOLDERS OR MEMBERS
sections.content: (a) 	A corporation or labor organization may make one or more direct campaign expenditures from its own property for the purpose of communicating directly with its stockholders or members, as appli- cable, or with the families of its stockholders or members. (b) 	An expenditure under this section is not reportable under Chapter 254. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. cross -refereNce DefinitionsΓÇöΓÇ£Principal PurposeΓÇ¥, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 26.5 P ractice Notes Keep a keen eye on this statute as well as the two after itΓÇö253.099 and 253.100ΓÇöregarding who the statutes apply to. This section allows a corporation/labor organization to make direct campaign expenditures to communicate with stockholders/members and their respective families. This is specifically worded to allow campaign-related communications for/against a candidate to be financed with corporate dollars as long as it is limited to this restricted class of people. The next section allows a corporation/labor organization to finance expenditures for GOTV and voter registration campaigns aimed at its stockholders/members and their respective families. However, 253.100(b) allows a corpo- ration/labor organization with a connected GPAC to use corporate dollars for PAC solicitations to stockholder/ members and their respective families as well as the corporation/labor organization employees. So while a corporate or labor entity can use corporate resources to solicit their employees for contributions to the PAC, they may not spend corporate resources on voter registration or GOTV aimed at their employees nor could they spend corporate dollars to communicate positions for/against candidates to their employees.

metadata.ethicsOpinions: COMMUNICATIONS TO RESTRICTED CLASS OF CORPORATIONS. The use of corporate resources to allow a particular candidate or a particular candidateΓÇÖs representative to address an audience and advocate his election would be a prohibited corporate contribution to the candidate. This would be true regardless of whether the candidate explicitly solicited contributions to his cam- paign. A corporation may make candidatesΓÇÖ campaign material available to corporate employees if it provides each candidate with the same opportunity to provide information, and handles the information provided in such a way that no candidate is given more advantageous treatment than any other. A corporation may invite all candidates for a particular office to address a corporate audience if all candidates are given the same opportu- nity to appear and the corporation does not endorse any particular candidate or present any candidate in a more advantageous way than any other candidate. An associa- tion may set up a ΓÇ£phone bankΓÇ¥ to urge its restricted class to vote for particular candidates or conduct a partisan get-out-the-vote drive aimed at its restricted class only if they are direct expendituresΓÇöthat is, expenditures made without the prior consent, approval, or cooper- ation of the candidate benefitted. If there is candidate involvement with the phone bank, the expenditures would be prohibited political contributions to the can- didate. Assuming that the preparation and issuance of a press release would involve the use of corporate resources, a press release to the general public would be a prohibited corporate expenditure under Texas law. An expenditure incurred in issuing a press release about the political committeeΓÇÖs political endorsements is not an ΓÇ£administrative expenseΓÇ¥ of a political committee under Election Code section 253.100(a). EAO 340. See also EAO 225, EAO 336, EAO 327, EAO 132, EAO 216. See generally ┬º253.098, Election Code. Affirmed by H.B. 2525, 81st Leg., R.S. (2009) (amending Elec. Code ┬º253.100(a), (c); adding Elec. Code ┬º253.100(d), (e)) DISCLOSURE NOT REQUIRED ON LETTER- HEAD 	STATIONARY 	COMMUNICATED 	TO MEMBERS ONLY. A ΓÇ£memberΓÇ¥ of a farm mutual insurance company, as provided for in chapter 16 of the Insurance Code, is a ΓÇ£memberΓÇ¥ of the farm mutual insurance company for purposes of section 253.098 of the Election Code. Because a disclosure statement is required only in circumstances in which there is a contract or other agreement to print, publish, or broadcast political adver- tising, no disclosure statement is required in the circum- stances described. EAO 227. See also EAO 225. STATE 	ORGANIZATION 	MAY 	SOLICIT CONTRI BUTIONS 	FROM 	MEMBERS 	OF ANY 	AFFILIATED 	INCORPORATED 	LOCAL ORGANIZATION. We can imagine instances in which we might find that the legislature did not intend the term ΓÇ£memberΓÇ¥ to encompass as broad a class as that specified in the bylaws of a membership association. For example, if a corporation defined a member as anyone who lived in Texas or anyone who had contributed to a particular candidate, without requiring the ΓÇ£memberΓÇ¥ to have any voluntary affiliation with the association, we would likely conclude that such members were not ΓÇ£membersΓÇ¥ for purposes of chapter 253 of the Election Code. Moreover, the Texas Chamber of Commerce could solicit contribu- tions from the members of any incorporated local orga- nizations even if those members were not also members of the statewide organization: an incorporated mem- bership association may solicit contributions from the employees and stockholders or members (and the families of employees and stockholders or members) of any of its incorporated members. A solicitation for contributions sent to a corporationΓÇÖs employees in accordance with section 253.100(b) of the Election Code may not contain express advocacy in regard to an identified candidate. EAO 225. See also EAO 223, EAO 163, EAO 168.

sections.title: NONPARTISAN VOTER REGISTRATION AND GET-OUT-THE-VOTE
sections.content: CAMPAIGNS (a) 	A corporation or labor organization may make one or more expenditures to finance nonpartisan voter registration and get-out-the-vote campaigns aimed at its stockholders or members, as applicable, or at the families of its stockholders or members. (b) 	An expenditure under this section is not reportable under Chapter 254. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. P ractice Notes This statute may be unenforceable at least as it relates to elections in which federal candidates are on the ballot. 11 CFR ┬º114.4(d) specifically allows corporations to conduct nonpartisan voter registration and get out the vote drives outside of the corporationΓÇÖs restricted class (stockholders or members + families of both). Additionally, 52 U.S.C. ┬º30143 specifically preempts and supersedes any provision of state law with respect to federal offices.

metadata.ethicsOpinions: CORPORATE FUNDS TO CREATE & MAINTAIN WEBSITE WITH INFO ON CANDIDATES. A corporation may make expenditures for creating and maintaining an Internet site containing photos and information relating to candidates in upcoming elections if all candidates in an election have access to the site on an equal basis and if the site is not used to support or oppose any candidate. EAO 327. See also EAO 198.

sections.title: EXPENDITURES FOR GENERAL-PURPOSE COMMITTEE
sections.content: (a) 	A corporation, acting alone or with one or more other corporations, may make one or more politi- cal expenditures to finance the establishment or administration of a general-purpose committee. In addition to any other expenditure that is considered permissible under this section, a corporation may make an expenditure for the maintenance and operation of a general-purpose committee, including an expenditure for: (1) 	office space maintenance and repairs; (2) 	telephone and Internet services; (3) 	office equipment; (4) 	utilities; (5) 	general office and meeting supplies; (6) 	salaries for routine clerical, data entry, and administrative assistance necessary for the proper administrative operation of the committee; (7) 	legal and accounting fees for the committeeΓÇÖs compliance with this title; (8) 	routine administrative expenses incurred in establishing and administering a general-purpose political committee; (9) 	management and supervision of the committee, including expenses incurred in holding meetings of the committeeΓÇÖs governing body to interview candidates and make endorsements relating to the committeeΓÇÖs support; (10) the recording of committee decisions; (11) 	expenses incurred in hosting candidate forums in which all candidates for a particular office in an election are invited to participate on the same terms; (12) expenses incurred in preparing and delivering committee contributions; or (13) creation and maintenance of the committeeΓÇÖs public Internet web pages that do not contain polit- ical advertising. (b) 	A corporation may make political expenditures, including fully or partially matching contributions to an organization that is exempt from federal income tax under Section 501(c)(3), Internal Revenue Code of 1986, to finance the solicitation of political contributions to a general-purpose committee assisted under Subsection (a) from the stockholders, employees, or families of stockholders or employ- ees of one or more corporations. (c) 	A labor organization may engage in activity authorized for a corporation by this section. For purposes of this section, the members of a labor organization are considered to be corporate stockholders. (d) 	A corporation or labor organization may not make expenditures under this section for: (1) 	political consulting to support or oppose a candidate; (2) 	telephoning or telephone banks to communicate with the public; (3) 	brochures and direct mail supporting or opposing a candidate; (4) 	partisan voter registration and get-out-the-vote drives; (5) 	political fund-raising other than from its stockholders or members, as applicable, or the families of its stockholders or members; (6) 	voter identification efforts, voter lists, or voter databases that include persons other than its stock- holders or members, as applicable, or the families of its stockholders or members; (7) 	polling designed to support or oppose a candidate other than of its stockholders or members, as applicable, or the families of its stockholders or members; or (8) 	recruiting candidates. (e) 	Subsection (d) does not apply to a corporation or labor organization making a campaign contribution to a political committee under Section 253.097 or an expenditure to communicate with its stock- holders or members, as applicable, or with the families of its stockholders or members as provided by Section 253.098. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 2003, 78th Leg., ch. 249, Sec. 2.26, eff. Sept. 1, 2003. Amended by Acts 2009, 81st Leg., R.S., Ch. 1306 (H.B. 2525), Sec. 1, eff. June 19, 2009. Amended by Acts 2019, 86th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1127 (H.B. 2586), Sec. 6, eff. September 1, 2019. Acts 2019, 86th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1239 (H.B. 3044), Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2019. cross -refereNce Name of General-Purpose Committee, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.409 Contributions to Direct Campaign Expenditure Only Committees, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º22.5 Corporations and Certain Associations Covered, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 24.1 Designation of Contribution for Administrative Purposes, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º24.18. P ractice Notes Note EAO 615 below: This is an important opinion for anyone in a trade association or nonprofit with a PAC. The requestor in this opinion was a nonprofit that defined ΓÇ£memberΓÇ¥ as anyone who ΓÇ£is informed by the NonprofitΓÇÖs website of the NonprofitΓÇÖs goals, checks a box indicating support of the NonprofitΓÇÖs goals, and then provides contact information to the corporation.ΓÇ¥ The TEC said in the opinion that the organizationΓÇÖs governing documents must also provide some rights in the organization to a person for that person to be considered a member. Other than that, the restrictions are minimal. The TEC even specifically discounted an FEC opinion as too restrictive because it required the member to have governance rights to confer membership. All corporate entities with a PAC should review this opinion and seek legal advice on how to adjust your bylaws regarding membership to make it easier for people to sign up. Doing so could gain you hundreds new ΓÇ£membersΓÇ¥ that could then be solicited for political contributions to your PAC. attorNey G eNeral oPiNioNs PUBLIC EMPLOYEE PAYROLL DEDUCTION REQUIRES SPECIFIC AUTHORIZATION. SCOTUS held in Janus v. American Federation of State, County, & Municipal Employees that a public employer may not deduct a fee from an employeeΓÇÖs wages to pay union fees or dues unless the employee affirmatively consents to pay. At a minimum, public employers must ensure that employee consent to a payroll deduction for membership fees or dues in a union or employee organization is voluntary, and a one-time perpetual consent is insufficient. [Ed.Note: Many groups want to do payroll deductions for PAC contributions, so this opinion is useful at least to see that the AGΓÇÖs office and SCOTUS are very specific about getting consent for these types of payroll deductions, even if it is limited here to public employers and union dues.] AttΓÇÖy Gen. Op. KP-0310 (2020)

metadata.caseLaw: Ex parte Ellis, 309 S.W. 3d 71 (Tex. Crim. App., 2010) ΓÇ£Under ┬º 253.100, a corporation may create its own political committee. The corporation may then use this political committee to solicit contributions from shareholders, employees, and their families. The corporation is permitted to make expenditures for the maintenance and operation of the committee. The Legislature set out a list of twelve items included as qualifying expenditures (e.g., office equipment and utilities) and a list of eight items for which expenditures may not be made. It appears that contributions made by a corporation to such a committee would not be considered to be expenditures. But even assuming that they could be considered the same, it is nevertheless clear that ┬º 253.100 contemplates expenditures made by a corporation for certain purposes. A contribution with no strings attached would not qualify as such an expenditure. To the extent that the court of appeals may have suggested that there is no such thing as an undesignated corporate political contribution, the error it made was minor. It would be more accurate to say that there is no such thing as a legal undesignated corporate political contribution. Individuals can legally make undesignated political contributions, but corporations cannot. A corporation must designate the purpose of the political contribution by contributing to a political committee that is exclusively devoted to measures, by making expenditures for maintenance or operation of a corporate political committee, or by contributing to a political party under certain narrowly defined conditions.ΓÇ¥ (p. 88) Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, 558 U.S. 310 (2010) The Supreme Court struck down portions of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (commonly referred to as the ΓÇ£McCain Feingold ActΓÇ¥) and a decision by the U.S. District Court in D.C. from Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce to state that prohibitions on independent expenditures by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment. The ruling upheld restrictions on corporate contributions directly to candidates but freed contributions and unions to spend directly on electioneering communications that advocate for the election or defeat of candidates. This is the seminal case that defined a corporation as a ΓÇ£personΓÇ¥ for the sake of constitutional (namely, First Amendment) protection. Fed. Election CommΓÇÖn v. NatΓÇÖl Right to Work Comm., 459 U.S. 197, 202 (1982) (analyzing the federal analog to Section 253.100(d)). A non-profit corporation without capital stock established a separate segregated fund, as required by 2 USCS 441b(b) (4)(C), in order to receive and make contributions on behalf of federal candidates. The corporation sent letters to individuals who had at one time contributed to the corporation, soliciting contributions to the fund. Another lobby- ing group subsequently filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission, asserting that the corporation had solicited contributions from persons who were not stockholders, executive or administrative personnel of the corpora- tion, or their families, in violation of the solicitation restrictions of 441b(b)(4). The corporation took the position that the recipients of its solicitation letters were ΓÇ£membersΓÇ¥ of the corporation within the meaning of the proviso set forth in 441b(b)(4)(C), and that it therefore did not violate the restrictions on the use of corporate funds to solicit contribu- tions. The Commission determined that there was probable cause to believe that the corporation had violated 441b by soliciting contributions from persons who were not its members. The District Court agreed, but the judgment of the District Court was reversed by the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which held that the term ΓÇ£memberΓÇ¥ must be given an elastic definition in order to prevent impermissible interference with associational rights. SCOTUS held that (1) the corporationΓÇÖs solicitations were not limited to its members, since those solicited were insufficiently attached to the corporate structure of the corporation to qualify as ΓÇ£membersΓÇ¥ under 2 USCS 441b(b)(4)(C), the solicitation letter making no reference to members, the members playing no part in the operation or administration of the corporation, and having no control of the expenditure of their contributions, and moreover, the corporationΓÇÖs own articles of incorporation explicitly disclaiming the existence of members.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: DEFINITION OF ΓÇ£MEMBERΓÇ¥ FOR CORPORATE PAC FUNDRAISING PURPOSES. To be a member of a nonprofit for purposes of Section 253.100(d)(5), an indi- vidual must 1) satisfy the requirements for membership as specified by the organizationΓÇÖs governing documents; 2) affirmatively accept the organizationΓÇÖs invitation to become a member; and 3) be conferred some rights in the organization. EAO 615. See also, EAO 495 (2010), EAO 383 (1997), EAO 239 (1994). POLITICAL PARTY COPORATE CONTRI BU- TIONS FOR ADMIN EXPENSES. The requestor represents a political party. The requestor would like to use funds from corporations or labor organizations to pay a contractorΓÇÖs invoice. Specifically, the requestor stated that the contractor would be ΓÇ£developing admin- istrative tools (spreadsheets, budgets, etc.) and a hiring plan related to [the] partyΓÇÖs coordinated campaign.ΓÇ¥ The spreadsheets would be used to track budget and cash flow. The political party may use funds from corpora- tions or labor organizations to pay a contractorΓÇÖs invoice because the contractor provided normal administrative services. EAO 611. See also, EAO 604 (2024), EAO 272 (DATE), EAO 176 (1993). PAC MAY USE CORPORATE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PAY FOR LOBBYIST. A committee that is oper- ated and maintained by a corporation and receives cor- porate money for administrative purposes (but not given specifically to compensate a lobbyist) may use a portion of its corporate contributions to hire a lobbyist. Although the acceptance of the corporate contributions must be disclosed as political contributions to the committee, the committeeΓÇÖs use of the contributions to hire a lobbyist would be a nonpolitical purpose for the use of those funds, and would not be regulated by title 15. EAO 528. See also EAO 131, EAO 168. GPAC MAY NOT USE CORP CONTRIBUTIONS IT RECEIVES TO THEN CONTRIBUTE TO POLITICAL PARTY. While a general purpose com- mittee may accept corporate contributions from corpo- rate sources for administrative & solicitation uses, and a political party may accept corporate contributions for administrative purposes as well, a general purpose committee may not use political contributions accepted from a corporation for its own administrative use to turn around and make a contribution of corporate money to a political party for the partyΓÇÖs administrative costs. EAO 527. See also EAO 489, EAO 383, EAO 221, EAO 176. PARENT 	CORPORATION 	MAY 	SOLICIT EMPLOYEES FROM SUBSIDIARY OF PARENT. A parent for-profit corporation that assists a gener- al-purpose committee under section 253.100(a) may solicit political contributions to the committee from the employees of a subsidiary for-profit corporation that it wholly owns and operates. EAO 509. See also EAO 447, EAO 225, EAO 223. GPAC 	CORPORATE 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	TO DEFRAY LAWSUIT EXPENSES. A general-pur- pose political committee may accept contributions from corporations to defray expenses incurred in defending against defamation lawsuits filed against the committee and its campaign treasurer. Such contribu- tions must be disclosed on the committeeΓÇÖs campaign finance reports. This conclusion is specifically limited to the stipulated facts set out herein. (Here, TEC stated that expenses in defending other lawsuits may not be considered administrative expenses, but that the facts herein supported the administrative argument). EAO 497. See also EAO 132, EAO 216. SOLICITING 	RESTRICTED 	CLASS 	FOR CONTRIBUTIONS TO AFFILIATED PAC. A cor- poration may make political expenditures to finance the solicitation of political contributions to a general-pur- pose committee assisted under section 253.100(a) from the stockholders, employees, or families of stockholders or employees of one or more corporations. EAO 485. PROMISING 	TO 	MATCH 	CONTRIBUTIONS AND DONATE TO CHARITY. An incorporated 501(c)(6) trade association and its corporate members may not do a ΓÇ£charitable match solicitation programΓÇ¥ in which the corporate members make contributions (dollar for dollar or otherwise) to one of three charities chosen in advance by an individual for any contributions the indi- vidual makes to the associationΓÇÖs PAC. EAO 475. See also EAO 280, EAO 217, EAO 362. Overruled by Tex. H.B. 3044, 86 th Leg., R.S. (2019), effective September 1, 2019 (amending Election Code, ┬º 253.100(b)) CANDIDATES 	CAN 	SPEAK 	TO 	MEMBERS, BUT MUST CONTROL WHAT THEY SAY, NO CAMPAIGN TALK. An incorporated organization with incorporated chapters may invite elected officials to address the organizationΓÇÖs membership regarding issues of interest to the membership if the intent of the organization is that it is not political in nature and if the officeholder does not create or control the presentation as a forum to communicate with his or her constituents or potential voters. The officeholder would not be creating or controlling a presentation as a forum to communicate with his or her constituents or potential voters if the orga- nization sets out to the officeholder the issues of interest to the membership and the officeholder addresses only those issues. We caution, however, that the organization would be making a prohibited political contribution by allowing the officeholder to essentially create or control the speaking engagement as a forum to communicate with his or her constituents or potential voters. The orga- nization would not be required to invite the officeholderΓÇÖs opponent to the speaking engagement. EAO 471. See also EAO 346, EAO 144. DELIVERING 	POLITICAL 	CONTRIBUTION FROM GPAC. An expenditure made by a corporation to deliver a political contribution in the form of a check from a general-purpose political committee to a candi- date would constitute an administrative expenditure if the delivery originates and is completed in the state of Texas. EAO 468. See also EAO 132. Affirmed by HB 2525 (2009), amending ┬º253.100 (a) & (c), add- ing ┬º253.100 (d) & (e) CORPORATE SOLICITABLE CLASS EXTENDS TO CORPORATE MEMBERS/STOCKHOLDERS, NOT TO THOSE CORPORATIONSΓÇÖ EMPLOYEES, FAMILIES OF EMPLOYEES. If a stockholder or mem- ber of a corporation is a business entity not subject to the restrictions in section 253.094 of the Election Code, the corporationΓÇÖs solicitable class does not include the own- ers or employees of the business or to the families of the owners and employees. The political committee itself, of course, may solicit contributions from the owners or employees of the business or the families of the owners and employees. EAO 447. See also EAO 225, EAO 223, EAO 163. POLITICAL 	PARTY 	GPAC 	MAY 	ACCEPT CORPORATE 	MONEY 	EARMARKED 	FOR SCHOLARSHIP FUND. A general-purpose political committee may accept corporate contributions ear- marked for a scholarship fund as long as the committeeΓÇÖs expenditures in connection with the scholarship fund are not made in connection with a campaign for elective office or on a measure or for officeholder purposes. EAO 409. See also EAO 131, EAO 132, EAO 168. ANYTHING SOLD TO CANDIDATES BELOW FAIR MARKET VALUE OF COST. It is critical that the terms of a contract between a corporation and a can- didate be typical of the terms the corporation offers to political and non-political customers. Because the cor- porate producer described in the request letter has no history of comparable transactions with other non-po- litical customers, we cannot conclude that the proposed transaction is permissible. EAO 398. See also EAO 35, EAO 143. GIFT TO COUNTY/DISTRICT CLERKS FROM CORPORATION 	TO 	DEFRAY 	ELECTION EXPENSES. A contribution from a corporation to a county or district clerk that is intended to defray the clerkΓÇÖs costs of running for an elective position with an association of county or district clerks is a prohibited ΓÇ£officeholder contributionΓÇ¥ unless the costs are reim- bursable with public money. For purposes of Penal Code section 36.08(d), a county or district clerk exercises discretion in regard to purchasing matters by making recommendations to the commissioners court even if the commissioners court makes the final decisions about purchasing matters. EAO 396. See also EAO 75, EAO 63, EAO 61, EAO 36. LABOR ORGANIZATION & REQUESTS FROM MEMBERS TO SEND PORTION OF DUES PAC. A labor organization would be making a political contribu- tion to a political committee if it honored a request from its members to transfer a portion of a memberΓÇÖs required membership dues to the political committee. EAO 379. See also EAO 132, EAO 38. INSURANCE COMPANY POLICYHOLDERS ARE ΓÇ£MEMBERSΓÇ¥ OF THE SOLICITABLE CLASS. Texas law expressly permits an insurance company to make political expenditures to solicit its ΓÇ£membersΓÇ¥ to contribute to a general-purpose political committee. Because its policyholders are its ΓÇ£members,ΓÇ¥ an Ohio domestic mutual insurance company may make expen- ditures to solicit contributions from its policyholders to its Texas general-purpose political committee. EAO 367. See also EAO 227. NOT ALL INDUCEMENTS TO CONTRIBUTE TO A PAC ARE CONSIDERED SOLICITATION COSTS. Awarding a prize in the form of a transfer of corporate money to an employee activity fund for an employee group that outperforms other employee groups in making contributions to the corporationΓÇÖs general-pur- pose political committee is not necessarily a ΓÇ£solicitation costΓÇ¥ for purposes of section 253.100(b). ΓÇ£Small token prizesΓÇ¥ for winning a skill contest at the event are per- missible solicitation costs. This is not a blanket approval, and is limited to the circumstances in the opinion. EAO 362. See also EAO 280. EARMARK 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	ONLY 	FOR ADMINISTRATIVE PURPOSES AT REQUEST OF CONTRIBUTOR. Whether a general-purpose political committee is willing to honor a request to use a contribution from an individual for administrative purposes only is a matter between the contributor and the committee. A contribution from an individual to a general-purpose political committee that is earmarked for administrative purposes must be reported. EAO 344. See also EAO 132. COMMUNICATIONS TO RESTRICTED CLASS OF CORPORATIONS. The use of corporate resources to allow a particular candidate or a particular candi- dateΓÇÖs representative to address an audience and advo- cate his election would be a prohibited corporate contri- bution to the candidate. This would be true regardless of whether the candidate explicitly solicited contributions to his campaign. A corporation may make candidatesΓÇÖ campaign material available to corporate employees if it provides each candidate with the same opportunity to provide information, and handles the information provided in such a way that no candidate is given more advantageous treatment than any other. A corpora- tion may invite all candidates for a particular office to address a corporate audience if all candidates are given the same opportunity to appear and the corporation does not endorse any particular candidate or present any candidate in a more advantageous way than any other candidate. An association may set up a ΓÇ£phone bankΓÇ¥ to urge its restricted class to vote for particular candidates or conduct a partisan get-out-the-vote drive aimed at its restricted class only if they are direct expendituresΓÇö that is, expenditures made without the prior consent, approval, or cooperation of the candidate benefitted. If there is candidate involvement with the phone bank, the expenditures would be prohibited political contributions to the candidate. Assuming that the preparation and issuance of a press release would involve the use of corpo- rate resources, a press release to the general public would be a prohibited corporate expenditure under Texas law. An expenditure incurred in issuing a press release about the political committeeΓÇÖs political endorsements is not an ΓÇ£administrative expenseΓÇ¥ of a political committee under Election Code section 253.100(a). EAO 340. See also EAO 225, EAO 336, EAO 327, EAO 132, EAO 216. See generally ┬º253.098, Election Code. Affirmed by H.B. 2525, 81st Leg., R.S. (2009) (amending Elec. Code ┬º253.100(a), (c); adding Elec. Code ┬º253.100(d), (e)) CANDIDATESΓÇÖ 	CAMPAIGN 	MATERIALS AVAILABLE TO CORPORATIONΓÇÖS EMPLOYEES. A corporation that provides all candidates the same opportunity to make campaign materials available to corporate employees would not be making a campaign contribution. In this context ΓÇ£the same opportunityΓÇ¥ means not only that all candidates must be given the opportunity to provide information, but also that the corporate communications to each candidate regarding the opportunity to provide information must be essen- tially the same and that the corporation must handle each candidateΓÇÖs information in the same way. EAO 336. See also EAO 198, EAO 327, EAO 37. Superseded, in part, by statuteΓÇöH.B. 2359, 82 nd Leg., R.S. (2011) (amending Elec. Code ┬º┬º253.094, 253.036, 254.061; adding Elec. Code Subchapter J, 254.261, 254.262; repealing Elec. Code ┬º┬º253.002, 253.097, 254.036(f), and Subchapter C, ┬º┬º253.061, 253.062, 253.063) WEBSITE WITH INFORMATION ON CANDI- DATES. A corporation may make expenditures for cre- ating and maintaining an Internet site containing photos and information relating to candidates in upcoming elections if all candidates in an election have access to the site on an equal basis and if the site is not used to support or oppose any candidate. EAO 327. See also EAO 198. ARTICLE 	DISTRIBUTED 	TO 	EDUCATE MEMBERS ABOUT CORPORATIONΓÇÖS PAC. An article published in a magazine distributed by a nonprofit association may be a solicitation of contributions to the political committee, depending on the particular facts and the content of the article. Even if it is a solicitation, Election Code section 253.100 permits the corporation to finance the article if the article is being sent only to the corporationΓÇÖs members. EAO 290. See also EAO 280. INCORPORATED 	HOSPITAL 	FUNDRAISER FOR GPAC. An incorporated hospital may finance the costs of green fees and small token prizes in connection with a golf tournament fundraiser for the hospitalΓÇÖs general-purpose committee to the extent that costs are attributable to stockholders or employees of the hospital or to the families of stockholders or employees. The hos- pital may pay for t-shirts sold to corporate employees and their families to raise funds for the political committee if the sale complies with the Federal Election CommissionΓÇÖs ΓÇ£one-thirdΓÇ¥ rule. T-shirts paid for by the hospital may be sold only to stockholders and employees of the hospital or to the families of stockholders and employees. EAO 280. See also EAO 163. CORPORATE CONTRIBUTIONS AND EXPEN- DITURES 	IN 	OTHER 	STATES. 	Although 	the restrictions on corporate political activity do not specify that they apply only to activity in connection with Texas elections, Title 15 of the Texas Election Code does not prohibit a Texas corporation from making contributions and expenditures in connection with elections in other states. EAO 277. See also EAO 208. POLITICAL PARTY CORPORATE CONTRIBU- TIONS FOR VOTER REGISTRATION DRIVES & ADS. ΓÇ£Normal overhead and administrative or oper- ating costsΓÇ¥ describe items such as expenditures for office space, utilities, and other usual costs of operating an organization. Neither brochures which describe a par- tyΓÇÖs philosophy and functions and includes solicitations for membership, contributions, and participation in the partyΓÇÖs primary nor expenditures for voter registration drives can be considered overhead or administrative costs. Therefore, a political party may not use corporate contributions for either of those purposes. EAO 272. See also EAO 176, EAO 177, EAO 37. Affirmed by H.B. 2525, 81st Leg., R.S. (2009) (amending Elec. Code ┬º253.100(a), (c); adding Elec. Code ┬º253.100(d), (e)) NONPROFIT CORPORATION FORMED FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES MUST REGISTER AS PAC AND REPORT. An officeholder who wishes to produce and distribute a newsletter as an officeholder activity cannot be reimbursed from public money to do so. As such, the expenditures would be subject to the campaign finance reporting requirements. Using a non- profit corporation established by various benefactors to produce the newsletter requires that it state in its official incorporation documents that it is a political committee incorporating for liability purposes only and that its only principal purpose is accepting political contributions and making political expenditures. Otherwise it would be a prohibited corporate contribution. EAO 242. STATE ORGANIZATION SOLICITING FROM MEMBERS 	OF 	ANY 	AFFILIATED 	INCOR- PORATED LOCAL ORGANIZATION. We can imagine instances in which we might find that the leg- islature did not intend the term ΓÇ£memberΓÇ¥ to encom- pass as broad a class as that specified in the bylaws of a membership association. For example, if a corporation defined a member as anyone who lived in Texas or anyone who had contributed to a particular candidate, without requiring the ΓÇ£memberΓÇ¥ to have any voluntary affiliation with the association, we would likely conclude that such members were not ΓÇ£membersΓÇ¥ for purposes of chapter 253 of the Election Code. Moreover, the Texas Chamber of Commerce could solicit contributions from the members of any incorporated local organizations even if those members were not also members of the statewide organization: an incorporated membership association may solicit contributions from the employ- ees and stockholders or members (and the families of employees and stockholders or members) of any of its incorporated members. A solicitation for contributions sent to a corporationΓÇÖs employees in accordance with section 253.100(b) of the Election Code may not contain express advocacy in regard to an identified candidate. EAO 225. See also EAO 223, EAO 163, EAO 168. FUNDS 	CONTRIBUTED 	BY 	CORPORATE MEMBERS TO SOLICIT ENTIRE SOLICITABLE CLASS. The solicitable class of an incorporated associ- ation includes the solicitable class of each of its member corporations. That conclusion applies to the solicitable class of any corporate member of the incorporated associ- ation described in the request letter. The general-purpose committee may use funds contributed by corporate members to solicit the entire solicitable class of the incor- porated association (including any solicitable classes of member corporations). EAO 223. See also EAO 163. EAO 217, EAO 225, EAO 132. CONTRIBUTION 	MADE 	BY 	PARTNERSHIP ATTRIBUTABLE TO A CORPORATE PARTNER. The Federal Election Commission has developed com- plex regulations governing the apportionment and attribution of partnership contributions and expen- ditures as to the individual partners in order to insure that corporate funds are not spent on political activity in violation of the law. The Ethics Commission believes that any similar treatment of contributions and expendi- tures under Texas law should result from the legislative process rather than from the Texas Ethics CommissionΓÇÖs rulemaking or advisory opinion functions. 	EAO 221. See also EAO 163, EAO 215, Fed. Elec. Commission AO 1980-132; 11 C.F.R. 110.1(e). PAYROLL DEDUCTION PLAN FOR EMPLOYEES TO CONTRIBUTE TO ASSOCIATED PAC. The corporation may also finance a payroll deduction plan benefitting the political committee of a trade association to which the corporation belongs and pays membership dues. The dues deposited in the trade associationΓÇÖs trea- sury finance the associationΓÇÖs activities, including the administration of its political committee. In this way, the member corporation ΓÇ£assistsΓÇ¥ the associationΓÇÖs political committee for purposes of Election Code section 253.100, permitting the corporation to solicit contributions to that committee. Assuming that a portion of the dues paid to a local chapter benefit the state organization, or that the corporate members otherwise pay dues to the state organization, we conclude the corporation may use its payroll deduction plan to solicit contributions to the state organizationΓÇÖs political committee as well. The families of the stockholders and employees may be solicited as well. EAO 217. See also EAO 163, EAO 132. ADMINISTRATIVE FINE LEVIED BY ETHICS COMMISSION 	AGAINST 	ASSOCIATED 	PAC TREASURER. Payment of a late fine is an admin- istrative expense because it is not directly related to a committeeΓÇÖs support of or opposition to candidates or measures. Therefore, a corporation may use treasury funds to pay an administrative fine assessed under title 15 against the treasurer of a general-purpose committee that the corporation sponsors. EAO 216. See also EAO 206, EAO 132. Affirmed by H.B. 2525, 81st Leg., R.S. (2009) (amending Elec. Code ┬º253.100(a), (c); adding Elec. Code ┬º253.100(d), (e)) JOINT VENTURE WHOSE PART-OWNER IS A CORPORATION. If a joint venture owned in part by a corporation made political contributions, corporate funds would be used to finance political activity. Moving the funds through a non-corporate account would not alter their corporate nature. Letter from John Hannah, Jr., Texas Secretary of State, to Charles E. Burt, Burt & Company, Inc., P.C.
