metadata.caseLaw: King Street Patriots et. al. v. Texas Democratic Party et. al., No. 15-0320 (Tex. June 30, 2017) ΓÇ£Adhering to the United States Supreme CourtΓÇÖs decision in Federal Election Commission v. Beaumont, as we are obliged to do, we conclude that legislatively enacted bans on corporate political contributions are constitutional under the First Amendment.ΓÇ¥ (p.4) ΓÇ£Section 253.094ΓÇÖs current incarnation reflects a 2011 amendment that removed a limitation on political expenditures in response to the United States Supreme CourtΓÇÖs decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission. Restrictions on corporate political contribu- tions remained intact, however, presumably because the Supreme CourtΓÇÖs Citizens United decision did not overturn its earlier holding in Federal Election Commission v. Beaumont that laws barring corporate political contributions are ΓÇ£consistent with the First AmendmentΓÇ¥ and are not subject to strict scrutinyΓÇ¥ (p.21) Only the Supreme Court has the ΓÇ£prerogative . . . to overrule one of its precedents.ΓÇ¥ Thus even if BeaumontΓÇÖs rationale is in doubt, we are bound to follow it unless and until the Supreme Court overrules it. Our unan- imous acknowledgment that Beaumont is binding Supreme Court precedent terminates our inquiryΓÇªOur role is simply to ΓÇ£say what the law is,ΓÇ¥ not prognosticate how the law could change. Applying Beaumont, we conclude sections 253.091 and 253.094 of the Texas Election Code are not unconstitutional.ΓÇ¥ (p.22) Van Hollen v. FEC, Nos. 15-5016, 15-5017 (D.C. Cir. 2016) The regulation in question (11 CFR 104.20(c)(9)) requires disclosure of only those donations made for the purpose of furthering electioneering communications. In reversing the U.S. District Court for the District of ColumbiaΓÇÿs 2014 decision, the appellate court upheld the Commission regulation as a reasonable interpretation of the disclosure provisions of the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA). In analyzing whether the regulation was ΓÇ£arbitrary and capricious,ΓÇ¥ the opinion described the CommissionΓÇÖs three explanations for the purpose requirement: ΓÇó 	A ΓÇ£Support Rationale.ΓÇ¥ Without the purpose requirement, individual contributors to a union or corporation who do not support the entityΓÇÖs electioneering communications could be mistakenly characterized as support- ing the messages. ΓÇó 	A ΓÇ£Burden Rationale.ΓÇ¥ The purpose requirement ensures disclosing entities are not obliged to create an exhaustive list of every individual who provided more than $1,000, which could be very costly and require an inordinate amount of effort. ΓÇó 	A ΓÇ£Privacy Rationale.ΓÇ¥ The Commission tailored its regulations in a way that both effectuates the lawΓÇÿs disclo- sure requirements and protects the constitutional interests in privacy. The court concluded, ΓÇ£Because we can reasonably discern the FECΓÇÖs analytical path from these three rationales, we uphold its purpose requirement against Van HollenΓÇÖs challenge.ΓÇ¥ Catholic Leadership Coalition of Texas v. Reisman, 764 F. 3d 409 (5th Cir. 2014) This case invalidated the 60 day layout period and 10 contributor minimum required before making over $500 in expenditures by a PAC. See practice notes of 20.401(d) of these rules for a full explanation of this case. Texans for Free Enterprise v. Texas Ethics Commission, 732 F. 3d 535 (5th Cir. 2013) Texans for Free Enterprise (TFE) was a political committee which, by its own admission, did not have any intention on making contributions to candidates but rather only made direct campaign expenditures. Based on the Citizens United decision, TFE sued the TEC and filed an injunction to keep the TEC from enforcing a long-standing pro- hibition on PACs accepting corporate contributions to use in political expenditures. TFE argued that this prohibi- tion under the circumstances violated the First Amendment as applied to TFE. Ultimately the 5th Circuit agreed, and as a result, the Ethics Commission announced that it would no longer enforce ┬º253.094(a), Election Code and ┬º253.003(b), Election Code in certain circumstances. This case led to the creation of Direct Campaign Expenditure- Only Committees in Texas, which operate like federal Super PACs in that they can accept and pool corporate money from multiple sources and then turn around and spend that money only on direct campaign expenditures supporting or opposing candidates/measures. These committees are still prohibited from using any of the corporate money to contribute to candidates. The issue of dark money contributions and expenditures is still a moving target in regards to regulation, but Ethics Commission rules ┬º22.5 and ┬º22.6 and some ethics opinions referenced below show the recent attempts by the Ethics Commission to reign in hidden political activity. Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, 558 U.S. 310 (2010) The Supreme Court struck down portions of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (commonly referred to as the ΓÇ£McCain Feingold ActΓÇ¥) and a decision by the U.S. District Court in D.C. from Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce to state that prohibitions on independent expenditures by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment. The ruling upheld restrictions on corporate contributions directly to candidates but freed contributions and unions to spend directly on electioneering communications that advocate for the election or defeat of candidates. This is the seminal case that defined a corporation as a ΓÇ£personΓÇ¥ for the sake of constitutional (namely, First Amendment) protection. Federal Election CommΓÇÿn v. Beaumont, 539 U.S. 146, 123 S.Ct. 2200, 156 L.Ed.2d 179 (2003) Contribution regulations are justified so long as they are ΓÇ£closely drawn to match a sufficiently important interest,ΓÇ¥ while expenditure regulations must be ΓÇ£narrowly tailored to serve a compelling government interest.ΓÇ¥ (p. 161) Osterberg v. Peca, 12 S.W.3d 31 at 43 (Tex., 2000) ΓÇ£Though complexly phrased and structured, the Election Code has an unambiguous intended effect: an individual must report direct expenditures that total over $100 or the unreported expenditures become illegal and the spender may face civil and criminal penalties; if the spender reports the expenditures, he or she faces no penalties. As Peca argues, these provisions operate to impose a reporting requirement on direct campaign expenditures, rather than a ban or ceiling on those expenditures. Because in a candidate election the ultimate burden of these requirements is substantially similar to that of the federal reporting requirements, they fall into the genus of requirements that Buckley upheld as ΓÇ£a reasonable and minimally restrictive method of furthering First Amendment values by opening the basic processes of [the] election system to public view.ΓÇ¥ Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1 at 82 (1976).ΓÇ¥ Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1 (1976) In Buckley, the Court upheld limitations on the amount of money a person may contribute to another personΓÇÿs campaign but struck down limitations on independent expenditures (ΓÇ£direct campaign expendituresΓÇ¥ in Texas). Although a limitation upon the amount of money a person or group may contribute to a candidate or political committee ΓÇ£entails only a marginal restriction upon the contributorΓÇÿs ability to engage in free communication,ΓÇ¥ a limitation upon independent expenditures ΓÇ£heavily burdens core First Amendment expression.ΓÇ¥ The Court found that contribution limitations were sufficiently justified by the danger of corruption or the appearance of corruption, while these dangers were not sufficient to justify limitations on independent expenditures.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: ΓÇ£PRINCIPAL PURPOSEΓÇ¥ OF A PAC DEPENDS ON CIRCUMSTANCE, BUT 20% OR LESS GOING TO DCE DOES NOT = PRINCIPAL PURPOSE. A 501(c) (4) nonprofit that plans to make direct campaign expen- ditures from 20% of its total expenditures and staff time to expressly advocate for the election or defeat of clearly identified candidates for state and local offices in Texas and make no contributions does not have a principal purpose of accepting political contributions or making political expenditures and is not required to register as a political committee. This opinion provides a safe har- bor at 20%. A political committee is defined as a group with ΓÇ£a principal purpose,ΓÇ¥ as opposed to the principal purpose, of accepting political contributions or making political expenditures. There are a number of factors to rely on when determining a principal purpose: 1. The proportion of the groupΓÇÖs total expenditures that constitute political expenditures; 2. The amount of the groupΓÇÖs staff or volunteer time, equipment, or other resources allocated to making political expenditures; 3. The content of the groupΓÇÖs public statements regard- ing its goals or support of or opposition to candidates, officeholders, or measures; 4. The groupΓÇÖs government filings and organizational documents, including mission statements; and 5. The groupΓÇÖs other activities that are unrelated to making political expenditures. EAO 518. See also EAO 168, EAO 131, EAO 331, EAO 440, EAO 77, EAO 74, EAO 320, EAO 242, EAO 332, EAO 177. See TEC rule 20.1(5), 20.1(14) and 20.1(20). TEC 	CANNOT 	ENFORCE 	┬º253.094 	OR ┬º253.002, 	ELECTION 	CODE 	TO 	PROHIBIT CORPORATIONS/LABOR 	ORGANIZATIONS FROM 	MAKING 	DIRECT 	CAMPAIGN EXPENDITURES. On January 21, 2010, the United States Supreme Court issued an opinion in the case of Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (hereaf- ter, Citizens United), in which it considered the consti- tutionality of certain federal statutes. The legislature intended title 15 to require a corporation, labor organi- zation, or other person that makes one or more direct campaign expenditures from its own property in con- nection with an election of a candidate to comply with section 253.062 as if it were an individual. Therefore, a corporation, labor organization, or other person that makes such expenditures must comply with the disclosure requirements that apply to an individual under section 253.062. EAO 489. See also EAO 331. Superseded by statute: H.B. 2359, 82 nd Leg. R.S. (2011) (amending Elec. Code ┬º┬º253.094, 253.036, 254.061; adding Elec. Code Subchapter J, 254.261, 254.262; repealing Elec. Code ┬º┬º253.002, 253.097, 254.036(f), and Subchapter C, ┬º┬º253.061, 253.062, 253.063) CANDIDATE 	OBLIGATION 	TO 	REPORT DIRECT CAMPAIGN EXPENDITURE. A candi- date is required to report a direct campaign expenditure (as opposed to a contribution) made to support him or her only if the candidate receives notice under sections 253.062(a)(1), 254.128(a), or 254.161 of the Election Code. Ed note: The group that made the direct campaign expenditure in question here had not filed an appoint- ment of campaign treasurer as a political committee and apparently was not required to file. Although the campaign treasurer of a political committee is required to give notice to a candidate of a direct expenditure the committee makes on a candidateΓÇÖs behalf, this require- ment is not applicable in this situation because there is no campaign treasurer subject to the requirement. The fact that no notice is required in the situation described may have been an unintended result of a 1993 change in the law that allowed a political committee to accept up to $500 in contributions or make up to $500 in expen- ditures before filing a campaign treasurer appointment. Previously, a political committee could not accept any political contributions or make any political expenditures without appointing a campaign treasurer. EAO 331. INDIVIDUAL 	THAT 	SPENDS 	FUNDS 	TO ENTERTAIN OTHERS TO SOLICIT CONTRI- BUTIONS FOR A CANDIDATE. If the expenditure is not a contribution, the money spent on the entertain- ment event is a direct campaign expenditure. If the host is an individual not acting in concert with another, and the direct campaign expenditure is more than $100, the individual must report the expenditure as if the person were a specific-purpose political committee. If the host is acting in concert with one or more other persons, the group of persons is a political committee and the direct expenditure is subject to the various requirements appli- cable to expenditures by political committees. EAO 116. See also EAO 13, EAO 50.

sections.title: TRAVEL EXPENSE
sections.content: A direct campaign expenditure consisting of personal travel expenses incurred by a person may be made without complying with Section 254.261.
