sections.title: REQUIRED DISCLOSURE ON POLITICAL ADVERTISING
sections.content: (a) 	A person may not knowingly cause to be published, distributed, or broadcast political advertising containing express advocacy that does not indicate in the advertising: (1) 	that it is political advertising; and (2) 	the full name of: (A) the person who paid for the political advertising; (B) the political committee authorizing the political advertising; or (C) the candidate or specific-purpose committee supporting the candidate, if the political advertis- ing is authorized by the candidate. (b) 	Political advertising that is authorized by a candidate, an agent of a candidate, or a political commit- tee filing reports under this title shall be deemed to contain express advocacy. (c) 	A person may not knowingly use, cause or permit to be used, or continue to use any published, dis- tributed, or broadcast political advertising containing express advocacy that the person knows does not include the disclosure required by Subsection (a). A person is presumed to know that the use of political advertising is prohibited by this subsection if the commission notifies the person in writing that the use is prohibited. A person who learns that political advertising signs, as defined by Section 259.001, that have been distributed do not include the disclosure required by Subsection (a) or include a disclosure that does not comply with Subsection (a) does not commit a continuing violation of this subsection if the person makes a good faith attempt to remove or correct those signs. A person who learns that printed political advertising other than a political advertising sign that has been distrib- uted does not include the disclosure required by Subsection (a) or includes a disclosure that does not comply with Subsection (a) is not required to attempt to recover the political advertising and does not commit a continuing violation of this subsection as to any previously distributed political advertising. (d) 	This section does not apply to: (1) 	tickets or invitations to political fund-raising events; (2) 	campaign buttons, pins, hats, or similar campaign materials; or (3) 	circulars or flyers that cost in the aggregate less than $500 to publish and distribute. (e) 	A person who violates this section is liable to the state for a civil penalty in an amount determined by the commission not to exceed $4,000. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 2003, 78th Leg., ch. 249, Sec. 2.23, eff. Sept. 1, 2003. Amended by Acts 2019, 86th Leg., R.S., Ch. 824 (H.B. 2554), Sec. 5, eff. September 1, 2019. cross -refereNce DefinitionsΓÇöΓÇ£Political AdvertisingΓÇ¥, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.1(13) Disclosure Statement, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 26.1 P ractice Notes Internet Posting The Texas Ethics Commission updated rule ┬º26.1 in 2018 and again in 2024 to clarify intent on posting and repost- ing content online. It now states that disclosure statements are not required on posted or reposted online content as long as the person doing it is not an officeholder, candidate, or PAC, they didnΓÇÖt pay more than $100 in a reporting period for it, and they didnΓÇÖt post/repost it in return for consideration ($$). The ΓÇ£considerationΓÇ¥ part was added in response to a sudden widespread tactic of paying social media influencers to post or repost political advertising that a consultant created in return for cash. Even if it is done by an officeholder, candidate, or PAC, the advertisement does not require a disclosure statement as long as it links to a page that does contain it, or to a page which is exempt from needing it. Pages that will not need a disclaimer now include any pages which clearly and conspicuously display the full name of the candidate or officeholder on it. Blocking Critics on Social Media Elected officials should take note of cases like Lindke v. Freed, 601 U.S. 187, 144 S. Ct. 756 (2024) in which the Supreme Court established a two-part test to determine if and when an elected official made use of a social media account for official purposes. The court stated: Like millions of Americans, James Freed maintained a Facebook account on which he posted about a wide range of topics, including his family and his job. Like most of those Americans, Freed occasionally received unwelcome comments on his posts. In response, Freed took a step familiar to Facebook users: He deleted the comments and blocked those who made them. For most people with a Facebook account, that would have been the end of it. But Kevin Lindke, one of the unwelcome [*191] commenters, sued Freed for violating his right to free speech. Because the First Amendment binds only the government, this claim is a nonstarter if Freed posted as a private citizen. Freed, however, is not only a private citizen but also the city manager of Port Huron, MichiganΓÇöand while Freed insists that his Facebook account was strictly personal, Lindke argues that Freed acted in his official capacity when he silenced LindkeΓÇÖs speech. When a government official posts about job-related topics on social media, it can be difficult to tell whether the speech is official or private. We hold that such speech is attributable to the State only if the official (1) possessed actual authority to speak on the StateΓÇÖs behalf, and (2) purported to exercise that authority when he spoke on social media. Elected officials will need to consider this opinion when operating and using social media pages in the future. attorNey G eNeral oPiNioNs UNENFORCEABLE AGAINST PRIVATE ANONYMOUS INDIVIDUAL ON ISSUES FLYERS. It is clear that section 255.001(a) of the Texas Election Code cannot constitutionally be enforced against a private individual who creates and/or distributes anonymous printed material from his own resources advocating a position on a particular issue, rather than the choice of a particular candidate, in an election. The statute may be constitutional in other contexts; and given that we do not possess a narrowing construction of the statute by the Texas Supreme Court or Court of Criminal Appeals, or an interpretation of the limits of McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission, 514 U.S. 334 (1995), by either the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit or ultimately the United States Supreme Court, we must presume such constitutionality in those respects. AttΓÇÖy Gen. Op. JC-243 (2000). Case law cited in JC-243: Osterberg v. Peca, 12 S.W.3d 31 (Tex. 2000) [narrow construction of def. of campaign expendituresΓÇöΓÇ£a ΓÇÿdirect campaign expenditureΓÇÖ by an individual in a candidate election includes only those expenditures that ΓÇÿexpressly advocateΓÇÖ the election or defeat of an identified candidateΓÇ¥]; McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission, 514 U.S. 334 (1995) [a similar Ohio statute prohibiting anonymous campaign literature violated the First Amendment]; State v. Doe, No. 5-99-01091-CR; State v. Antonelli, No. 5-99-01907-CR.

metadata.ethicsOpinions: RADIO POL AD DISCLOSURE STATEMENT. Based on section 26.1 of the Texas Ethics CommissionΓÇÖs rules, political advertising that is broadcast by radio is not required to include a disclosure statement. Such a result is an unintended consequence of the rule, and the commission will amend rule 26.1 to clarify the manner in which a disclosure statement, when required by section 255.001 of the Election Code, must appear in political advertising that is broadcast by radio. EAO 540. See also EAO 202 (1994). Superseded by ruleΓÇö1 T.A.C. ┬º 26.1(a) CAMPAIGN MATERIALS REFRIGERATOR MAGNET. The refrigerator mag- net at issue prominently displays an individual photo- graph of a public officer standing in front of a represen- tation of a city seal. Below the photograph, the name of the public officer appears in a print type size that is larger than any other text on the magnet. Additionally, the magnet includes the name of the public office held, the public officerΓÇÖs contact information, and the Internet website address for information about the public officer on the cityΓÇÖs website. When viewed as a whole, the mag- net constitutes ΓÇ£political advertisingΓÇ¥ as defined in sec- tion 251.001(16) of the Election Code and for purposes of section 255.003 of the Election Code. Consequently, public funds may not be used to pay for the magnet. EAO 506. See also EAO 102, EAO 211, EAO 476. DISCLAIMER ON SOCIAL MEDIA. The advertise- ment may comply with the disclosure requirement under section 255.001(a) of the Election Code if either: 1) the full disclosure statement appears on the face of the adver- tisement or, in the alternative, 2) a direct link to another Internet landing page that displays the full disclosure statement appears on the face of the advertisement and the direct link contains the words ΓÇ£political advertising,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£pol ad,ΓÇ¥ or another recognizable abbreviation. (In other words, the link must take the Internet user directly to the page that contains the full disclosure statement.) If the advertisement includes a direct link in order to comply with the disclosure requirement, the Internet landing page to which the direct link refers must be operational and freely accessible during the time the advertisement is visible on the social networking website. EAO 491. CAMPAIGN SHIRTS NOT REQUIRED TO HAVE DISCLAIMER. A shirt is similar to a campaign button or hat because it is intended to be worn. Therefore, a shirt that bears a candidateΓÇÖs political logo is not required to include a political advertising disclosure statement. EAO 457. BUSINESS 	CARDS 	NOT 	NOVELTY 	ITEMS. Business cards, in our opinion, do not belong in the cate- gory of ΓÇ£novelty itemsΓÇ¥ which do not require a disclosure statement. Therefore, political advertising in the form of a business card must include the information required by section 255.001(a). EAO 435. See also EAO 424, EAO 390, EAO 387, EAO 184. CANDY 	WRAPPERS 	WITH 	CAMPAIGN SLOGAN. Small candies wrapped in paper imprinted with a campaign slogan with a print area of approxi- mately one and an eighth square inches would be ΓÇ£politi- cal advertising,ΓÇ¥ as that term is defined in Election Code section 251.001(16). In this case, we conclude that the small candy wrappers are similar to buttons, pins, and hats and are therefore not required to bear a political advertising disclosure statement. EAO 424. See also EAO 387, EAO 184. CAMPAIGN 	BALLOONS, 	CAMPAIGN MATERIALS PAID FOR AND REPORTED IN PREVIOUS CAMPAIGN NOT REQUIRED TO BE REPORTED AGAIN. Words on the balloons urge vot- ers to re-elect the candidate. Campaign balloons are not required to contain the disclosure statement described in Election Code section 255.001. A candidate is not required to report his use in a current campaign of mate- rials paid for and reported in connection with a previous campaign. EAO 390. See also EAO 116, EAO 387, EAO 184. WOODEN 	NICKELS 	WITH 	CANDIDATEΓÇÖS LOGO. Section 255.001 of the Election Code does not require that wooden nickels printed with a candidateΓÇÖs political logo include a political advertising disclosure statement. EAO 387. See also EAO 184. ENVELOPE 	USED 	TO 	SEND 	POLITICAL ADVERTISING. In our view, an envelope is normally not a separate communication from the material con- tained in the envelope. Consequently, we conclude that the disclosure information required by Election Code section 255.001 is not required on an envelope that is used to transmit political advertising, even if the enve- lope itself bears a message supporting or opposing a candidate, officeholder, or ballot measure. The political advertising in the envelope must, of course, comply with the requirements of Election Code section 255.001. EAO 380. HOLIDAY 	CARDS 	PAID 	FOR 	BY CONTRIBUTIONS. 	An 	Ethics 	Commission 	rule excepts from the disclosure requirement ΓÇ£political adver- tising printed on letterhead stationery, if the letterhead contains the [name and address of the person who had the political advertising published].ΓÇ¥ 1 T.A.C. ┬º 26.5. Although that rule is not expressly applicable to holiday greeting cards, holiday greeting cards fit within the spirit of the ruleΓÇöthat the disclosure is not necessary since the source and the nature of the communication are clear. Therefore, holiday greeting cards sent by an officeholder and paid for with political contributions are not required to contain a political advertising disclosure as long as the name and address of the officeholder sending the cards appear on the card itself or on the envelope. EAO 289. See also EAO 190. BROCHURE LISTING DETAILS OF THE OFFICE OF JUSTICE OF THE PEACE. The Office of the Justice of the Peace produces and distributes the bro- chure on a regular basis, and the justice of the peace hands out the brochure when speaking at meetings. The text of the brochure merely describes the duties of the justice of the peace court. The name of the incumbent justice of the peace appears only on the letterhead, and this is not done in an unduly conspic- uous way or in a way that would lead one to believe that the purpose of the brochure was to support the incumbent. No facts are indicated that would lead the commission to believe that distribution of the brochure is campaign related. Therefore, we do not believe that the brochure provided for our inspection constitutes political advertising as that term is defined in section 251.001(16) of the Election Code. EAO 211. OFFICEHOLDER 	NON-FUNDRAISER 	OPEN HOUSE 	& 	OTHER 	INCIDENTAL 	SMALL CAMPAIGN MATERIALS. Lapel stickers, pens, mag- nets, and emery boards bearing political messages are not required to carry the political disclosure prescribed in Election Code section 255.001. The requestor explains that ΓÇ£the open house is in no way a fundraiser. It will merely acquaint constituents with the district office.ΓÇ¥ We conclude that the disclosure statement is not required on political advertising in the form of an invitation to an open house. EAO 184. PERIODICAL 	WITH 	COMMENTARY 	NOT PUBLISHED FOR CONSIDERATION. We assume the legislature intended to distinguish written communi- cations disseminated solely in connection with a particu- lar election from a publisherΓÇÖs own political commentary in a periodical the publisher produces whether or not an election is imminent. In our view, the regular newsletter under discussion qualifies as a periodical. Because the political communications in the newsletter were not pub- lished in return for consideration, they do not constitute ΓÇ£political advertising.ΓÇ¥ Therefore, the regular newsletter is not required to carry a political advertising disclosure. EAO 183. Modified by Acts 2003, 78th Leg., ch. 249, ┬º 2.23 (amending Elec. Code ┬º 255.001) CORPORATELY 	SPONSORED 	TELEVISION PROGRAM SUPPORTING STATE LEGISLATOR. ΓÇ£Political advertisingΓÇ¥ includes a paid television broad- cast supporting or opposing a candidate for nomination or election to a public office or supporting or opposing a public officer. If the television show in question fits that definition, the show must include the information required by section 255.001. Although we have not been provided with a script or other information that precisely demonstrates the nature of the proposed program, it is our opinion that such a program will usually be political advertising. EAO 144. See also EAO 143. MAGAZINE ADVERTISEMENT FROM PUBLIC OFFICIAL CONGRATULATING SPORTS TEAM. Whether 	a 	particular 	communication 	supports 	or opposes a candidate or a public officer is a fact question. We think, however, that an advertisement congratulat- ing a sports team that identifies a candidate or public officer as such would almost always be political advertis- ing and therefore would have to contain the information required by section 255.001. EAO 102. USE OF OFFICEHOLDER TITLE POLITICAL ADVERTISING FOR A CANDIDATE MUST USE THE WORD ΓÇ£FORΓÇ¥. A piece of political advertising that does not contain the word ΓÇ£forΓÇ¥ when the candidate supported by the political advertising does not hold the office sought, would be a violation of section 255.006(a). Likewise, a violation of section 255.006(c) would occur if the piece were used as a campaign com- munication. EAO 442. See also EAO 198, EAO 385, EAO 376. PAC MAY USE NAME IN POL. AD. PRIOR TO CAMPAIGN TREASURER APPOINTMENT. The Election Code does contain several provisions that reg- ulate the names of certain types of political committees, but nothing in the Election Code prevents a political committee from using its name before it files a campaign treasurer appointment. EAO 404. POLITICAL ADVERTISING THAT LEAVES OUT ΓÇ£FORΓÇ¥ IS MISLEADING. The material in question here is a campaign communication supporting an individual who is not an incumbent in the office sought and it does not include the word ΓÇ£for.ΓÇ¥ Therefore, the material does not comply with section 255.006(b). Use of the campaign material in question would not violate sec- tion 255.006(a), because the contract or agreement was entered into before the effective date of Election Code section 255.006(c). Section 255.006(b), however, makes it an offense to ΓÇ£representΓÇ¥ in a campaign communica- tion that a candidate holds an office the candidate does not hold. Consequently, the candidate may not use the leftover campaign materials in a new campaign unless the word ΓÇ£forΓÇ¥ is inserted before the name of the office sought. EAO 376. CURRENT OFFICEHOLDER MAY ADVERTISE USING 	CURRENT 	TITLE 	FOR 	DIFFERENT OFFICE. Although a candidate may not suggest in political advertising and campaign communications that the candidate holds an office he or she does not hold, a candidate who is an officeholder is free to accurately identify himself or herself as the holder of a particular office. The laws under the jurisdiction of the Texas Ethics Commission do not require that political adver- tising contain a disclaimer stating that the advertising was not paid for with public funds, but an officeholder may wish to include such a disclaimer to assure the pub- lic that public funds have not been used for campaign purposes. EAO 321. USE OF TERM ΓÇ£JUDGEΓÇ¥ IN ADVERTISING BY RETIRED JUDGE SITTING BY ASSIGNMENT. A retired judge who hears cases by assignments exercises the authority of a judge. In our opinion, therefore, the use of the title ΓÇ£JudgeΓÇ¥ by a retired judge who sits by assignment does not, by itself, represent that the former judge holds an office he does not hold. EAO 303. See also EAO 198, Attorney General Opinion H-526. Superseded, in part, by statute Acts 1997, 75 th Leg., ch. 1134, ┬º 9 (adding Elec. Code ┬º 255.006(c)) Superseded, in part, by statute Acts 1999, 76 th Leg., ch. 737, ┬º 1 (amending Elec. Code ┬º 255.006(c)) APPOINTED 	DISTRICT 	ATTORNEY 	MAY NOT REPRESENT SELF AS DA IN CAMPAIGN LITERATURE. A person appointed by a judge to perform the duties of a district attorney under Local Government Code section 87.017(a), and who is a candidate for that office, is not the district attorney, and does not ΓÇ£holdΓÇ¥ that office within the meaning of Election Code section 255.006. Accordingly, a candidate appointed to perform the duties of a district attorney under Local Government Code section 87.017(a) may not describe himself in campaign literature as the holder of the office. EAO 196. FORMER 	JUDGE 	MAY 	NOT 	REPRESENT SELF AS CURRENT JUDGE IN POLITICAL ADVERTISING. As a general rule, it would not be a violation of section 255.006 for a person who is currently a judge to use the title ΓÇ£ judgeΓÇ¥ in political advertising or campaign communications. It would be a violation of subsection (a) of section 255.006 for a former judge to enter into an agreement to print, publish, or broadcast political advertising suggesting that the person is cur- rently a judge. It would be a violation of subsection (b) for a former judge to represent in a campaign commu- nication that he or she currently holds a judicial office. EAO 171.

sections.title: RATES FOR POLITICAL ADVERTISING
sections.content: (a) 	The rate charged for political advertising by a radio or television station may not exceed: (1) 	during the 45 days preceding a general or runoff primary election and during the 60 days preced- ing a general or special election, the broadcasterΓÇÖs lowest unit charge for advertising of the same class, for the same time, and for the same period; or (2) 	at any time other than that specified by Subdivision (1), the amount charged other users for com- parable use of the station. (b) 	The rate charged for political advertising that is printed or published may not exceed the lowest charge made for comparable use of the space for any other purposes. (c) 	In determining amounts charged for comparable use, the amount and kind of space or time used, number of times used, frequency of use, type of advertising copy submitted, and any other relevant factors shall be considered. (d) 	Discounts offered by a newspaper or magazine to its commercial advertisers shall be offered on equal terms to purchasers of political advertising from the newspaper or magazine. (e) 	A person commits an offense if the person knowingly demands or receives or knowingly pays or offers to pay for political advertising more consideration than permitted by this section. (f) 	An offense under this section is a Class C misdemeanor. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. cross -refereNce Definitions ΓÇ£DiscountΓÇ¥, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.1(22) Discount, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 20.66 Restrictions on Certain Payments, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 22.23 Payments to a Corporation of the Candidate or Officeholder, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 24.15 attorNey G eNeral oPiNioNs TX POL AD RATES STATUTE ONLY PREEMPTED BY FECA IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS/TX STATUTE NOT APPLICABLE TO OUT OF STATE ADVERTISING. When the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971was enacted, it contained the following provision:Sec. 403(a) Nothing in this Act shall be deemed to invalidate or make inapplicable any provision of any State law, except where compliance with such provision of law would result in a violation of a provision of this Act. In 1974, this provision, codified as 2 U.S.C. section 453, was amended as follows: The provisions of this Act, and of rules prescribed under this Act, supersede and preempt any provision of State law with respect to election to Federal office. As a consequence, Congress has expressly limited the boundaries of preemption exclusively to elections for federal office, and accordingly, Article 14.09(B) [now 255.002, Election Code] would not apply to such elections. If a broadcaster in Texas accepts advertising from candidates for state or local offices in other states, or on issues to be voted upon in other states, he need not charge the rates prescribed by article 14.09(B) [255.002, Election Code] for that advertising. AttΓÇÖy Gen. Op. MW-488 (1982). See also, H-588 (1975); H-433 (1974). Case law cited in MW-488: KVUE-TV, Inc. v. Moore, C.A. No. A-81-CA-446 (W.D. Tex. March 18, 1982); United States v. Tonry, 605 F.2d 144 (1979) [regulation of state elections is wholly within the authority of the individual states]; Oregon v. Mitchell, 400 U.S. 112 (1970). NEWSPAPER MAY ACCEPT POL ADS FROM MORE THAN ONE CANDIDATE. Assuming that the adver- tising rates of the Tilden Tribune are reasonable and in proportion to its circulation, the paper is not prohibited from accepting political advertisements from more than one candidate for office. AttΓÇÖy Gen. Op. O-2054 (1940).

sections.title: UNLAWFUL USE OF PUBLIC FUNDS FOR POLITICAL ADVERTISING
sections.content: (a) 	An officer or employee of a political subdivision may not knowingly spend or authorize the spending of public funds for political advertising. (b) 	Subsection (a) does not apply to a communication that factually describes the purposes of a measure if the communication does not advocate passage or defeat of the measure. (b-1) An officer or employee of a political subdivision may not spend or authorize the spending of public funds for a communication describing a measure if the communication contains information that: (1) 	the officer or employee knows is false; and (2) 	is sufficiently substantial and important as to be reasonably likely to influence a voter to vote for or against the measure. (c) 	A person who violates Subsection (a) or (b-1) commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. (d) 	It is an affirmative defense to prosecution for an offense under this section or the imposition of a civil penalty for conduct under this section that an officer or employee of a political subdivision reasonably relied on a court order or an interpretation of this section in a written opinion issued by: (1) 	a court of record; (2) 	the attorney general; or (3) 	the commission. (e) 	On written request of the governing body of a political subdivision that has ordered an election on a measure, the commission shall prepare an advance written advisory opinion as to whether a particu- lar communication relating to the measure does or does not comply with this section. (f) 	Subsections (d) and (e) do not apply to a port authority or navigation district. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. Amended by Acts 2009, 81st Leg., R.S., Ch. 644 (H.B. 1720), Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2009; Acts 2009, 81st Leg., R.S., Ch. 843 (S.B. 2085), Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2009. cross -refereNce Newsletter of Public Officer of a Political Subdivision, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 26.2 P ractice Notes Via footnote 9 of EAO 550, note that this statute applies to officers of a political subdivision. ΓÇ£Political subdivisionΓÇ¥ includes a county, city, or school district or any other government entity that possesses authority for subordinate self-government through officers selected by it. Elec. Code ┬º 1.005(13)(C). By contrast, section 39.02 of the Penal Code applies to any public servant. While the TEC must respond to the issue/question at hand rather than hypotheticals, EAO 625 below does potentially open the door to misleading logos and other campaign paraphernalia with the advent of AI. And although not discussed in the opinion, there is also potentially a ΓÇ£true source of communicationΓÇ¥ (┬º255.004) concern in this opinion as to who the logo actually represents if it is so close to the official city logo that a rea- sonable person would be confused. As of now, the issue is not settled, but I would expect to see a similar opinion soon construing that statute as it relates to campaign materials created by AI that too closely resemble official government documents. attorNey G eNeral oPiNioNs LINKING TO CANDIDATE WEBSITE FROM PUBLIC FUNDS. Tex. Educ. Code Ann. ┬º 11.169 prohibits a board of trustees of a school district from using public funds to work for a particular measure or candidate; in addition, Tex. Elec. Code Ann. ┬º 255.003(a) makes it a criminal offense for an officer or employee of a school district to knowingly spend or authorize the spending of public funds for political advertising; a court would likely conclude that the use of public funds to link to an Internet website promoting a specific candidate or measure is itself a communication supporting or opposing a candidate or measure in violation of these sections. AttΓÇÖy Gen. Op. KP-0177 (2018). SCHOOL DISTRICT USE OF RESOURCES FOR PARTISAN COMMUNICATIONS. This statute prohibits the use of school district staff, facilities, or other resources where school districts electronically distributed links to Internet websites that were partisan in nature. KP-177 (2018).

metadata.caseLaw: Guaranty Petroleum Corp. v. Armstrong, 609 S.W.2d 529, 531 (Tex. 1980) The Texas Election Code defines ΓÇ£political subdivisionΓÇ¥ to mean a county, city, or school district or any other govern- mental entity that (1) embraces a geographic area with a defined boundary, (2) exists for the purpose of discharging functions of government, and (3) possesses authority for subordinate self-government through officers selected by it. Tex. Elec. Code ┬º 1.005(13) The Texas Supreme Court has further defined ΓÇ£political subdivisionsΓÇ¥ as having ΓÇ£the power to assess and collect taxes ΓÇª.ΓÇ¥ However, the Supreme Court of Texas has refused to construe the open-courts provision as guaranteeing the public a right to access court proceedings, and has permitted, for example, excluding the public to preserve the trade secrets of litigants. In re M-I L.L.C., 505 S.W.3d 569, 577-78 (2016) (ΓÇ£To the extent the open-courts provision might confer a right of public access, this right clearly would not be absolute, but instead would be subject to reasonable limitations imposed to protect countervailing interests, such as the preservation of trade secrets.ΓÇ¥). State law also permits judges to conduct certain proceedings privately, at their discretion. For example, the Texas Family Code allows judges to exclude the public from certain hearings involving juveniles, and presumes that hear- ings involving a child under the age of 14 would be closed to the public unless the judge ΓÇ£finds that the interest of the child or the interests of the public would be better served by opening the hearing to the public.ΓÇ¥ Tex. Fam. Code ┬º 54.08. In re Turner, 558 S.W. 3d 796, 800 (Tex. App.ΓÇöHouston [14th Dist.] 2018, no pet.) ΓÇ£...255.003(a) was not intended to ΓÇÿinhibit discussion of matters pending before a government body.ΓÇÖΓÇ¥
metadata.ethicsOpinions: PAC LOGO RESEMBLING POLICE DEPTΓÇÖS NOT A VIOLATION. A logo created by a PAC that closely resembles the local police departmentΓÇÖs logo is not a viola- tion of the statute assuming the requestor did not directly copy or repurpose the city-made logo or have access to it specifically because of his employment with the city as a police officer. EAO 625. See also, EAO 561 (2021), EAO 532 (2015), EAO 443 (2002), EAO 45 (1992). FACTUAL INFORMATION IS OKAY, BUT ANY AMOUNT OF ADVOCACY IS NOT. City published educational materials with factual descriptions of the ballot measure is not advocacy. ΓÇ£No matter how much factual information about the purposes of a measure election is included in a communication, any amount of advocacy is impermissible under Section 255.003(a).ΓÇ¥ EAO 594. See also EAO 211 (1994), EAO 476 (2007), EAO 564 (2021). COMMUNICATION 	ASKING 	ΓÇ£WHY 	DO 	WE NEED A VATRE?ΓÇ¥ IS POLITICAL ADVERTISING. A public communication about a voter-approved tax rate election put out by a superintendent of an ISD that contains that question ΓÇ£Why do we need a VATRE?ΓÇ¥ advocates for the passage of a measure and is political advertising. Thus, public funds cannot be used for it. EAO 593. See also EAO 476 (2003), EAO 559 (2021), EAO 565 (2021), EAO 582 (2022). EXPENDITURES TO ENCOURAGE DONATIONS TO 	CHARITY 	= 	REPORTABLE 	POLITICAL EXPENDITURES. A local mayor wanted to make an offer on his campaign facebook page to give lottery tick- ets (paid out of personal money, not public) to anyone that donates to a local food bank. The promotion of the event is permissible under 255.003, but since the mayor is using his campaign social media to promote it, it is considered ΓÇ£in connection withΓÇ¥ his campaign and is thus reportable as a political expenditure. EAO 584. See also EAO 550 (2019), EAO 102 (1992). FACTUAL 	ONE-PAGERS 	WITHOUT 	A ΓÇ£MOTIVATIONAL 	SLOGAN 	OR 	CALL 	TO ACTIONΓÇ¥ OKAY. As long as a communication by the school district does not contain express advocacy and is merely factual about the tax rate election, even in com- paring the tax rate to previous years, is not prohibited by 255.003. EAO 582. See also, EAO 565 (2021), EAO 559 (2021). SPECIAL 	PURPOSE 	DISTRICT 	NOT PROHIBITED FROM USING PUBLIC FUNDS FOR INFORMATIONAL COMMUNICATION. An officer of the district is not prohibited from using public funds to send educational materials to voters regarding an election to incorporate as a municipality if the infor- mation is factual in nature and does not contain political advertising. EAO 565. See also, EAO 559 (2021), EAO 476 (2007). HOME 	RULE 	CHARTER 	ELECTION COMMUNICATION. An officer of a subdivision is not prohibited from sending the specific communication described to the CommissionΓÇöa cover letter sent to all registered voters with a copy of the Home Rule Charter document that is to be voted on with factual information about the election. EAO 564. See also, EAO 476 (2007), EAO 211 (1994). USE 	OF 	PUBLIC 	FUNDS 	AND 	CAMPAIGN- RELATED ACTIVITY. This opinion addresses three distinct questions around the use of public funds. 1) using the name of a public officer in the name of an event like ΓÇ£MayorΓÇÖs Fun RunΓÇ¥ and using public funds to advertise and produce it, 2) announcing during a public meeting that an officer will have a booth at the event to distrib- ute merchandise purchased with public funds, and 3) using public funds to set up tents/tables/food at a food distribution event where other officials will be passing out campaign materials. The Commission found that 1) 255.003 of the Election Code does not broadly prohibit use of public funds for events that simply contain the title ΓÇ£MayorΓÇ¥ in it, but circumstances may make it political advertising if there were any other language included that supported the official in their campaign; 2) 255.003 does not broadly prohibit officers from discussing mat- ters during public meetings, but it does prohibit members of the body from arranging a conversation on the record about an item not before the body in the hopes that it is broadcast to voters and influences the outcome of the election; and 3) 255.003 does prohibit the use of public funds to facilitate the distribution of political advertise- ments, and the cityΓÇÖs production of an event deliberately designed to effectuate that distribution is prohibited. EAO 563. See also EAO 560 (2020), EAO 550 (2019), EAO 476 (2007), EAO 211 (1994), EAO 102 (1992). USE 	OF 	PUBLIC 	DOMAIN 	PHOTOS 	FOR JUDICIAL 	POLITICAL 	PURPOSES. 	Section 255.003(a) of the Texas Election Code does not apply to district judges because they are not officers or employees of political subdivisions. Section 39.02(a)(2) of the Penal Code prohibits judges from using their courtrooms to create political advertisements, but not from repurposing material that is created lawfully. EAO 562. See also EAO 550 (2021), EAO 395 (1998), EAO 372 (1997), EAO 134 (1993). SWAG PROMOTING A BIKE-SHARE PROGRAM IS POL. AD. WHEN STATING ΓÇ£PAID FOR BYΓÇ¥ A PUBLIC OFFICIAL ON IT. The requestor is an elected public official that wants to know whether or not he can use political subdivision funds to print graphic designs and put them on bicycle-sharing stations, hats, t-shirts, etcΓÇª in connection with the bicycle-sharing program funded by the political subdivision. Each design has the name of the program and the name of the requestorΓÇÖs office, as well as the following statement in smaller print: ΓÇ£Funding for this Station Provided by [requestor]ΓÇ¥ including his name and office. This is a political advertisement that benefits the requestor, and as such the political subdivision may not use public funds to support it. EAO 560. See also EAO 476 (2007), EAO 211 (1994), EAO 102 (1992). STATED DENIALS OF SUPPORT/OPPOSITION IN AN AD NOT ENOUGHΓÇöMUST LOOK AT WHOLE 	COMMUNICATION. 	When 	asked 	to consider whether a specific written communication constitutes political advertising for purposes of the Election Code, we view the communication as a whole. A significant factor in determining whether a particular communication is a political advertisement is whether it provides information without promoting a public officer or measure. The mere fact that a communication includes an express disclaimer of support or opposition is not determinative. [here, the ad stated in large bold text: ΓÇ£[t]his document is to be used for informational purposes and is not intended to advocate passage or failure of any issue on the bal- lot.ΓÇ¥] However, the specific communications considered in this opinion are not political advertisements for pur- poses of section 255.003 of the Election Code because they are entirely informational and do not include any advocacy. EAO 559. See also EAO 476 (2007), EAO 211 (1994), EAO 102 (1992). CITY-OWNED 	RENTAL 	SPACE 	USED 	FOR CANDIDATE 	DEBATES 	AND 	POLITICAL ADVERTISING. A city does not violate 255.003 by renting out city-owned space to a sponsor for a candidate debate/forum where candidates display political adver- tising to the public as long as it is at the standard rental rate charged to others and nonpublic funds are used to pay the rental fee. As long as a city employee does not specifically authorize any particular campaign/candi- date to post political advertising in the hallways leading to the rented room or in the parking lot entrance to the building (which are not rented), the TEC believes that the legislature did not intend 255.003 to require an employee of the city to prevent the display of political advertising and in that case, the employee does not ΓÇ£authorize the spending of public funds for political advertisingΓÇ¥. EAO 552. See also EAO 550, EAO 532, EAO 516, EAO 443, EAO 45. Note: Footnote 5 of this opinion states ΓÇ£We do not conclude that a city employee must always allow the display or distribution of political advertising, but only that the city employee does not authorize the spending of public funds in the circumstances before us.ΓÇ¥ PUBLIC 	OFFICER 	MAY 	NOT 	USE 	GOVT RESOURCES IN POL AD. A public officer, including a statewide officer, legislator, county officer, municipal officer, or school district officer, would be prohibited from using government resources, such as the officerΓÇÖs office in a government building, to create a photograph, video, or other communication for political advertising because the officer has custody or possession of the gov- ernment resources by virtue of holding the public office. EAO 550. See also, EAO 443, EAO 45. See also e.g. for previous decisions by TEC of violations of 255.003, In re Brooks (SC-3180260) (2018) (use of a county-owned vehicle dedicated to the officerΓÇÖs use), In re Wilson (SC- 31712183) (2018) (use of a county Facebook page main- tained by the officer), In re Joiner (SC-31605137) (2017) (use of newsletter headlined as from officerΓÇÖs desk), In re Hawkins (SC-31011409) (2012) (use of space in a city util- ity bill), In re Downs (SC-240588) (2004) (use of space in a city water bill), In re McRae (SC-240226) (2004) (use of city letterhead), In re Clark (SC-240225) (2004) (use of city letterhead), In re Bowman (SC-240218) (2004) (use of emergency services district letterhead), In re Lord (SC- 230963) (2004) (use of city-contracted video production), In re Williams, et. al. (SC-211170) (2001) (use of space in city water bill and airtime on city cable channel), In re Morgan (SC-210541) (2001) (use of internal mail system), and In re Williams (SC-991032) (1999) (use of special edition of sheriffΓÇÖs report). BROCHURE 	BY 	CITY 	RE: 	EMERGENCY SERVICES DISTRICT MEASURE. The brochure in question contains facts about the district and the city, such as the current property and sales tax rates, esti- mated sales tax revenue if the measure passes, certain budgetary figures for the district and the city, prospec- tive growth figures, land use information, and how the sales tax revenue is used. The brochure also explains certain effects if the measure passes, including that the city would be unable to collect a sales tax in future areas annexed by the city within district boundaries because those areas would already be assess the maximum local sales tax rate of two percent, which would be collected by the district. For purposes of section 255.003 of the Election Code, the attached brochure is not political advertising and, therefore, public funds may be used to distribute the brochure unless an officer or employee of the city authorizing such use of public funds knows that the brochure contains false information. EAO 538. See also EAO 476. CITY 	LETTERHEAD 	& 	LOGO 	ARE 	NOT USABLE FOR POLITICAL ADVERTISING. An officer or employee of the political subdivision may not use letterhead that is created by city staff or with city resources, and that contains the cityΓÇÖs logo and slogan that were designed with city funds, to write and distrib- ute political advertising. EAO 532. See also EAO 443, EAO 45. DISCUSSION 	OF 	MEASURE 	ONLY 	IS 	NOT POLITICAL ADVERTISING. Information and dis- cussion of a measure without promoting the outcome of the measure does not constitute political advertising, and thus public funds to distribute is permissible. EAO 531. See also EAO 476. INFORMATIONAL NEWSLETTER ON MEASU RE ELECTION BY CITY NOT PROHIBITED. A news- letter created and disseminated in print and online by a city that provides information and discussion of a measure without promoting the outcome of the measure and does not constitute political advertising as the term is defined in section 251.001(16) of the Election Code. Therefore, the use of public funds for the newsletter would not violate section 255.003(a) of the Election Code, but an officer or employee authorizing the use may not do so knowing that the communications contain information that is false. EAO 526. See also EAO 476. OFFICER OR EMPLOYEE OF CITY MAY NOT USE CITY TIME, EQUIPMENT OR FACILITIES FOR POLITICAL ADVERTISING. ΓÇ£SpendingΓÇ¥ of public funds includes the use of political subdivision employeesΓÇÖ work time, the use of existing political sub- division equipment, and the use of facilities maintained by a political subdivision. Thus, an officer or employee of a city may not use or authorize the use of the cityΓÇÖs employeesΓÇÖ work time, equipment, or facilities for polit- ical advertising. The prohibition in section 255.003 applies to any use of a political subdivisionΓÇÖs resources for political advertising, regardless of whether a political subdivision shows a preference for political advertising from a particular source. A city may not use its resources to create or maintain political advertising bearing the name of a political committee pursuant to the ΓÇ£adopt-a- parkΓÇ¥ program described in this opinion. EAO 516. See also EAO 443, EAO 102. CITY COUNCIL MEMBERΓÇÖS REFRIGERATOR MAGNET. The refrigerator magnet at issue prominently displays an individual photograph of a public officer standing in front of a representation of a city seal. Below the photograph, the name of the public officer appears in a print type size that is larger than any other text on the magnet. Additionally, the magnet includes the name of the public office held, the public officerΓÇÖs contact infor- mation, and the Internet website address for information about the public officer on the cityΓÇÖs website. The magnet also prominently features the phrase ΓÇ£DEDICATION to . . .ΓÇ¥ and a list of three items relating to activities of the public office. When viewed as a whole, the magnet constitutes ΓÇ£political advertisingΓÇ¥ as defined in section 251.001(16) of the Election Code and for purposes of sec- tion 255.003 of the Election Code. Consequently, public funds may not be used to pay for the magnet. EAO 506. See also EAO 102, EAO 211, EAO 476. CITY 	COMMUNICATION 	RE: 	MEASURE ELECTION STATING ONLY FACTS. A fact sheet provides information and discussion of a measure with- out promoting the outcome of the measure and there- fore does not constitute political advertising as the term is defined in section 251.001(16) of the Election Code. Therefore, for the use of public funds to distribute the fact sheet to be permissible under section 255.003(b-1), an officer or employee of the city authorizing the use may not do so knowing that the fact sheet contains informa- tion that is false. EAO 504. See also EAO 476. PROVIDING 	TRUTHFUL 	INFORMATION ABOUT 	A 	BALLOT 	MEASURE 	WITHOUT ADVOCATING. Whether a particular communication supports or opposes a measure is a fact question. A fac- tor in determining whether a particular communication supports or opposes a measure is whether the commu- nication provides information and discussion of the measure without promoting the outcome of the measure. In our opinion, the brochure provides information and discussion of a measure without promoting the outcome of the measure and therefore does not constitute political advertising as the term is defined in section 251.001(16) of the Election Code. Therefore, for the use of public funds to distribute the brochure to be permissible under section 255.003(b-1), the officer or employee of the county authorizing the use may not do so knowing that the brochure contains information that is false. EAO 501. See also EAO 476. ΓÇ£REIMBURSABLE 	WITH 	PUBLIC 	MONEYΓÇ¥ DOES 	NOT 	REQUIRE 	IMMEDIATE REIMBURSEMENT. 	For 	purposes 	of 	sections 251.001(4) and 251.001(9) of the Election Code, the phrase ΓÇ£reimbursable with public moneyΓÇ¥ means the governmental body has the authority to reimburse an officeholder for an expense and, at the time the expense is incurred, allows the reimbursement of the particular category of expense, such as continuing legal education. The phrase does not require the governmental body to actually reimburse the expense or to have funds avail- able for such reimbursement at the time the expense is incurred. EAO 495. See also EAO 476. CITY TASK FORCE REPORT THAT PROVIDES NO INFORMATION ABOUT ELECTION. A report issued by a city task force and the introductory article to the report that provide information about the task force, its objectives, and an analysis of ridership data produced by the FWTA do not provide information about the election nor do they support or oppose withdrawal from the FWTA and, therefore, do not constitute political advertising as the term is defined in section 251.001(16) of the Election Code. Therefore, for the use of public funds to publish the communications to be permissible, an officer or employee of the city may not authorize the use of public funds if the officer or employee knows the communications contain information that is false. EAO 494. See also EAO 476. PAMPHLET DISSEMINATING INFORMATION FOR CITIZENS. A pamphlet that relates to the City of CrowleyΓÇÖs Crime Control and Prevention District (here- after, CCPD) which is designed to disseminate informa- tion for citizens to understand how sales tax money is spent through CCPD is not ΓÇ£political advertisingΓÇ¥ and, therefore, public funds may be used to publish it unless an officer or employee of the city authorizing such use of public funds knows that the pamphlet contains false information. EAO 490. CITY FLYER DISCUSSING VOTER ISSUE WITH FACTUAL 	STATEMENTS 	NOT 	POLITICAL ADVERTISING. The requestor of the advisory opin- ion provides that the communication at issue relates to a special election the city is holding in which the voters will consider reauthorizing a Crime Control and Prevention District (hereafter, District). The requestor states that all of the statements of fact contained in the communication are true. For purposes of section 255.003 of the Election Code, the attached communication is not ΓÇ£political advertising,ΓÇ¥ and, therefore, may be included in a city newsletter that is paid for with public funds unless an officer or employee of the city authorizing such inclusion knows that the communication contains false informa- tion. EAO 488. CITY 	TASKFORCE 	REPORT 	ON 	POSSIBLE ACTION BY CITY. A city created task force that issues a report evaluating the various transportation options available to the city is not political advertising. This is so even if the report is submitted and published to the public prior to an election on transportation bonds, and therefore may be posted on a cityΓÇÖs Internet website unless an officer or employee of the city authorizing such posting knows that the report contains false information. EAO 487. PUBLIC OFFICER NEWSLETTER. A public offi- cerΓÇÖs newsletter that excessively uses pictures in which the public officer appears will almost always be political advertising. In our opinion, a public officerΓÇÖs newsletter that contains no more than two pictures of the public officer per page is not excessive use if the total amount of area covered by the pictures is no more than 20 percent of any page on which the pictures appear. Additionally, we caution on the use of personally phrased references, such as the use of the public officerΓÇÖs name, in particular when those references are set apart from other text. EAO 476. See also EAO 102, EAO 211. CITY PUBLIC MEETINGS & OPINIONS ON BALLOT MEASURES. A city may broadcast a tape of a public meeting if the broadcast is in keeping with the cityΓÇÖs regular practice of broadcasting meetings. In that situation, city resources would not be used ΓÇ£forΓÇ¥ political advertising even if an incidental effect of broadcasting the tape would be to broadcast statements supporting or opposing a ballot measure. EAO 456. See also EAO 45. ΓÇ£SPENDINGΓÇ¥ OF PUBLIC FUNDS INCLUDES USE OF PUBLIC FACILITIES. The prohibition in section 255.003 of the Election Code applies to any use of a political subdivisionΓÇÖs resources for political advertising including the use of facilities maintained by a political subdivision. This opinion does not apply to the use of the facilities of a political subdivision in a situation in which the facilities function as a public forum. EAO 443. See also EAO 45, EAO 343. POLITICAL SUBDIVISION MAY NOT EXCLUDE CANDIDATES FROM CANDIDATE FORUMS. Excluding candidates from a candidate forum makes the forum itself a communication in support of those included because the exclusion of certain candidates lends the sponsorΓÇÖs tacit support to those included as the candidates worthy of consideration by the audience. EAO 343. See also EAO 336. USE OF SCHOOL DISTRICT INTERNAL MAIL SYSTEM. An officer or employee of a school district is prohibited from spending public funds for political advertising. Expenditures for distribution of a circular or other written materials are within that prohibition. EAO 45.

sections.title: UNLAWFUL USE OF INTERNAL MAIL SYSTEM FOR POLITICAL
sections.content: ADVERTISING (a) 	An officer or employee of a state agency or political subdivision may not knowingly use or authorize the use of an internal mail system for the distribution of political advertising. (b) 	Subsection (a) does not apply to: (1) 	the use of an internal mail system to distribute political advertising that is delivered to the prem- ises of a state agency or political subdivision through the United States Postal Service; or (2) 	the use of an internal mail system by a state agency or municipality to distribute political advertis- ing that is the subject of or related to an investigation, hearing, or other official proceeding of the agency or municipality. (c) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. (d) 	In this section: (1) 	ΓÇ£Internal mail systemΓÇ¥ means a system operated by a state agency or political subdivision to deliver written documents to officers or employees of the agency or subdivision. (2) 	ΓÇ£State agencyΓÇ¥ means: (A) a department, commission, board, office, or other agency that is in the legislative, executive, or judicial branch of state government; (B) a university system or an institution of higher education as defined by Section 61.003, Education Code; or (C) a river authority created under the constitution or a statute of this state.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 2003, 78 th Leg., ch. 229, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 2003.

sections.title: TRUE SOURCE OF COMMUNICATION
sections.content: (a) 	A person commits an offense if, with intent to injure a candidate or influence the result of an election, the person enters into a contract or other agreement to print, publish, or broadcast political advertis- ing that purports to emanate from a source other than its true source. (b) 	A person commits an offense if, with intent to injure a candidate or influence the result of an election, the person knowingly represents in a campaign communication that the communication emanates from a source other than its true source. (c) 	An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. (d) 	A person commits an offense if the person, with intent to injure a candidate or influence the result of an election; (1) 	creates a deep fake video; and (2) 	causes the deep fake video to be published or distributed within 30 days of an election. (e) 	In this section, ΓÇ£deep fake videoΓÇ¥ means a video, created with the intent to deceive, that appears to depict a real person performing an action that did not occur in reality. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987. Amended by Acts 2019, 86th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1339 (S.B. 751), Sec. 1, eff. September 1, 2019.

metadata.caseLaw: Ex parte Stafford, No. PD-0310-23, (Crim. App. Sep. 4, 2024) Although the State has a compelling interest in fair and honest elections and preventing fraud on the electorate, the statute is not narrowly tailored to achieve that goal. While the governmentΓÇÖs interest to protect voters from confusion, fraud, and undue influence by preventing misleading communications is certainly compelling, we agree with the court of appeals that 255.004(b) encompasses communications that are not arguably false or misleading and it is not narrowly tailored to achieve the interests advanced by the State because there is no requirement of materiality. It criminalizes anonymous, un-signed, and factually accurate political communications. There is no exception for social media reposts. The statute also lends itself to prosecuting anonymous communications and even imitation, impersonation, sarcasm, parody, surrogacy, or pen names because it is subject to an individualΓÇÖs perception of the communication. We hold that ┬º 255.004(b) on its face, violates the First Amendment to the United States Constitution.

sections.title: MISREPRESENTATION OF IDENTITY
sections.content: (a) 	A person commits an offense if, with intent to injure a candidate or influence the result of an election, the person misrepresents the personΓÇÖs identity or, if acting or purporting to act as an agent, misrep- resents the identity of the agentΓÇÖs principal, in political advertising or a campaign communication. (b) 	An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 864, Sec. 249, eff. Sept. 1, 1997. P ractice Notes In 2024, the FEC released an ΓÇ£Interpretive RuleΓÇ¥ on existing regulations instead of new regulations on the use of AI in campaigns. This interpretation stated briefly that the commission did not have the statutory authority to issue broader rules and confirmed that existing federal rules on fraudulent misrepresentation prohibitions already apply to AI-generated content, as it is ΓÇ£technology neutral.ΓÇ¥ At the moment, it seems like the TEC is taking the same stance and applying ┬º255.004 and ┬º255.005 to potential misuses of AI in campaigns.

sections.title: MISLEADING USE OF OFFICE TITLE
sections.content: (a) 	A person commits an offense if the person knowingly enters into a contract or other agreement to print, publish, or broadcast political advertising with the intent to represent to an ordinary and pru- dent person that a candidate holds a public office that the candidate does not hold at the time the agreement is made. (b) 	A person commits an offense if the person knowingly represents in a campaign communication that a candidate holds a public office that the candidate does not hold at the time the representation is made. (c) 	For purposes of this section, a person represents that a candidate holds a public office that the candi- date does not hold if: (1) 	the candidate does not hold the office that the candidate seeks; and (2) 	the political advertising or campaign communication states the public office sought but does not include the word ΓÇ£forΓÇ¥ in a type size that is at least one-half the type size used for the name of the office to clarify that the candidate does not hold that office. (d) 	A person other than an officeholder commits an offense if the person knowingly uses a representation of the state seal in political advertising. (e) 	An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor. Amended by Acts 1987, 70 th Leg., ch. 899, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1987; Acts 1993, 73rd Leg., ch. 300, Sec. 30, eff. Aug. 30, 1993; Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 864, Sec. 250, eff. Sept. 1, 1997; Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 1134, Sec. 9, eff. Sept. 1, 1997; Acts 1999, 76th Leg., ch. 62, Sec. 5.17, eff. Sept. 1, 1999; Acts 1999, 76th Leg., ch. 737, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1999. cross -refereNce Disclosure Statement, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 26.1 Use of the Term ΓÇ£Re-ElectΓÇ¥ in Political Advertising, 1 Tex. Admin. Code, ┬º 26.7

metadata.ethicsOpinions: WEARING JUDICIAL ROBES, USING JUDICIAL TITLE CURRENTLY HELD. The law generally does not prohibit a judge from using the title ΓÇ£ judgeΓÇ¥ in political advertising or campaign communications for another judicial office as long as the communications do not suggest that the judge holds a public office the person does not hold. Section 255.006 of the Election Code does not prohibit an associate judge from wearing judicial robes or referring to the judge in political advertising as ΓÇ£Associate Judge, 1000 th District Court, Texas County.ΓÇ¥ EAO 548. See also EAO 171. OFFICEHOLDER 	WHOSE 	DISTRICT 	WAS RENUMBERED USING ΓÇ£RE-ELECTΓÇ¥. In certain circumstances, the term ΓÇ£re-electΓÇ¥ may represent that a non-incumbent candidate holds a public office and would therefore be prohibited by section 255.006 of the Election Code. However, for purposes of that prohibi- tion, the crucial issue is whether the candidate ΓÇ£holdsΓÇ¥ the particular office, which is not necessarily determined by whether the candidate acquired the office by election. EAO 512. See also Atty General Opinion 93-45, Atty General Opinion JC-483. POLITICAL ADVERTISING FOR A CANDIDATE MUST USE THE WORD ΓÇ£FORΓÇ¥. A person who does not hold the office he or she is seeking must use the word ΓÇ£forΓÇ¥ in certain campaign materials to clarify that the candidate does not hold the office sought. Because the piece of political advertising at issue does not contain the word ΓÇ£forΓÇ¥ and because the candidate supported by the political advertising does not hold the office sought, a violation of section 255.006(a) would occur if a person knowingly entered into a contract or other agreement to print or publish the political advertising. Likewise, a violation of section 255.006(c) would occur if the piece were used as a campaign communication. EAO 442. See also EAO 198, EAO 385, EAO 376. POLITICAL ADVERTISING THAT LEAVES OUT ΓÇ£FORΓÇ¥ 	IS 	MISLEADING 	AND 	REPRESENTS THAT THE CANDIDATE IS AN INCUMBENT. The material in question here is a campaign communi- cation supporting an individual who is not an incumbent in the office sought and it does not include the word ΓÇ£for.ΓÇ¥ Therefore, the material does not comply with sec- tion 255.006(b). Use of the campaign material in ques- tion would not violate section 255.006(a), because the contract or agreement was entered into before the effec- tive date of Election Code section 255.006(c). Section 255.006(b), however, makes it an offense to ΓÇ£represent ΓÇ£ in a campaign communication that a candidate holds an office the candidate does not hold. EAO 376. CURRENT OFFICEHOLDER MAY ADVERTISE USING 	CURRENT 	TITLE 	FOR 	DIFFERENT OFFICE, NOT MISLEADING. Although a candidate may not suggest in political advertising and campaign communications that the candidate holds an office he or she does not hold, a candidate who is an officeholder is free to accurately identify himself or herself as the holder of a particular office. The laws under the jurisdiction of the Texas Ethics Commission do not require that political advertising contain a disclaimer stating that the advertising was not paid for with public funds, but an officeholder may wish to include such a disclaimer to assure the public that public funds have not been used for campaign purposes. EAO 321. USE OF TERM ΓÇ£JUDGEΓÇ¥ IN ADVERTISING BY RETIRED JUDGE. A retired judge who hears cases by assignments exercises the authority of a judge. In our opinion, therefore, the use of the title ΓÇ£JudgeΓÇ¥ by a retired judge who sits by assignment does not, by itself, represent that the former judge holds an office he does not hold. EAO 303. See also EAO 198, Attorney General Opinion H-526. Superseded, in part, by statute Acts 1997, 75 th Leg., ch. 1134, ┬º 9 (adding Elec. Code ┬º 255.006(c)) Superseded, in part, by statute Acts 1999, 76 th Leg., ch. 737, ┬º 1 (amending Elec. Code ┬º 255.006(c)) APPOINTED 	DISTRICT 	ATTORNEY 	MAY NOT REPRESENT SELF AS DA IN CAMPAIGN LITERATURE. While the person appointed by the judge under section 87.017(a) has the right and duty to perform the duties of the district attorney during the pendency of the removal trial, he is not the district attor- ney, and does not ΓÇ£holdΓÇ¥ that office within the meaning of Election Code section 255.006. Accordingly, a candi- date appointed to perform the duties of a district attorney under Local Government Code section 87.017(a) may not describe himself in campaign literature as the holder of the office. EAO 196. FORMER 	JUDGE 	MAY 	NOT 	REPRESENT SELF AS CURRENT JUDGE IN POLITICAL ADVERTISING. As a general rule, it would not be a violation of section 255.006 for a person who is currently a judge to use the title ΓÇ£ judgeΓÇ¥ in political advertising or campaign communications. It would be a violation of subsection (a) of section 255.006 for a former judge to enter into an agreement to print, publish, or broadcast political advertising suggesting that the person is cur- rently a judge. It would be a violation of subsection (b) for a former judge to represent in a campaign commu- nication that he or she currently holds a judicial office. EAO 171. BUMPER STICKER & CANDIDATE OFFICE. A bumper sticker that contains the candidateΓÇÖs name in large type and in smaller type, the words ΓÇ£A Needed Change for the BETTERΓÇ¥ without stating the office the candidate is seeking may not violate the Election Code. Even if the word ΓÇ£forΓÇ¥ does not precede the office the bumper sticker at issue does not, as a whole, repre- sent that the candidate holds the office he is seeking. Therefore, we conclude that this particular bumper sticker does not violate section 255.006 of the Election Code. Nonetheless, we caution that a candidate who is not an incumbent in the office sought should avoid uncertainty about the application of section 255.006 by using words such as ΓÇ£forΓÇ¥ before the name of the office sought, or ΓÇ£electΓÇ¥ before the candidateΓÇÖs name. EAO 210. Modified by Acts 1997, 75th Leg., R.S., ch. 1134, ┬º 9 (amend- ing Elec. Code ┬º 255.006; Acts 1999, 76 th Leg., ch. 737, ┬º 1 (amending Elec. Code ┬º 255.006)

sections.title: DISCLOSURE ON POLITICAL ADVERTISING FOR JUDICIAL OFFICE
sections.content: (a) 	This section applies only to a candidate or political committee covered by Subchapter F, Chapter 253. (b) 	Political advertising by a candidate who files a declaration of intent to comply with the limits on expenditures under Subchapter F, Chapter 253, or a specific-purpose committee for supporting such a candidate may include the following statement: ΓÇ£Political advertising paid for by (name of candidate or committee) in compliance with the voluntary limits of the Judicial Campaign Fairness Act.ΓÇ¥ (c) 	Political advertising by a candidate who files a declaration of intent to comply with the limits on expenditures under Subchapter F, Chapter 253, or a specific-purpose committee for supporting such a candidate that does not contain the statement prescribed by Subsection (b) must comply with Section 255.001. (d) 	Political advertising by a candidate who files a declaration of intent to exceed the limits on expen- ditures under Subchapter F, Chapter 253, or a specific-purpose committee for supporting such a candidate must include the following statement: ΓÇ£Political advertising paid for by (name of candidate or committee), (who or which) has rejected the voluntary limits of the Judicial Campaign Fairness Act.ΓÇ¥ (e) 	The commission shall adopt rules providing for: (1) 	the minimum size of the disclosure required by this section in political advertising that appears on television or in writing; and (2) 	the minimum duration of the disclosure required by this section in political advertising that appears on television or radio. (f) 	A person who violates this section or a rule adopted under this section is liable for a civil penalty not to exceed: (1) 	$15,000, for a candidate for a statewide judicial office or a specific-purpose committee for support- ing such a candidate; (2) 	$10,000, for a candidate for chief justice or justice, court of appeals, or a specific-purpose commit- tee for supporting such a candidate; or (3) 	$5,000, for a candidate for any other judicial office covered by Subchapter F, Chapter 253, or a specific-purpose committee for supporting such a candidate. (g) 	Section 253.176 applies to the imposition and disposition of a civil penalty under this section.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1995, 74 th Leg., ch. 763, Sec. 6, eff. Sept. 1, 1995.

sections.title: PRINCIPAL POLITICAL COMMITTEE OF POLITICAL PARTY
sections.content: The state or county executive committee of a political party may designate a general-purpose committee as the principal political committee for that party in the state or county, as applicable.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.19, eff. Jan. 1, 1992.

sections.title: REQUIREMENTS RELATING TO CORPORATE OR LABOR UNION
sections.content: CONTRIBUTIONS (a) 	A political party that accepts a contribution authorized by Section 253.104 may use the contribution only to: (1) 	defray normal overhead and administrative or operating costs incurred by the party; or (2) 	administer a primary election or convention held by the party. (b) 	A political party that accepts contributions authorized by Section 253.104 shall maintain the contri- butions in a separate account.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.19, eff. Jan. 1, 1992.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: POLITICAL PARTY COPORATE CONTRI BU- TIONS FOR ADMIN EXPENSES. The requestor represents a political party. The requestor would like to use funds from corporations or labor organizations to pay a contractorΓÇÖs invoice. Specifically, the requestor stated that the contractor would be ΓÇ£developing admin- istrative tools (spreadsheets, budgets, etc.) and a hiring plan related to [the] partyΓÇÖs coordinated campaign.ΓÇ¥ The spreadsheets would be used to track budget and cash flow. The political party may use funds from corpora- tions or labor organizations to pay a contractorΓÇÖs invoice because the contractor provided normal administrative services. EAO 611. See also, EAO 604 (2024), EAO 272 (DATE), EAO 176 (1993). POLITICAL PARTY MAY USE CONTRIBUTIONS FROM 	CORPORATIONS 	FOR 	NORMAL OVERHEAD COSTS. In this case, a county political party wanted to accept contributions from a corporation to purchase a storage trailer that would be used to store campaign and other political party items. This is an acceptable overhead/admin cost for a political party. EAO 604. See also, EAO 272 (1995), EAO 176 (1993). CORPORATE 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	FOR 	PUR- CHASE 	OF 	POLITICAL 	PARTY 	HEAD- QUARTERS. Costs associated with obtaining and maintaining a headquarters are clearly administrative operating costs. The political party therefore may accept corporate contributions for the purpose described. GPACΓÇÖs administered by corporations may also contrib- ute to the political partyΓÇÖs efforts to raise money for a headquarters since they do not operate under the same restrictions on political activity as do corporations, and so are free to contribute to a political party for this or any other lawful purpose. EAO 176. Affirmed by H.B. 2525, 81st Leg., R.S. (2009) (amending Elec. Code ┬º253.100(a), (c); adding Elec. Code ┬º253.100(d), (e))

sections.title: REPORT REQUIRED
sections.content: (a) 	A political party that accepts contributions authorized by Section 253.104 shall report all contribu- tions and expenditures made to and from the account required by Section 257.002. (b) 	The report must be filed with the commission and must include the information required under Section 254.031 as if the contributions or expenditures were political contributions or political expenditures. (c) 	Sections 254.001 and 254.032-254.037 apply to a report required by this section as if the party chair were a campaign treasurer of a political committee and as if the contributions or expenditures were political contributions or political expenditures. (d) 	The commission shall prescribe by rule reporting schedules for each primary election held by the political party and for the general election for state and county officers.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.19, eff. Jan. 1, 1992. Amended by Acts 1997, 75th Leg., ch. 864, Sec. 251, eff. Sept. 1, 1997.
metadata.ethicsOpinions: PRECINCT CHAIR OF A PARTY WISHING TO SOLICIT CONTRIBUTIONS. A precinct chair of a political party wishing to solicit political contributions to be used on campaign activities for his partyΓÇÖs candi- dates must file an appointment of campaign treasurer of a general-purpose committee before exceeding $500 in political contributions or political expenditures, because the precinct chair would necessarily be working in con- cert with contributors to accept political contributions and make political expenditures. The treasurer of the committee would be required to follow the recordkeep- ing and reporting requirements of chapter 254 of the Election Code. EAO 320.

sections.title: RESTRICTIONS ON CONTRIBUTIONS BEFORE GENERAL
sections.content: ELECTION (a) 	Beginning on the 60 th day before the date of the general election for state and county officers and continuing through the day of the election, a political party may not knowingly accept a contribution authorized by Section 253.104 or make an expenditure from the account required by Section 257.002. (b) 	A person who violates this section commits an offense. An offense under this section is a felony of the third degree.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.19, eff. Jan. 1, 1992.

sections.title: CANDIDATE FOR STATE OR COUNTY CHAIR OF POLITICAL PARTY
sections.content: (a) 	Except as provided by this section, the following are subject to the requirements of this title that apply to a candidate for public office: (1) 	a candidate for state chair of a political party with a nominee on the ballot in the most recent gubernatorial general election; and (2) 	a candidate for election to the office of county chair of a political party with a nominee on the ballot in the most recent gubernatorial general election if the county has a population of 350,000 or more. (b) 	A political committee that supports or opposes a candidate covered by Subsection (a) is subject to the provisions of this title that apply to any other committee that supports or opposes candidates for public office, except as provided by this section. (c) 	The reporting schedules for a candidate covered by Subsection (a) or a political committee supporting or opposing the candidate shall be prescribed by commission rule. (d) 	Except as provided by this section, each contribution to and expenditure by a candidate covered by Subsection (a) is subject to the same requirements of this title as a political contribution to or a political expenditure by a candidate for public office. Each contribution to and expenditure by a political com- mittee supporting or opposing a candidate covered by Subsection (a) is subject to the same require- ments of this title as a political contribution to or political expenditure by any other specific-purpose committee. (e) 	Section 251.001(1) does not apply to this section.

metadata.ethicsOpinions: PARTY PRECINCT CHAIR NOT REQΓÇÖD TO FILE CTA OR CAMPAIGN FINANCE REPORTS. Title 15 of the Texas Election Code requires candidates for public office and certain candidates for state and county party offices to designate campaign treasurers and file campaign finance reports. It does not require candidates for precinct offices of political parties to designate cam- paign treasurers or file campaign finance reports. EAO 576 (2022). CORPORATE 	CONTRIBUTIONS 	TO CANDIDATE 	FOR 	COUNTY 	CHAIR 	OF POLITICAL PARTY. Title 15 of the Election Code does not prohibit a corporation from making contribu- tions to a candidate for county chair of a political party. EAO 301. See also EAO 198. Superseded, in part, by statute Acts 2003, 78 th Leg., ch. 249, ┬º2.24, 2.25 (amending Elec. Code ┬º257.005)

sections.title: CRIMINAL PENALTY FOR FAILURE TO COMPLY
sections.content: (a) 	Except as provided by Section 257.004, a person who knowingly uses a contribution in violation of Section 257.002 or who knowingly fails to otherwise comply with this chapter commits an offense. (b) 	An offense under this section is a Class A misdemeanor.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.19, eff. Jan. 1, 1992.

sections.title: RULES
sections.content: The commission shall adopt rules to implement this chapter.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1991, 72 nd Leg., ch. 304, Sec. 5.19, eff. Jan. 1, 1992.

sections.title: SHORT TITLE
sections.content: This chapter may be cited as the Fair Campaign Practices Act.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1997, 75 th Leg., ch. 168, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1997.

sections.title: PURPOSE
sections.content: (a) 	The purpose of this chapter is to encourage every candidate and political committee to subscribe to the Code of Fair Campaign Practices. (b) 	It is the intent of the legislature that every candidate and political committee that subscribes to the Code of Fair Campaign Practices will follow the basic principles of decency, honesty, and fair play to encourage healthy competition and open discussion of issues and candidate qualifications and to discourage practices that cloud the issues or unfairly attack opponents.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1997, 75 th Leg., ch. 168, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1997.

sections.title: DELIVERY OF COPY OF CODE
sections.content: (a) 	When a candidate or political committee files its campaign treasurer appointment, the authority with whom the appointment is filed shall give the candidate or political committee a blank form of the Code of Fair Campaign Practices and a copy of this chapter. (b) 	The authority shall inform each candidate or political committee that the candidate or committee may subscribe to and file the code with the authority and that subscription to the code is voluntary.

metadata.addedBy: Added by Acts 1997, 75 th Leg., ch. 168, Sec. 1, eff. Sept. 1, 1997.

sections.title: TEXT OF CODE
sections.content: The Code of Fair Campaign Practices reads as follows: code of fair camPaiGN Practices There are basic principles of decency, honesty, and fair play that every candidate and political committee in this state has a moral obligation to observe and uphold, in order that, after vigorously contested but fairly conducted campaigns, our citizens may exercise their constitutional rights to a free and untrammeled choice and the will of the people may be fully and clearly expressed on the issues. THEREFORE: (1) 	I will conduct the campaign openly and publicly and limit attacks on my opponent to legitimate challenges to my opponentΓÇÖs record and stated positions on issues. (2) 	I will not use or permit the use of character defamation, whispering campaigns, libel, slander, or scurrilous attacks on any candidate or the candidateΓÇÖs personal or family life. (3) 	I will not use or permit any appeal to negative prejudice based on race, sex, religion, or national origin. (4) 	I will not use campaign material of any sort that misrepresents, distorts, or otherwise falsifies the facts, nor will I use malicious or unfounded accusations that aim at creating or exploiting doubts, without justification, as to the personal integrity or patriotism of my opponent. (5) 	I will not undertake or condone any dishonest or unethical practice that tends to corrupt or under- mine our system of free elections or that hampers or prevents the full and free expression of the will of the voters, including any activity aimed at intimidating voters or discouraging them from voting. (6) 	I will defend and uphold the right of every qualified voter to full and equal participation in the elec- toral process, and will not engage in any activity aimed at intimidating voters or discouraging them from voting. (7) 	I will immediately and publicly repudiate methods and tactics that may come from others that I have pledged not to use or condone. I shall take firm action against any subordinate who violates any provision of this code or the laws governing elections. I, the undersigned, candidate for election to public office in the State of Texas or campaign treasurer of a political committee, hereby voluntarily endorse, subscribe to, and solemnly pledge myself to conduct the campaign in accordance with the above principles and practices. __________________ 	__________________ Date 	Signature

sections.title: NOTICE REQUIREMENT ON POLITICAL ADVERTISING SIGNS
sections.content: (a) 	The following notice must be written on each political advertising sign: ΓÇ£NOTICE: IT IS A VIOLATION OF STATE LAW (CHAPTERS 392 AND 393, TRANSPORTATION CODE), TO PLACE THIS SIGN IN THE RIGHT-OF-WAY OF A HIGHWAY.ΓÇ¥ (b) 	A person commits an offense if the person: (1) 	knowingly enters into a contract to print or make a political advertising sign that does not contain the notice required by Subsection (a); or (2) 	instructs another person to place a political advertising sign that does not contain the notice required by Subsection (a). (c) 	An offense under this section is a Class C misdemeanor. (d) 	It is an exception to the application of Subsection (b) that the political advertising sign was printed or made before September 1, 1997, and complied with Subsection (a) as it existed immediately before that date. (e) 	In this section, ΓÇ£political advertising signΓÇ¥ means a written form or political advertising designed to be seen from a road but does not include a bumper sticker.
